lights.t: The Muslim year counts from a departure, not a birth
lights.s: Around 638 CE the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab and his advisers had to decide where the Muslim calendar should begin. They did not choose the birth of the Prophet ﷺ, or the first revelation, or a victory. They chose the Hijra, the migration from Makkah to Yathrib, because that was when a scattered community became a society with obligations to one another. By the standard reckoning the first day of Muharram in year 1 falls on 16 July 622 in the Julian calendar. Every Islamic date since is counted from a group of refugees arriving in a town that agreed to take them in.
lights.d: Set under Umar ibn al-Khattab · c. 638 CE

lights.t: Medina's founding document named Jews as part of one community
lights.s: Soon after arriving in Yathrib in 622, the Prophet ﷺ set out the terms on which a mixed town would live. The text, preserved by the early biographer Ibn Ishaq and usually called the Sahifa or Constitution of Medina, lists the tribes by name, including the Jewish clans, and states that they form one community alongside the believers. It guarantees them their religion, fixes who pays blood money for whom, requires joint defence of the town, and says disputes go to arbitration rather than feud. Historians treat it as one of the earliest written constitutional documents anywhere, and it was written for a place with more than one faith in it.

lights.t: The first Muslim refugees were sheltered by a Christian king
lights.s: Around 615 CE, with the Makkan boycott closing in, the Prophet ﷺ told a small group of his followers to cross the Red Sea to Abyssinia, telling them there was a king there under whom no one was wronged. A first party of about a dozen went, and more followed. Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to demand their return. The Aksumite ruler, called the Negus in Arabic sources, heard both sides, listened to a passage of the Qur'an about Jesus and Mary read aloud in his court, and refused to hand them over. The first migration in Islamic history was not to a Muslim country. It was asylum granted by someone of another faith.

lights.t: Badr is the only battle the Qur'an names outright
lights.s: On 17 Ramadan in year 2 of the Hijra, which converts to 13 March 624, a small Muslim force met a far larger Makkan army at the wells of Badr, southwest of Madinah. The traditional count puts the Muslims at 313 men against roughly a thousand. The Qur'an refers to the day directly in Surah Al Imran, naming the place and reminding the community that it was given victory at Badr while it was weak. Prisoners taken that day were treated in a way that surprised their own side, and some literate captives were released in exchange for teaching Muslim children to write. It remains the single engagement the Qur'an mentions by name.
lights.d: Wells of Badr · 17 Ramadan 2 AH, 13 March 624

lights.t: Umar prayed outside the church so it would stay a church
lights.s: In 637 CE, some sources say 638, Jerusalem's Patriarch Sophronius handed the city over to the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab, who came in plain clothes and on foot for part of the way. The written terms, known as the Umariyya covenant, guaranteed the safety of the inhabitants, their churches and their crosses, and stated that no church would be seized or destroyed. Later chroniclers report that when the hour of prayer came while Umar was inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, he stepped outside to pray, saying that if he prayed there Muslims after him would claim the spot. A small mosque stands opposite the church door to this day.

lights.t: The oldest dated Qur'anic text is written on a wall
lights.s: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem was completed under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik, and the mosaic inscription running around its inner octagon gives the year 72 of the Hijra, which is 691 to 692 CE. That band of gold on blue, some 240 metres of it, carries Qur'anic verses and is the oldest securely dated Qur'anic text that survives anywhere in the world. It is older than any surviving complete manuscript. The building itself is not a mosque but a shrine over the rock, and its octagonal plan and dome were built by craftsmen working in a late Roman and Byzantine tradition, for a new patron and a new text.

lights.t: Gibraltar is a rock named after a Berber commander
lights.s: In 711 a force led by Tariq ibn Ziyad, a Berber commander in Umayyad service, crossed the strait from North Africa and landed at the great rock at its northern end. The Arabic name for the place became Jabal Tariq, the mountain of Tariq, and that is what Spanish and then English wore down into Gibraltar. Within a few years most of the Iberian peninsula was under Muslim rule, and it would remain so in part for nearly eight hundred years. Millions of people say the name of a seventh century North African officer every time they mention the strait, the rock, or the airport built on the isthmus below it.

lights.t: Baghdad was built as a perfect circle and nothing remains
lights.s: In 762 the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur laid out a new capital on the Tigris and called it Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. It was circular, a double ring of walls with four equidistant gates, the mosque and the palace at the exact centre, and the chroniclers describe tens of thousands of workers brought in to build it. Within a century it was among the largest cities on earth and the place where Greek, Persian, Syriac and Sanskrit books were translated into Arabic. Not one stone of the Round City has been located with certainty today. The plan survives only in the descriptions of the geographers who walked through its gates.

lights.t: The numbers we use came to Baghdad from India in 773
lights.s: In 773 an embassy from Sind reached the court of the caliph al-Mansur carrying an Indian astronomical work, a Siddhanta, most likely Brahmagupta's. It was translated into Arabic as the Zij al-Sindhind, and with it came the decimal place value system and the zero, which Indian mathematicians had developed. Arabic writers were clear about the debt and called the figures al-arqam al-hindiyya, the Indian numerals. When the system reached Europe through Arabic books, Europeans called them Arabic numerals, after the language they had read them in. The digits on every phone screen carry two civilisations in their name, and the older claim belongs to India.

lights.t: A paper mill in Baghdad changed what a book cost
lights.s: Papermaking was invented in China. It reached Central Asia through Samarkand, and around 794, during the reign of Harun al-Rashid, a paper mill was set up in Baghdad, credited to his vizier al-Fadl ibn Yahya. Paper was cheaper than parchment and harder to erase than papyrus, which made it good for both scholarship and government records. Within a generation the state chancery had moved to paper, booksellers filled a street of their own, and the copying of books became an ordinary trade rather than a luxury craft. The translation movement and the libraries that followed rested on a Chinese invention passed westward, and on a mill by a river.

lights.t: Two teams walked in opposite directions to measure the earth
lights.s: Around 830 the caliph al-Ma'mun sent surveyors to the flat plain of Sinjar, north of the Tigris, with a task: find the length of one degree of latitude. Two parties started from the same point, one walking north and one south, measuring the ground as they went, until each found the pole star had shifted by one degree. Their answer was about 56 and two thirds Arabic miles per degree. Converted into a circumference for the whole earth it comes close to the modern figure, though how close depends on which mile they were using, and that is still argued. What is not in doubt is the method: not a calculation from books, but people counting paces across a plain.

lights.t: A caliph's wife paid for the water on the Makkah road
lights.s: Zubayda bint Ja'far, wife of Harun al-Rashid, made the hajj and saw pilgrims dying of thirst on the route from Kufa to Makkah. She spent her own fortune on the problem: wells, cisterns, paved stretches, milestones and waystations along some 1,500 kilometres of desert road, and a spring channel at Makkah itself that carried water into the city. The road has been called Darb Zubayda, Zubayda's Road, ever since, and the archaeological remains of its pools and wells are still mapped across Iraq and Saudi Arabia. She died in 831. Her name survived not through a battle or a dynasty but through drinking water.

lights.t: A marble column in Cairo set the year's tax rate
lights.s: On Rawda Island in the Nile stands a stone pit with a marble column at its centre, marked off in cubits. It was rebuilt in 861 under the caliph al-Mutawakkil, and the astronomer Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Farghani is named as its designer. Each summer the river rose, and the height it reached on that column decided everything: too low meant famine, too high meant destroyed villages, and a good flood meant the year's taxes could be levied. Officials read the mark and criers announced the number in the streets. The nilometer still stands, its Kufic inscriptions intact, one of the oldest Islamic structures in Egypt and a piece of public infrastructure that doubled as a public forecast.

lights.t: He spent sixteen years deciding what to leave out
lights.s: Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari was born in Bukhara in 810 and died in 870. He travelled for years through Khurasan, Iraq, the Hijaz, Syria and Egypt collecting reports of what the Prophet ﷺ said and did, and interrogating the people who transmitted them: where they lived, whether they had actually met their teacher, whether anyone doubted their memory or honesty. The point of the work was subtraction. His Sahih contains roughly 7,275 reports counting repetitions, sifted out of a far greater mass he had gathered and rejected. The discipline he helped build, weighing a chain of names before weighing the text, is one of the earliest systematic methods for testing testimony.

lights.t: Codebreaking was invented by counting letters in Arabic
lights.s: Al-Kindi, the philosopher of Baghdad who died around 873, wrote a short treatise on deciphering encrypted messages. In it he explains that if you know the language a message is written in, you take a long ordinary text in that language, count how often each letter appears, then count the symbols in the cipher and match the most frequent to the most frequent. That is frequency analysis, and it broke every simple substitution cipher for the next seven hundred years. The manuscript was lost for centuries and was rediscovered in 1987 in the Ottoman archive in Istanbul. Scholars of the Qur'an had already been counting letters and word frequencies, which is where the habit came from.

lights.t: Cordoba declared itself a caliphate in January 929
lights.s: On 16 January 929, Abd al-Rahman III, ruler of a fractured al-Andalus he had spent seventeen years pulling back together, stopped calling himself emir and took the titles of caliph and commander of the faithful. It was a direct claim against Baghdad and against the Fatimids in North Africa, and it made Cordoba the seat of a third caliphate. Under him and his son the city grew into one of the largest in Europe, with paved and lit streets, public baths, a court that employed Muslims, Christians and Jews, and a library that scholars crossed the continent to use. The caliphate he proclaimed lasted just over a century before civil war broke it apart.

lights.t: A little cloud in his star book was another galaxy
lights.s: In 964 the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi finished his Book of Fixed Stars in Isfahan. He went through Ptolemy's catalogue constellation by constellation, checked every star with his own eyes, corrected magnitudes and positions, drew each constellation twice, as seen on a globe and as seen in the sky, and recorded the Arabic names Bedouin observers already used. In Andromeda he described a small cloud, a faint patch that was not a star. It is the earliest known record of the Andromeda galaxy, which no one would understand as a separate galaxy until the 1920s. His book was copied and translated for six hundred years, and many star names in use today come through it.

lights.t: Cairo was laid out as a private city for one dynasty
lights.s: In 969 the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli, a former slave of Sicilian origin, took Egypt for the caliph al-Mu'izz and marked out a walled enclosure north of the existing town of Fustat. It was called al-Qahira, the victorious, and it was not built for the public: it held the palaces, the guard and the administration, and ordinary Egyptians lived outside it. Within two centuries the walls had been overtaken and the name had spread to the whole city. Europeans took al-Qahira into their languages as Cairo. Egyptians still often call it simply Misr, the name of the country itself, because for a long time the city and the country were spoken of as one thing.

lights.t: Al-Azhar was founded by one sect and outlived it
lights.s: Construction of the mosque of al-Azhar in Cairo began in 970 under the Fatimids, and the first Friday prayer was held there in 972. It was built to teach and spread Ismaili Shi'i doctrine, and for two centuries that is what it did. When Salah ad-Din ended Fatimid rule in 1171 the mosque was turned to Sunni teaching, and it has taught, with one long interruption, ever since. Its method was circles on the floor: a teacher against a pillar, students around him, a licence granted by the teacher rather than the institution. More than a thousand years later it is still one of the central seats of Sunni learning, in a building begun by the people whose theology it now teaches against.

lights.t: Cordoba's caliph read the books before he shelved them
lights.s: Al-Hakam II, who ruled Cordoba from 961 to 976, was a collector on a state scale. He sent agents to Baghdad, Cairo and Damascus with orders to buy or copy anything worth having, paid scribes in several cities to work for him, and according to the sources built a library whose catalogue alone ran to 44 volumes. The figure usually given for the collection is 400,000 volumes, which comes from later writers and may be generous, but no one disputes it was the largest in Europe. Marginal notes in his own hand survive in some manuscripts. After his death much of it was dispersed or burned during the civil wars that broke the caliphate apart.

lights.t: He learned Sanskrit to describe Hinduism in its own words
lights.s: Al-Biruni finished his book on India around 1030. He had gone there with Mahmud of Ghazna's campaigns, but what he wrote was not a conqueror's report. He learned Sanskrit, read the Puranas and the Bhagavad Gita, sat with Brahmins, and stated his method at the start: he would report what Hindus themselves say, in their own terms, and would not argue with them in the telling. He compared their astronomy with Greek astronomy, described their weights, calendars, castes and festivals, and noted where he thought they were mistaken and where he thought his own side was. The book is still used by historians as the best outside account of eleventh century India.

lights.t: The Seljuk state paid students to study, from 1065
lights.s: Nizam al-Mulk, vizier to the Seljuk sultans, began building the Nizamiyya of Baghdad in 1065 and opened it in 1067. What was new was not teaching, which had always happened in mosques, but the funding: a permanent endowment, a waqf, paid the professors a salary, gave students stipends and lodging, and maintained a library, so that a poor student could study without a patron. He founded sister colleges in Nishapur, Isfahan, Basra and other cities. Al-Ghazali held the chair in Baghdad. The model, an endowed college with salaried teachers and funded students, spread across the Muslim world and is one of the ancestors of the modern university.

lights.t: One August day in 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement
lights.s: On 26 August 1071 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan met the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes near Manzikert, in what is now eastern Turkey. Alp Arslan had been trying to avoid the battle and had offered terms. He won it, and captured the emperor, who by most accounts was treated courteously and released for a ransom that was never fully paid. The consequences were not military so much as demographic. Byzantine control of the Anatolian interior collapsed into civil war, Turkoman groups moved in over the following decades, and the region that had been Greek speaking for well over a thousand years slowly became the Turkish speaking country it is today.

lights.t: Omar Khayyam helped fix a calendar still used in Iran
lights.s: The Seljuk sultan Malik Shah asked for a solar calendar that would keep the seasons in place, and a committee of astronomers, among them the poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam, worked at an observatory in Isfahan to produce one. The Jalali calendar they delivered begins on 15 March 1079, with the year starting at the exact moment the sun crosses the equator at the spring equinox rather than by a fixed rule. Its year tracks the sun more closely than the Julian calendar then in use in Europe, and more closely than the Gregorian reform that came five centuries later. A direct descendant of it is the official calendar of Iran and Afghanistan today.

lights.t: The most famous teacher in Baghdad walked away in 1095
lights.s: Al-Ghazali held the chair at the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, the most prestigious teaching post in the Muslim world, with hundreds of students. In 1095 he had a breakdown he described plainly in his own account: he found he could not speak in the lecture hall, could not swallow food, and could not tell whether he was teaching for God or for his reputation. He gave away most of what he owned, left the city under the cover of going on pilgrimage, and spent about eleven years in Damascus, Jerusalem, Makkah and back home in Tus. Out of that came the Revival of the Religious Sciences, still one of the most widely read books in Islam.

lights.t: He drew the world with south at the top
lights.s: Al-Idrisi, born in Ceuta and trained in Cordoba, spent about fifteen years at the Norman court of Roger II in Palermo, interviewing travellers and merchants and checking their accounts against each other. In 1154 he delivered a book of geography and a world map engraved on a great disc of silver, which was later broken up and lost. The maps that survive in the manuscripts show south at the top, following a convention of the time, so the familiar shape of Africa and Arabia sits upside down to a modern eye. His work was made for a Christian king by a Muslim scholar using Norman, Arab, Greek and Jewish informants, and it stayed a standard reference in Europe for three centuries.

lights.t: Jerusalem changed hands in 1187 without a massacre
lights.s: On 2 October 1187, corresponding to 27 Rajab 583, Salah ad-Din took Jerusalem after a short siege. The terms were negotiated with Balian of Ibelin: the inhabitants could buy their freedom at a fixed rate per head, and those who could not pay were to be enslaved. In the event large numbers were released without payment, some ransomed by Salah ad-Din and his brother from their own funds, and the Christian population was allowed to leave with what it could carry. Eastern Christians were permitted to stay, and Jews were allowed to resettle in the city. The contrast with the sack of 1099 was noted by chroniclers on both sides at the time.

lights.t: Salah ad-Din died owning one gold piece and no property
lights.s: Salah ad-Din died in Damascus on 4 March 1193, in his mid fifties, after a fever of about two weeks. He had ruled Egypt and Syria and had commanded armies for twenty years. His secretary and biographer Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, who was present, records that when the estate was counted there were 47 silver dirhams and one piece of gold in the treasury, and that he owned no house, no garden, no village and no farm. There was not enough money on hand to pay for the funeral, and the sum had to be borrowed. His tomb, a modest chamber next to the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, can still be visited.

lights.t: A palace engineer drew fifty machines and how to build them
lights.s: In 1206, at the Artuqid court in Diyarbakir, al-Jazari finished the Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices. It describes about fifty machines with exploded diagrams and step by step instructions: water clocks including an elephant clock combining Indian, Greek, Chinese and Arab parts, hand washing basins that pour and refill, musical automata, and pumps for raising water. Historians of technology point to his use of the crankshaft joined to a connecting rod, and of segmental gears and a camshaft, in working machines. He wrote that he would describe nothing he had not built and tested himself. He died the year the book was completed.

lights.t: He corrected Galen on the heart and was lost for centuries
lights.s: Around 1242, in Cairo, the Syrian physician Ibn al-Nafis wrote a commentary on the anatomy in Ibn Sina's Canon and disagreed with both Ibn Sina and Galen. The accepted view was that blood passed from the right side of the heart to the left through invisible pores in the wall between them. Ibn al-Nafis wrote that the wall is solid, with no pores, and that the blood must travel from the right chamber to the lungs, mix with air there, and return to the left. That is the pulmonary circulation, described three centuries before European anatomists. His text sat unread until a physician, Muhyi al-Din al-Tatawi, found it in a Berlin manuscript and published on it in 1924.

lights.t: A former slave ruled Egypt with coins in her own name
lights.s: When the sultan al-Salih Ayyub died in 1249 with a French army in the Nile delta, his widow Shajar al-Durr, who had been bought as a slave, concealed his death, kept issuing orders in his name, and held the campaign together until his son arrived. The son was killed by the army months later, and in 1250 the commanders made her sultan. Coins were struck in her name and the Friday sermon was said for her, the two public marks of sovereignty. Her rule lasted about three months before pressure from Baghdad forced her to marry her commander Aybak and rule beside him. Her reign is generally taken as the start of the Mamluk state in Egypt.

lights.t: Baghdad fell in February 1258 and the books went to Maragha
lights.s: Hulagu's Mongol army reached Baghdad in January 1258. The caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered on 10 February, and the city was sacked over the following week. Five centuries of libraries were destroyed, and the canal system that fed the region was damaged past easy repair. One thing was saved deliberately: the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, who was travelling with Hulagu, secured books and instruments and persuaded him to fund an observatory. It was built at Maragha, in what is now northwest Iran, and within a few years it held a large library and a team of astronomers from as far as China. The tables they produced there corrected Ptolemy and were read for centuries.

lights.t: The Mongol advance west stopped at a spring in Galilee
lights.s: On 3 September 1260 a Mamluk army from Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars met a Mongol force under Kitbuqa at Ayn Jalut, the Spring of Goliath, in Galilee. The Mongols had taken Baghdad two years earlier and Aleppo and Damascus that spring, and had not been defeated in a pitched battle in the region. They were beaten at Ayn Jalut and their commander was killed. The Mamluks drew them in with a feigned retreat of the kind the Mongols themselves favoured. Historians debate how decisive one battle can be, since Hulagu had already withdrawn most of his army eastward, but the westward advance never resumed.

lights.t: Rumi called the night he died his wedding night
lights.s: Jalal ad-Din Rumi died in Konya on 17 December 1273. He had told those around him not to mourn, because he understood death as a meeting rather than an ending, and the anniversary is still called Sheb-i Arus, the wedding night. The early accounts of his funeral describe Christians, Jews and Muslims in the same procession, each group reading from its own scripture, and say the crowd took most of a day to reach the grave. He wrote in Persian, some 25,000 couplets in the Masnavi alone, and his son organised his followers into the order later known in the West as the whirling dervishes. Konya still marks the date every December.

lights.t: A Cairo hospital was endowed to turn nobody away
lights.s: The Mamluk sultan Qalawun founded a hospital in Cairo in 1284, on the site of a former Fatimid palace, as part of a complex that also held a school and his tomb. Its endowment deed, a legal document that survives, set out how it was to run: separate wards for different illnesses, a pharmacy, a library, a salaried staff of physicians, oculists and surgeons, and treatment funded by the endowment so that payment was never required of the patient. Sick people who could not work were given an allowance on discharge. Endowed hospitals of this kind, called bimaristans, existed across the Muslim world from the ninth century. The Cairo site has served the sick almost continuously since, and an eye hospital still operates there.

lights.t: The grandson of Baghdad's destroyer became a Muslim ruler
lights.s: In 1295 Ghazan, great grandson of Hulagu who had sacked Baghdad, accepted Islam shortly before taking the Ilkhanid throne in Iran, and much of the Mongol army in the region followed. Within four decades of the destruction of 1258 the conquering dynasty had adopted the religion of the conquered, and Ghazan spent his short reign rebuilding: a currency reform, a fixed land tax to stop soldiers extorting villages, roads and post stations, and endowed hospitals and schools in Tabriz. He commissioned Rashid al-Din, a physician of Jewish birth who had become Muslim, to write a history of the world including the Franks, the Chinese and the Indians. It is one of the first histories written on that scale anywhere.

lights.t: A gravestone in Sumatra dates Islam in Southeast Asia
lights.s: At Pasai, on the north coast of Sumatra, stands the tombstone of Sultan Malik al-Salih, carved with the date 696 of the Hijra, which is 1297. It is the earliest firmly dated evidence of a Muslim ruler anywhere in Southeast Asia, and the stone itself appears to have been imported from Cambay in Gujarat, which says something about who was sailing where. Marco Polo, passing the same coast in 1292, noted that the people of the port of Perlak had become Muslim through contact with merchants. Islam reached the region not by conquest but along the monsoon trade routes, carried by traders and teachers, and it is now the religion of more people in Southeast Asia than in the Arab world.

lights.t: Mansa Musa's hajj was still being discussed in Cairo years later
lights.s: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, crossed the Sahara for the hajj with a very large caravan. In Cairo he gave away and spent so much gold that, according to the Egyptian official al-Umari who was writing about twelve years afterwards, the price of gold in the city had still not recovered and local people were talking about it. On the way home he recruited scholars and an architect from Granada, Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, who worked at Timbuktu and Gao. The Djinguereber mosque at Timbuktu dates from that return. European mapmakers, hearing the reports, began drawing a king with a gold nugget in the middle of Africa.
lights.d: Mansa Musa of Mali · hajj of 1324

lights.t: An East African island city impressed the world's great traveller
lights.s: In 1331 Ibn Battuta sailed down the East African coast to Kilwa, an island town in what is now Tanzania, and wrote that it was one of the finest and most substantially built towns he had seen. Kilwa lived on the Indian Ocean trade, exporting gold brought north from the Zimbabwe plateau through Sofala, and importing Chinese porcelain, glass and cloth. Its ruler built the Husuni Kubwa palace, with an octagonal bathing pool cut into the cliff, and a great mosque roofed with coral stone domes. The ruins of both stand today. The Swahili language and the stone towns of the coast grew out of centuries of Africans and Arabs and Persians and Indians trading in the same ports.

lights.t: He invented a science of society in five months
lights.s: Ibn Khaldun, out of political favour and living in a castle in what is now Algeria, wrote the first draft of the Muqaddimah in 1377. He says it took him about five months. It was meant as the introduction to a history of the Arabs and Berbers, but it turned into something else: an argument that history should be tested like any other report, that a chronicle full of impossible numbers should be rejected on the grounds of what economies and armies can actually sustain, and that dynasties rise and fall by a pattern in group solidarity that he called asabiyya. He gave the subject a name, the science of human social organisation. Sociologists and economists still read it.
lights.d: Ibn Khaldun · Qal'at Ibn Salama, 1377 CE

lights.t: A Samarkand mathematician held the record for pi for 180 years
lights.s: In 1424, working at Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand, Jamshid al-Kashi wrote a short treatise on the circumference of the circle. Using a polygon of more than eight hundred million sides, he calculated two pi correct to sixteen decimal places, and explained why he had gone that far: he wanted the error in a circle the size of the known universe to be less than the width of a horse's hair. Nobody improved on his figure for about 180 years, until Ludolph van Ceulen in the Netherlands. Al-Kashi also set out decimal fractions systematically in his Key to Arithmetic three years later, and gave an iterative method for solving cubic equations.

lights.t: A prince measured a thousand stars and timed the year
lights.s: Ulugh Beg was a grandson of Timur and governor of Samarkand, and he was more interested in the sky than in ruling. In the 1420s he built an observatory whose main instrument was a sextant arc about forty metres in radius, sunk into a trench in the rock so it could not shift. In 1437 his team completed the Zij-i Sultani, a catalogue of 1,018 stars measured fresh rather than copied from Ptolemy, along with a value for the length of the year that is within about a minute of the modern figure. He was killed in 1449. The buried arc of his instrument was rediscovered by excavation in 1908 and can be visited.

lights.t: A twenty one year old took Constantinople in May 1453
lights.s: On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II entered Constantinople after a siege of about seven weeks. He was twenty one. The walls that had held for a thousand years were broken by cannon cast for the purpose, some of them by a Hungarian founder who had offered his services to both sides. Mehmed made the city his capital and set about refilling it: he brought in Greeks, Armenians, Jews and Turks by decree and incentive, confirmed a Greek patriarch, and within decades the population had grown several times over. He collected Greek manuscripts and had his portrait painted by the Venetian Gentile Bellini. The city has been called Istanbul ever since.

lights.t: Al-Andalus ended with a treaty that was broken in ten years
lights.s: On 2 January 1492 Muhammad XII, the last Nasrid ruler of Granada, handed the keys of the city to Ferdinand and Isabella, ending nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia. The surrender terms were generous on paper: Muslims could keep their religion, their mosques, their language, their property and their law, and no one was to be forced to convert. Within a decade the terms had been abandoned. Forced conversions began in 1499, Arabic books were burned in the squares of Granada, and by 1502 Islam was banned in Castile. The Alhambra survived because the new rulers wanted to live in it, which is why its rooms of carved plaster and poetry are still standing.

lights.t: A teenager took Tabriz and changed Iran's religion
lights.s: In 1501 Ismail, about fourteen years old and the head of a Sufi order with a devoted military following, took Tabriz and declared himself shah. He made Twelver Shi'ism the official religion of his state, in a country that was then largely Sunni, and imported scholars from Lebanon and Bahrain to teach it because there were not enough locally. The change took generations and was not gentle, but it is the reason Iran is a Shi'i country today and its neighbours are not. The Safavid state he founded lasted more than two centuries, gave Persian painting and carpet weaving a great period, and rebuilt Isfahan into one of the most admired cities in the world.

lights.t: An Ottoman admiral's map lists its own sources
lights.s: In 1513 Piri Reis, an Ottoman naval captain, drew a world map on gazelle skin. Only the left third survives, showing the Atlantic, the coasts of Iberia and West Africa, and part of South America. What makes it unusual is that he wrote his method on the map itself: he names about twenty source charts he compiled from, including Portuguese and Arab charts and, he says, a map used by Columbus, which he had obtained from a Spanish sailor taken prisoner. He later wrote a detailed pilot's book of the Mediterranean. The surviving fragment was found in the Topkapi Palace archives in 1929, more than four centuries after it was drawn.

lights.t: Babur won an empire with cannon and a diary
lights.s: On 21 April 1526 at Panipat, north of Delhi, Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi with a much smaller force by lashing carts together as a firing line, placing field guns behind them, and sending cavalry around both flanks. The victory founded the Mughal empire, which lasted in some form until 1857. Babur was a great grandson several times over of both Timur and Genghis Khan, and he had spent years losing Samarkand before he ever saw India. He also kept a diary in Chaghatai Turkish, the Baburnama, in which he complains about the Indian climate, catalogues its fruits and birds, and admits to his own fears and drinking. Few founders of empires left so candid a record.

lights.t: He called his 1,600 books the smallest library in the family
lights.s: When a Moroccan army took Timbuktu, its scholars were arrested, and in 1593 Ahmad Baba was taken in chains across the Sahara to Marrakesh. He was held for years and then taught there, becoming well known enough that Moroccan scholars sought him out. He later wrote that his library, seized when he was arrested, held 1,600 volumes, and that his had been the smallest library among his relatives. He returned to Timbuktu in 1607 and wrote more than forty works, including a legal opinion arguing that being African was no ground for enslaving anyone, and that the only relevant question in law was belief, not origin.
lights.d: Ahmad Baba · Timbuktu and Marrakesh, 1593 CE

lights.t: Isfahan was rebuilt around a square used for polo
lights.s: In 1598 Shah Abbas I moved the Safavid capital to Isfahan and had a new centre laid out beside the old city: a rectangular open space about 160 metres by 500, with a mosque at one end, a bazaar entrance at the other, a palace pavilion on one side and a smaller mosque on the other. It was a market, a parade ground and a polo field, and the stone goalposts are still in place at each end. Its name, Naqsh-e Jahan, means image of the world. Armenian craftsmen and merchants were resettled in a quarter across the river with their own churches. The square is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and people still picnic on it.

lights.t: The Taj Mahal is a tomb built for one named woman
lights.s: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, and construction of her tomb at Agra began in 1632 on the orders of her husband, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. The main mausoleum took about twelve years and the wider complex around twenty. The building is almost exactly symmetrical, its four minarets lean very slightly outward so that they would fall away from the dome in an earthquake, and the white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan with inlaid stones brought from as far as Afghanistan and Sri Lanka. The sources name Ustad Ahmad Lahori as the chief architect. It is one of the few world famous monuments built as a private act of grief for a specific person.

lights.t: Four women ruled Aceh in a row for fifty eight years
lights.s: In 1641, on the death of her husband, Safiatuddin Syah became ruler of Aceh in northern Sumatra, then one of the strongest states in Southeast Asia and a hub of the pepper trade. She reigned for thirty four years, and three more women followed her, so that Aceh was ruled by sultanas continuously from 1641 to 1699. Under them the state kept its independence, its scholars kept writing in Malay, and Dutch and English traders negotiated with a woman's court. The line ended when opponents obtained a ruling from Makkah against female rule. Two centuries later, Acehnese women again led resistance to Dutch conquest, among them Cut Nyak Dhien.

lights.t: The first Ottoman press printed a dictionary in 1729
lights.s: Ibrahim Muteferrika, born in Hungary and a convert to Islam, obtained permission from Sultan Ahmed III and a legal opinion from the chief mufti, and in 1729 produced the first book printed with Arabic type by an Ottoman press: a two volume Arabic to Turkish dictionary. The permission excluded the Qur'an and religious texts, which stayed with the copyists, and his list ran to seventeen titles including geography, history and a treatise on military reform. Printing in Istanbul was not new. Jewish, Armenian and Greek presses had been working in the city since the 1490s, in their own scripts. What was new in 1729 was Arabic type, and the argument that had to be won first.

lights.t: He wrote the Qur'an from memory on Robben Island
lights.s: Tuan Guru, born Abdullah ibn Qadi Abd al-Salam, was a prince from Tidore in the Indonesian archipelago, exiled by the Dutch and held on Robben Island off Cape Town from 1780. In prison he wrote out the Qur'an from memory, and also compiled a book of belief in Malay and Arabic. Copies survive. Released in 1793, he founded a school and then, in 1794, the Auwal Mosque in the Bo-Kaap, the first mosque in South Africa, in a property made available by Saartjie van de Kaap, a freed slave woman who owned it. The mosque is still in use, and much of the Cape Muslim community traces itself to those exiles.

lights.t: An enslaved man in Carolina wrote his life in Arabic
lights.s: Omar ibn Said was born around 1770 in Futa Toro, in what is now Senegal, studied for about twenty five years, and was captured and shipped to Charleston in 1807. In 1831, enslaved in North Carolina, he wrote fifteen pages in Arabic setting out his life. It is the only known autobiography written in Arabic by an enslaved person in the United States. He opens not with his own name but with Surah al-Mulk written out from memory, and he describes being taken from a place where he had prayed and studied. The manuscript was bought by the Library of Congress in 2017, digitised, and put online, where anyone can read his handwriting.

lights.t: She built a network of women teaching women across Sokoto
lights.s: Nana Asma'u, born in 1793, was the daughter of Usman dan Fodio and one of the most learned figures of the Sokoto Caliphate in what is now northern Nigeria. She read and wrote Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa and Tamacheq, and more than sixty of her works survive: poems, elegies, instruction in law and medicine, and a verse history of her father's movement. Her lasting work was organisational. She trained older women as itinerant teachers, the jaji, who travelled between villages teaching women in their own homes, each carrying a cloth or a symbol marking her as a teacher. The network she set up in the 1830s is called the yan taru, and it still operates in northern Nigeria. She died in 1864.

lights.t: A poet in Sialkot wrote in Persian to reach further
lights.s: Muhammad Iqbal was born on 9 November 1877 in Sialkot, in what was then British India and is now Pakistan. He studied philosophy at Cambridge and took a doctorate at Munich on metaphysics in Persia, then practised law in Lahore while writing the poetry he is known for. He wrote much of it in Persian rather than Urdu, because Persian was still read from Istanbul to Delhi and he wanted the wider audience. His theme was self hood, khudi: that a person and a community come alive by taking responsibility rather than waiting. In 1930 he argued for a separate Muslim political unit in northwest India. He died in 1938, nine years before Pakistan existed.

lights.t: Pilgrims funded a railway to Madinah by subscription
lights.s: On 1 September 1908 the first train from Damascus reached Madinah, about 1,300 kilometres to the south, cutting a camel route of some forty days to under four. The Hejaz Railway was built between 1900 and 1908 and paid for in large part by public donation from Muslims across the world, from India to North Africa, collected in mosques and by newspaper appeal. Much of the labour was done by Ottoman soldiers. It is often recounted that near Madinah the rails were laid on felt so that the noise would not disturb the Prophet's ﷺ resting place. The line ran for less than a decade before the First World War, and the stations and rolling stock still stand rusting in the Jordanian and Saudi desert.

lights.t: Azerbaijan gave women the vote before Britain did
lights.s: On 28 May 1918 the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic declared independence, the first secular parliamentary republic in the Muslim world. Its electoral law gave the vote to all citizens over twenty regardless of sex, religion or ethnicity, which put Azerbaijani women at the ballot box before women in Britain had equal franchise, which came in 1928, and before women in the United States, who got it in 1920. The parliament included Armenian, Russian, Jewish and Georgian members. The republic lasted twenty three months before the Red Army entered Baku in April 1920. Its flag and its independence day were both taken up again when Azerbaijan became independent a second time in 1991.

lights.t: The caliphate was ended by a vote in March 1924
lights.s: On 3 March 1924 the Grand National Assembly in Ankara abolished the caliphate, an institution that had existed in some form since 632, and the last caliph, Abdulmecid II, left Istanbul by train the following night. The office had been almost powerless for centuries and had already been separated from the sultanate in 1922, but its ending mattered far beyond Turkey. In India it had already produced the Khilafat movement, one of the first mass political campaigns on the subcontinent. Muslims elsewhere held congresses in Cairo and Makkah to consider what to do, and agreed on nothing. The question of who, if anyone, speaks for the whole community has been open since that day.

lights.t: Indonesia was declared in a front garden in 35 words
lights.s: On the morning of 17 August 1945, two days after the Japanese surrender and before the Dutch could return, Sukarno stood in the front garden of his house in Jakarta and read out a proclamation of two short sentences, typed that night after a long argument among younger and older nationalists. There was no ceremony to speak of, a flag sewn by Sukarno's wife Fatmawati was raised, and a few hundred people were present. Four years of war followed before the Netherlands recognised it in 1949. Indonesia is now the country with the largest Muslim population on earth, and Islam arrived there not by conquest but along the trade routes, centuries earlier.

lights.t: Pakistan was created on a date chosen for convenience
lights.s: Pakistan became independent on 14 August 1947 and India the following day, because the last viceroy Louis Mountbatten had moved the whole transfer of power forward by about ten months and the two ceremonies had to be held on separate days so he could attend both. The boundary line between the two countries was drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India before, working from maps and census returns in five weeks. It was not published until after independence. The migration that followed was one of the largest in human history, and the border he drew still runs through Punjab and Bengal today.

lights.t: Malaya's independence was announced with one word, seven times
lights.s: On 31 August 1957 at the Merdeka Stadium in Kuala Lumpur, Tunku Abdul Rahman read the proclamation of independence and then raised his hand and called out merdeka, freedom, seven times, with the crowd answering each one. The word is Malay, borrowed long before from the Sanskrit maharddhika, and it is still the name of the day. The constitution agreed that year made Islam the religion of the federation while guaranteeing the practice of other religions, and set up a rotating monarchy in which nine hereditary Malay rulers elect one of their number as king every five years, an arrangement that exists nowhere else in the world.

lights.t: Algeria chose the anniversary of its own conquest
lights.s: Algeria proclaimed its independence on 5 July 1962, and the date was not an accident. French troops had entered Algiers on 5 July 1830, so the new state closed the account exactly 132 years later, to the day. The war that ended in 1962 had lasted almost eight years and cost hundreds of thousands of lives, and afterwards close to a million European settlers left within months. The country's first task was practical and enormous: at independence the great majority of the population could not read, and teachers had to be recruited from Egypt, Syria and elsewhere to staff the schools of a country the size of Western Europe.

lights.t: He built a physics institute for scientists with no equipment
lights.s: On 10 December 1979 Abdus Salam of Pakistan received the Nobel Prize in Physics with Sheldon Glashow and Steven Weinberg, for work showing that electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force are two aspects of one force. He was the first Muslim to win a Nobel Prize in a science. He accepted it in Punjabi dress and a turban. Long before the prize, in 1964, he had founded the International Centre for Theoretical Physics in Trieste so that physicists from poor countries could spend part of each year working with equipment and colleagues and then return home rather than emigrate. Thousands have passed through it. He is buried in Pakistan.

lights.t: The first Muslim in space watched the crescent from orbit
lights.s: On 17 June 1985 the space shuttle Discovery lifted off with Sultan bin Salman al-Saud aboard as a payload specialist for the launch of an Arab communications satellite. He was twenty eight, the first Muslim, the first Arab and the first member of a royal family to go into space. He carried a Qur'an with him. He also carried a practical question that later Muslim astronauts would have to answer formally: how to keep prayer times and face Makkah in a vehicle that circles the earth roughly every ninety minutes.

lights.t: In 1988 a woman took office as prime minister of Pakistan
lights.s: Benazir Bhutto was sworn in as prime minister of Pakistan on 2 December 1988, the first woman to lead the government of a Muslim majority country in modern times. She was thirty five. Her father, a former prime minister, had been hanged nine years earlier, and she had spent much of the intervening period in prison or in exile. Her opponents argued that a woman could not hold the office at all; the electorate and the courts settled it otherwise. Her two terms were both cut short. She was assassinated in Rawalpindi in 2007. Women have since led governments in Bangladesh, Turkey, Indonesia, Senegal, Kosovo and Kyrgyzstan.

lights.t: Malaysia wrote the rules for praying in orbit
lights.s: Before Sheikh Muszaphar Shukor launched to the International Space Station on 10 October 2007, Malaysia's national fatwa council convened scholars and scientists and published a short document, Guidelines for Performing Islamic Rites at the International Space Station. The problems were concrete. The station circles the earth about sixteen times a day, so which sunrise starts a fast. There is no down, so how do you bow and prostrate. The direction of Makkah changes second by second, so the guidance says face it as best you can at the start and continue, and if that is impossible, face anywhere. Prayer times were to follow the launch site. Old rules for travellers and the sick were applied to a new place.

lights.t: Timbuktu's manuscripts were smuggled out in footlockers
lights.s: When armed groups took Timbuktu in 2012, the city's libraries held centuries of manuscripts on law, astronomy, medicine, poetry and mathematics, many still owned by the families who had copied them. Abdel Kader Haidara, a librarian, organised an evacuation. Volunteers packed manuscripts into metal footlockers and rice sacks, moved them out of the city a few at a time by car, donkey and boat down the Niger, through checkpoints, and stored them in houses in Bamako. By early 2013 an estimated 350,000 manuscripts had been moved. Some were burned in Timbuktu, but far fewer than first reported. The collections are now being conserved and digitised in the south of the country.

lights.t: Two leaves in Birmingham dated to within a lifetime of revelation
lights.s: On 22 July 2015 the University of Birmingham announced the results of radiocarbon dating on two parchment leaves that had sat in its Mingana Collection, uncatalogued alongside another manuscript, since the 1920s. The parchment dated to between 568 and 645 CE with 95.4 per cent probability. The text, parts of chapters 18 to 20 in an early Hijazi script, matches the standard Qur'an in use today. The date is of the animal skin rather than the ink, so it gives an upper limit rather than an exact age, and scholars continue to discuss what that means. The leaves are among the oldest Qur'anic manuscripts known, and they were found by a doctoral student looking properly at a box.

lights.t: An Arab probe reached Mars orbit in February 2021
lights.s: On 9 February 2021 the Emirates Mars Mission, called Hope, fired its engines for twenty seven minutes and entered orbit around Mars. It was the first interplanetary mission by an Arab country, and only about half of all Mars missions to that point had succeeded. The spacecraft was built in six years by a team whose average age was in the early thirties, working with the University of Colorado, and the science lead was Sarah al-Amiri. Its orbit was chosen to see the whole planet at all times of day, which no earlier mission had done, and it studies how the Martian atmosphere is escaping into space. Its data is released publicly to anyone who asks for it.

lights.t: Maragha was an observatory with a budget and a staff
lights.s: In 1259 Nasir al-Din al-Tusi began building an observatory at Maragha, in what is now northwest Iran, with Hulagu's backing and, more usefully, a share of endowment income assigned to it so that it did not depend on one ruler's mood. That was the new thing. Earlier observatories had been the project of a single astronomer and closed when he died or lost his patron. Maragha had a director, a library, a workshop, salaried staff drawn from Damascus to Andalusia, and a Chinese astronomer named in the sources. Its instruments were designed by Mu'ayyad al-Din al-Urdi. The tables it produced, the Zij-i Ilkhani, were finished in 1272 and used for centuries. The pattern it set, a funded institution outliving its founder, was copied at Samarkand and Istanbul.

lights.t: Letters home from Samarkand describe how an observatory ran
lights.s: Two letters written by Jamshid al-Kashi to his father in Kashan survive from the 1420s, and they are the closest thing anyone has to an eyewitness account of a great observatory at work. Al-Kashi describes the staff at Ulugh Beg's institution in Samarkand, dozens of scholars with the ruler himself among the working astronomers, and reports that Ulugh Beg could carry long calculations in his head. He is blunt about colleagues he thought incompetent. He also admits that he had no manners at court and that Ulugh Beg overlooked it. The observatory was attached to a madrasa where astronomy and mathematics were taught, so the staff trained their own replacements, and one of those students, Ali Qushji, later carried the work west to Istanbul.

lights.t: Istanbul's observatory was demolished three years after it opened
lights.s: Taqi al-Din, chief astronomer to Sultan Murad III, built an observatory at Tophane in Istanbul in the 1570s, at almost the same time as Tycho Brahe was building Uraniborg on an island in Denmark. The instruments were of comparable size and design. Taqi al-Din observed the great comet of 1577, as Tycho did, and read it as a good omen for the campaign against Iran. The campaign went badly, plague came to the city, and the chief mufti gave the opinion that prying into the secrets of the heavens brought misfortune. In January 1580 the building was pulled down on the sultan's order by a detachment of the navy. Uraniborg ran for twenty years and produced the observations Kepler used to find the orbit of Mars.

lights.t: He measured the year and was off by two minutes
lights.s: Al-Battani observed from Raqqa, on the Euphrates, from about 877 until 918, with instruments he had built and checked himself. He put the length of the solar year at 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes and 24 seconds, which is about two minutes and twenty seconds short of the modern value. He also found that the point at which the sun is furthest from the earth had shifted since Ptolemy recorded its position, which meant the Greek tables were not simply to be copied forward. His own tables were translated into Latin in the twelfth century, he was known in Europe as Albategnius, and Copernicus cites him repeatedly in the book of 1543. There is a crater on the moon carrying his Latin name.

lights.t: One hill in the Punjab was enough to measure the earth
lights.s: Around 1018, at the fort of Nandana in what is now Pakistan, al-Biruni measured the height of a hill by sighting its summit from two places on the plain below. He then climbed it and measured how far the horizon had dropped below the level line. From those two numbers and some trigonometry he obtained the radius of the earth. His answer works out at about 6,340 kilometres, within a fraction of a per cent of the modern figure. He liked the method mainly because it needed one person and one instrument, where the caliph al-Ma'mun's astronomers had needed survey parties pacing across a plain. Historians note that his instrument could not really support that much accuracy, so part of the agreement is luck.

lights.t: His eclipse timings were still useful eight hundred years later
lights.s: Ibn Yunus worked in Cairo under the Fatimids and finished his great set of astronomical tables, the Hakimi Zij, around 1003. What sets it apart is that he wrote down the raw observations, his own and other people's, rather than only the conclusions drawn from them: dozens of planetary conjunctions and about thirty lunar eclipses, each with its date and its measured time, including older records he had dug out of earlier astronomers' papers. Extracts were printed in Paris in 1804, and nineteenth century astronomers used his eclipse times, along with other early records, to test whether the moon's motion around the earth is slowly changing. It is. Ibn Yunus was not answering that question. He simply wrote the numbers down and kept them.

lights.t: Two rolling circles turn a circle into a straight line
lights.s: Ptolemy's planetary models needed a device called the equant, a point about which a planet swept equal angles although it was not the centre of the circle it moved on. It predicted well and it broke the rule that motion in the heavens is uniform and circular, and astronomers had complained about it for centuries. In 1247 Nasir al-Din al-Tusi published a way round it. Roll a small circle inside a circle of twice its diameter, and any point on the small circle traces a straight line, back and forth. Circular motions alone can therefore produce oscillation. The construction is called the Tusi couple. It appears, drawn the same way and with no attribution, in Copernicus's book of 1543, and how it got there is a standing question.

lights.t: A mosque timekeeper's lunar model matches Copernicus exactly
lights.s: Ibn al-Shatir kept the prayer times at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus and built the sundial for its minaret. He also rebuilt planetary astronomy, discarding Ptolemy's equant and off centre circles and assembling his models from uniform circular motions only. In 1957 Victor Roberts, working with E. S. Kennedy in Beirut, showed that Ibn al-Shatir's model of the moon is mathematically identical to the one Copernicus published in 1543, and that several parameters match. What nobody has found is a route. No Latin translation of Ibn al-Shatir is known and Copernicus never names him. Some scholars argue for transmission through Byzantine Greek manuscripts, others for two men solving the same problem the same way. Ibn al-Shatir kept the earth at the centre. Copernicus moved it.

lights.t: He argued nothing observable rules out a turning earth
lights.s: Ali Qushji learned his astronomy at Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand and worked on its star tables. After Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449 he moved west, and in the early 1470s Mehmed II brought him to Istanbul to teach. He made two arguments unusual for his time. The first was that astronomy does not need Aristotle's physics underneath it and should be built on observation and geometry alone. The second followed from it: everything seen in the sky would look the same whether the earth stands still or turns, so observation cannot settle the matter, and no astronomical result requires a motionless earth. He did not claim the earth moves. He said the case that it does not was weaker than people assumed.
lights.d: Ali Qushji · Samarkand and Istanbul, died 1474

lights.t: The caliph's best mathematician was not a Muslim
lights.s: Thabit ibn Qurra came from Harran in upper Mesopotamia and belonged to the Sabians, a small community with its own religion and its own regard for the stars. He was working as a money changer when one of the Banu Musa brothers noticed him and brought him to Baghdad. He kept his religion, wrote in Syriac for his own people and in Arabic for the court, and became one of the finest mathematicians of the ninth century. He revised the Arabic Euclid, translated Archimedes and Apollonius, found the area under a parabola by a method close to integration, and gave the first general rule for producing amicable numbers, pairs in which each is the sum of the other's divisors. He died in 901. His son and grandsons were scientists too.
lights.d: Thabit ibn Qurra · Harran and Baghdad, died 901

lights.t: Algebra had no symbols for four hundred years
lights.s: Abu Kamil, an Egyptian calculator working a generation or so after al-Khwarizmi, wrote everything out in words. An equation was a sentence: a square and ten roots equal thirty nine dirhams. There was no x, no equals sign, no notation for a power, and the proofs were geometrical, drawn as actual squares and rectangles. Inside that constraint he did serious work. He allowed irrational quantities as coefficients and as answers, which al-Khwarizmi had not, handled powers up to the eighth, and solved systems in several unknowns. One of his puzzles about buying birds has 2,676 whole number solutions, and he counted every one of them and recorded that he was pleased with himself. Fibonacci took problems from him into the book that brought algebra to Latin Europe.

lights.t: The man who freed algebra also wrote about underground water
lights.s: Al-Karaji worked in Baghdad around the year 1000. Before him algebra was tied to geometry, because a square meant an area and a cube meant a volume, and a fourth power meant nothing anyone could draw. He cut the tie, treating the powers of the unknown as a ladder you can climb in either direction, with reciprocals going down, and gave rules for multiplying and dividing them. He set out the triangle of binomial coefficients that Europe would later name after Pascal, supported by reasoning historians describe as an early form of mathematical induction. He then left the capital and wrote a manual on locating groundwater and digging qanats, the underground channels that watered Iran, thought to be the oldest surviving text on the subject.

lights.t: He wrote his algebra book at nineteen
lights.s: Al-Samawal was born in Baghdad to a Jewish family from Morocco. He worked through the mathematics available in the city, found by his late teens that he had exhausted it, and wrote al-Bahir, the Brilliant, at about nineteen. In it he divided one polynomial by another by setting the coefficients out in a table, which is the long division of algebra, stated the laws of exponents including the negative ones, and recorded that any quantity raised to the power zero is one. He used repeated division to carry a quotient to as many places as he wanted, coming close to the idea of an unending decimal. He became a Muslim in 1163 and wrote his own account of why. He died around 1180 at Maragha.

lights.t: Khayyam solved cubic equations by crossing two curves
lights.s: Omar Khayyam is read in English as a poet, on the strength of a loose Victorian version of verses attributed to him. In Persian and Arabic he is a mathematician. Around 1070 he wrote a treatise sorting cubic equations into fourteen kinds that cannot be reduced to anything simpler, and giving each kind a solution by drawing two conic sections, a circle with a parabola or a hyperbola, and measuring where they cross. He said plainly that he had found no way to solve them by arithmetic and hoped somebody would. Somebody did, in Italy, four and a half centuries later. He also led the committee that produced the Jalali solar calendar, and wrote on the parallel postulate that troubled geometers until the nineteenth century.
lights.d: Omar Khayyam · Samarkand and Isfahan, c. 1070

lights.t: The sine of one degree, to ten sexagesimal places
lights.s: Every table of sines has to start somewhere, and the hard case is one degree, which cannot be reached by the usual halving and adding of angles already known. At Samarkand in the 1420s, Jamshid al-Kashi turned it into a cubic equation and solved that equation by repeated approximation, each round of arithmetic adding another correct digit, until he had the value to ten places in the base sixty notation astronomers used. No instrument of his day, or for a long time after, could measure an angle anywhere near that finely. He did the same with the circumference of a circle, taking the value of what we call pi far past any practical need. Ulugh Beg's star tables were built on his figures.

lights.t: He moved arithmetic off the dust board and onto paper
lights.s: In Damascus in 952 a mathematician known as al-Uqlidisi wrote a book on calculating with the Indian numerals. Reckoning was then done on a takht, a board spread with fine dust, where each step was wiped out as the next was written. He argued for ink and paper instead, partly because the dust board was the tool of street fortune tellers and carried their reputation, and partly because on paper the working stays where you can check it. In the same book he uses a mark to separate a whole number from the fraction following it, which is the earliest known use of a decimal fraction. Al-Kashi set decimal fractions out systematically in 1427, and Simon Stevin made them ordinary in Europe in 1585.

lights.t: Your digits came west through the Maghrib and Spain
lights.s: The numerals reached the Arabic speaking world from India, and Arabic writers called them the Indian figures, which is what they were. They then split into two families of shapes. In the east, from Egypt to Iran, the forms still printed on Egyptian number plates and Iranian banknotes took hold. In the west, in the Maghrib and al-Andalus, a different set developed, called ghubar or dust figures after the boards they were written on. Those are the ones Europe learned. Gerbert of Aurillac, later Pope Sylvester II, met them in Catalonia in the tenth century, and Fibonacci learned them properly as a boy at Bugia on the coast of what is now Algeria, where his father was a customs official.
lights.d: Maghrib to Europe · tenth to thirteenth centuries

lights.t: Zero and cipher are one word borrowed twice
lights.s: The Indian mathematicians who made place value work called the empty column shunya, meaning void. Arabic translators rendered that as sifr, meaning empty. When the system moved into Latin, sifr was written down two ways, as zephirum and as cifra. Zephirum became the Italian zefiro and then zero. Cifra became the French chiffre and the English cipher, which first meant zero, then meant any digit at all, and then, because the new figures looked like a code to people who could not read them, came to mean a secret code. So a cipher is a zero, a zero is an emptiness, and the English word for a person who counts for nothing is the Sanskrit word for the void, carried west in Arabic.
lights.d: Sanskrit to Arabic to Latin · one word's route

lights.t: Sine is a mistranslation of a misread Arabic word
lights.s: Indian astronomers worked with the half chord of an arc and called it jya. When their tables were translated into Arabic the word was carried across by sound as jiba, which means nothing in Arabic. Written without vowels, those same letters spell jayb, which means a fold, or the opening at the breast of a garment where things are kept. Later readers naturally read it that way, because it was a real word. When the Arabic was translated into Latin in twelfth century Spain, the translator rendered the meaning he found, and jayb became sinus, the Latin for a fold or a bay. English shortened that to sine. The function is Indian, the name is an accident, and the tangent began separately as the length of a shadow.
lights.d: India to Baghdad to Toledo · one word's route

lights.t: His sine table was right to eight decimal places
lights.s: Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani came from Khurasan to Baghdad as a young man and stayed for the rest of his life. He treated all six trigonometric quantities as functions rather than as lines in a diagram, gave the addition formula for sines, and computed a fresh table at intervals of fifteen minutes of arc. His value for the sine of half a degree is correct to eight decimal places, and was not improved on for a long time. The spherical law of sines, the rule that makes triangles on a globe calculable, is credited to him and to two contemporaries, Abu Nasr Mansur and al-Khujandi, and which of the three had it first has never been settled. He also wrote a book of geometrical constructions for craftsmen.

lights.t: A book that made trigonometry a subject of its own
lights.s: Trigonometry had always been a tool for something else. You calculated triangles in order to find where a planet would be, and the tables lived inside astronomy books, in the chapters before the interesting part. Around 1260 Nasir al-Din al-Tusi wrote the Treatise on the Complete Quadrilateral, five books setting out plane and spherical trigonometry as a subject with its own problems and its own proofs and no astronomy in it at all. Historians usually call it the first work to do that, while noting that Abu al-Wafa and Abu Nasr Mansur had already gone much of the way. It was printed with a French translation at Istanbul in 1891, which is when European mathematicians could finally read it.

lights.t: He tabulated the direction of Makkah for every latitude
lights.s: Facing Makkah from anywhere else on earth is a problem in spherical trigonometry. You need the shortest path over a sphere between two points whose latitudes and longitudes you know, and then the angle that path makes with north. Exact solutions were worked out in the ninth century, and al-Biruni wrote a whole book on pinning down the coordinates that go into them. In the fourteenth century Shams al-Din al-Khalili, timekeeper at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, computed the answer in advance for every combination of latitude and longitude difference across the inhabited world, close to three thousand entries, by hand. When his table was checked against modern computation in the twentieth century, almost every entry proved correct.

lights.t: Two brass maps give the direction to Makkah from anywhere
lights.s: Two engraved brass world maps came to light in the 1990s, made in Iran and generally dated to the seventeenth century. They look ornamental until you understand what the grid is doing. Makkah sits at the centre, and the curved lines around it are laid out so that a ruler pivoted at that centre reads off both the direction of Makkah and the distance to it for any place marked on the plate, with no calculation at all. David King, the historian who published them, argued that the mathematics behind the grid is much older than the objects themselves and goes back to methods worked out around the eleventh century. A hard problem in spherical trigonometry, compressed into a disc of metal you can hold.
lights.d: Safavid Iran · published by David King

lights.t: An astrolabe is a model of the sky you hold
lights.s: You sight a star or the sun through the bar on the back of an astrolabe, read its height above the horizon off the rim, turn the openwork grid on the front until it matches, and the instrument tells you the time of day or night, the direction you are facing, where any other star has got to, and the height of the tower across the street. No arithmetic is needed. The flattening of the sphere onto a disc is Greek geometry and goes back to Hipparchus. Muslim makers turned it into a standard object made in quantity, with prayer times and the direction of Makkah engraved on it. Chaucer wrote a manual for one in English, for his ten year old son.
lights.d: Oldest dated example by Nastulus · 927 CE

lights.t: One line in one book records a woman who made astrolabes
lights.s: In the catalogue of books he compiled at Baghdad around 987, Ibn al-Nadim lists the makers of astrolabes, and among them names the daughter of al-Ijli, saying she made the instruments and worked at the court of Sayf al-Dawla in Aleppo. That is the whole record. He gives no first name, no instrument by her is known to survive, and nothing further about her life has been found. Modern accounts often call her Mariam, which is a later addition rather than anything the source says. What the single line does establish is that a woman making precision instruments in tenth century Aleppo was worth listing without comment, alongside the men. An asteroid is named al-Ijliya after her.
lights.d: Al-Ijliyya of Aleppo · named in the Fihrist, c. 987

lights.t: Mosques put an astronomer on the payroll
lights.s: The five prayers are defined by the sun: first light, the moment a stick's shadow reaches a set length, sunset. Working out when those moments fall on a given day at a given latitude is astronomy, and from the thirteenth century mosques in Egypt and Syria employed a salaried official to do it, the muwaqqit. He kept the tables, checked them against the sky, and set the times for the muezzin. The post drew serious people: Ibn al-Shatir held it in Damascus, and so did al-Khalili. Their everyday tool was the sine quadrant, a quarter circle of brass or wood with a plumb line and a grid of curves, on which the day's trigonometry could be read by sliding a bead along a thread.
lights.d: The muwaqqit · Egypt and Syria, from the 1200s

lights.t: The largest instrument yet built sank under its own weight
lights.s: Around 994, near Rayy in northern Iran, al-Khujandi built the Fakhri sextant, named after the ruler who paid for it. It was an arc of sixty degrees set in a north to south trench and roofed over, its radius long enough that a single degree on the scale could be divided into seconds, which no smaller instrument allowed. A small aperture let a disc of sunlight fall on the scale at noon. As far as is known it was the largest astronomical instrument built up to that time. His measurement of the tilt of the earth's axis came out about two minutes of arc short. Al-Biruni, who examined it and wrote about it, concluded that the aperture had sunk as the masonry settled.

lights.t: A dark room with a pinhole gave the camera its name
lights.s: Make a small hole in the wall of a dark room and the scene outside appears on the opposite wall, upside down. The effect was noticed long before anyone explained it. It is described in the Chinese Mozi text around the fourth century BCE, and a Greek work handed down under Aristotle's name notes that gaps between leaves cast crescents on the ground during an eclipse. Ibn al-Haytham, in Cairo in the early eleventh century, turned it into an experiment. He set several lamps outside the aperture and showed their images stayed separate on the wall, which means light travels in straight lines and rays do not mix. His term was the dark room. Kepler put that into Latin in 1604 as camera obscura.
lights.d: Ibn al-Haytham · Cairo, early eleventh century

lights.t: He built a glass raindrop to explain the rainbow
lights.s: Around 1309 in Tabriz, Kamal al-Din al-Farisi was working through Ibn al-Haytham's Optics at the suggestion of his teacher Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, and reached the rainbow. Rather than argue about it he built a model: a large clear glass sphere filled with water, standing in for one drop, set up in a darkened room. Tracing the light through it, he found that the main bow comes from two refractions and one reflection inside each drop, and the fainter outer bow from an extra reflection, which is also why its colours run the other way. At almost the same time Theodoric of Freiberg in Germany reached the same conclusion by the same kind of experiment. There is no sign either knew of the other.

lights.t: The Book of Optics reached Kepler through a Basel printer
lights.s: Ibn al-Haytham finished his Book of Optics in Cairo in the 1020s. Around 1200 it was translated into Latin under the name Alhazen, and it became the foundation of the subject in Europe. Roger Bacon used it, Witelo rewrote it at length, and John Peckham made a students' textbook out of it that was copied for two hundred years. In 1572 a printer at Basel, Friedrich Risner, issued the Latin Alhazen and Witelo together in a single volume. That book was on Kepler's desk. His own optics of 1604 is titled as a set of additions to Witelo, and it corrects Ibn al-Haytham on how the eye forms an image while working entirely inside the tradition that his book began.

lights.t: Many of the brightest stars still carry Arabic names
lights.s: Look up on a clear night and you are mostly reading Arabic. Altair is al-nasr al-ta'ir, the flying eagle, and Vega is al-nasr al-waqi, the swooping one, two birds on opposite banks of the Milky Way. Aldebaran is al-dabaran, the follower, because it rises behind the Pleiades. Deneb is a tail, Rigel a foot, Fomalhaut the mouth of the fish, Algol the ghoul. Some are worn past recognition. Betelgeuse is usually explained as a misreading of the Arabic for the hand of the Jawza, one letter taken for another by a copyist. The names entered Latin through translations of Ptolemy and through star tables, and when the International Astronomical Union began fixing official spellings in 2016, a large share of the list was Arabic.
lights.d: Star names in English · from Arabic star lists

lights.t: Europe read his geography for centuries under a wrong name
lights.s: Al-Idrisi finished his geography for Roger II of Sicily in January 1154. Its structure is a grid: the inhabited world divided into seven bands of climate, each band cut into ten sections, giving seventy sectional maps that fit together into one map of the world, with a chapter of description for each. Fewer than a dozen manuscripts survive. In 1592 an abridged Arabic version was printed at Rome, among the first Arabic books printed in Europe with movable type. A Latin translation followed in 1619, and its editors, not knowing who had written it, called it the Geographia Nubiensis. For most of two centuries European scholars cited an anonymous geographer from Nubia who had never existed.

lights.t: An admiral wrote sailing directions for every Mediterranean harbour
lights.s: Piri Reis is remembered for a fragment of a world map, but his working book was the Kitab-i Bahriye, the Book of the Sea. He compiled it in 1521 and expanded it in 1526 for Sultan Suleiman: around two hundred charts of the Mediterranean coasts, harbour by harbour, each with facing text on the depths, the anchorages, the currents and the winds, where to take on water and where the rocks lie. It is a pilot's manual rather than a display piece, and much of it records what he had seen himself in a lifetime at sea. He was executed at Cairo around 1553, in his eighties, after a campaign in the Gulf went wrong. Copies of the book kept being made regardless.

lights.t: Columbus sailed on a number he had converted wrongly
lights.s: Al-Farghani wrote an introduction to astronomy at Baghdad in the 830s, thirty short chapters with almost no mathematics in them, which is exactly why it served as the standard textbook for seven hundred years. Translated twice into Latin in the twelfth century, it is where Dante took his figures for the size of the heavens. It also carried the caliph al-Ma'mun's measurement of the earth, given as fifty six and two thirds miles to one degree of latitude. Those were Arabic miles, longer than Roman ones. Columbus, working from that figure, used the shorter mile, and so calculated an earth about a quarter smaller than it is, with Asia correspondingly nearer. How much was error and how much was wishful thinking is still argued.

lights.t: A Toledo instrument maker ended up correcting Ptolemy
lights.s: Al-Zarqali began as a metalworker in Toledo, making instruments to order for the astronomers of the city, who noticed how well he understood what he was building and gave him books. He went on to lead the group that produced the Toledan Tables around 1070. Translated into Latin, those were the tables Europe used for two centuries, until the Alfonsine Tables replaced them, and those were compiled in the same city. He tracked the slow drift of the point where the sun is furthest from the earth, which al-Battani had shown was moving but had not measured. He also designed an astrolabe plate that works at any latitude, as did a contemporary in Toledo, so a traveller no longer needed a separate disc for every city.

lights.t: Hospitals were paid for by endowments, not by patients
lights.s: The bimaristan, from a Persian word meaning place of the sick, was funded by waqf, a permanent endowment. A donor signed over shops, farms or a bathhouse, and the rent paid the staff and the drugs from then on. The deed set the rules, and several survive. The Adudi hospital in Baghdad opened around 981 and Nur al-Din's in Damascus in 1154, and both had wards divided by complaint, including for mental illness, with salaried physicians, oculists, surgeons, bone setters and pharmacists, a kitchen and a library. Treatment was free because the endowment said so, not because a state had decided to provide health care.
