The system depended on wealthy people wanting a charity that outlived them, and it decayed wherever the endowments were seized or lost.

lights.t: Al-Razi wrote down the cases where he was wrong
lights.s: Abu Bakr al-Razi, born in Rayy near modern Tehran in the middle of the ninth century, ran hospitals there and in Baghdad. The book he is best known for, the Hawi, was not written by him for readers. After his death his students assembled it from his working notebooks, which is why it reads as it does: an authority quoted, then Greek and Indian opinion, then a mark meaning mine, followed by what he had seen at the bedside. His case notes record particular patients, the treatment given and whether it worked, including the times it did not. He also wrote a book of doubts about Galen, arguing that medicine advances only when a physician trusts a careful observation over a great name, and that Galen's own method demanded it.
lights.d: Al-Razi · Rayy and Baghdad, died c. 925

lights.t: The first book to tell smallpox from measles
lights.s: Al-Razi's treatise on smallpox and measles sets the two diseases side by side and separates them by what a physician can see and ask: the pattern of fever, the back pain, the state of the eyes, the itching in the nose, how the eruption comes on and how it differs between the two. It is the earliest known clinical account to distinguish them. His management is practical, and much of it is about protecting the eyes, because blindness was the outcome he was trying to prevent. He had no notion of a virus and explained both diseases by the humoral theory of his day, which was wrong. The value of the book is the description, and it was accurate enough that European physicians kept printing it from the fifteenth century into the nineteenth.

lights.t: One textbook was taught in Europe for six centuries
lights.s: Ibn Sina finished the Canon of Medicine around 1025. It is five books: general principles, some eight hundred simple drugs, diseases taken organ by organ from head to foot, diseases affecting the whole body, and a formulary of compound remedies. Its success was organisation. What Greek, Persian, Indian and Arabic medicine held was arranged so that a physician could find the passage he needed, which made it teachable. Gerard of Cremona translated it at Toledo in the twelfth century, it was printed in Latin in the 1470s, and it was still set reading in Italian and French medical faculties in the sixteenth century. That was also the trouble with it. A book good enough to be the syllabus is a book people stop testing, and physicians from Ibn al-Nafis onward had to argue against it.
lights.d: Ibn Sina · Canon of Medicine, c. 1025

lights.t: Ibn Sina set the conditions for judging a drug
lights.s: In the second book of the Canon, Ibn Sina asks how anybody can know that a drug works, and lays down conditions. The drug must be pure and unspoiled, so that nothing else is being tested. It must be tried on a single disease and not on a mixture of complaints. Its strength must be matched against the strength of the illness. The time it takes to act must be noted. The effect must appear again and again in many cases, because a result seen once may be chance. And the trial must be made on human beings, since what a drug does to a horse proves nothing about a man. This is not a controlled trial, and there is no comparison group anywhere in it. It is a set of rules for not being fooled.
lights.d: Ibn Sina · Canon, Book Two, c. 1025

lights.t: Nobody knows whether Europe read Ibn al-Nafis on the heart
lights.s: Writing in Cairo around 1242, Ibn al-Nafis said that the wall between the two sides of the heart is solid, that no blood seeps through it, and that blood must therefore travel from the right chamber out to the lungs, mix with air there, and return to the left. Three centuries later Michael Servetus in 1553 and Realdo Colombo in 1559 described the same route in Europe. Whether they knew of him is an open question. A Venetian physician, Andrea Alpago, had spent about thirty years in Damascus and translated Ibn al-Nafis into Latin, printed in Venice in the 1540s, so a channel existed. No European text of the period cites him, and independent rediscovery is entirely possible. Historians have argued both sides since an Egyptian doctor found the Arabic passage in a Berlin manuscript in 1924.

lights.t: He tried the operation on a goat first
lights.s: Abu Marwan ibn Zuhr, who died at Seville around 1162, is the plainest experimenter in Andalusi medicine. Before performing a tracheotomy on a person he did it on a goat, watched the animal recover, and only then accepted the procedure. For patients who could not swallow he fed them through a silver tube into the gullet, and by nutrient enema. He wrote his book of particular treatments, the Taysir, at the request of his friend Ibn Rushd, who was writing the general work and wanted the practical half from a man who actually saw patients. Ibn Zuhr is often credited with the first description of the mite that causes scabies. The passage is short, and historians disagree about whether it says what modern readers want it to say.

lights.t: Only one of his thirty volumes is about surgery
lights.s: Al-Zahrawi worked at Madinat al-Zahra outside Cordoba and finished his medical encyclopedia, the Tasrif, around the year 1000. It runs to thirty treatises, and the famous one is the last: surgery, with about two hundred instruments drawn on the page so that a reader could have them made. The other twenty nine are the ordinary business of medicine, on diet, on drugs and how to prepare them, on childbirth, on the teeth, and a long section on what would now be called cosmetics, which he treated as a branch of medicine rather than a vanity. Gerard of Cremona translated the surgical volume at Toledo, and it remained the standard surgical text in Europe for roughly five hundred years, printed in Latin under the name Albucasis.

lights.t: A surgeon in Cordoba stitched with thread the body dissolves
lights.s: Animal gut had been used as thread before al-Zahrawi. What he set down, in the surgical volume of the Tasrif, was its use inside the body, where the point is that the thread is absorbed and nothing has to be taken out again. He describes closing a wound with two needles on one thread, using the mandibles of large ants as clips to hold the edges of a torn intestine, tying off a bleeding vessel, and cauterising. He also describes a family whose boys bled to death from small cuts, which is often read as the earliest clinical account of an inherited bleeding disorder. His warning to readers was blunt: anyone who cuts without knowing anatomy will kill the patient, and in his day almost nobody was taught it.

lights.t: Pharmacy split from medicine and got its own book
lights.s: Sabur ibn Sahl, a physician who died in 869, compiled the earliest known Arabic formulary standing on its own: a book of compound remedies, each with its ingredients, quantities, method of preparation, dose and use. Books of this kind, called aqrabadhin, were kept in hospital pharmacies and copied for the shops, and later hospitals commissioned their own. The trade was policed from outside. A market inspector, the muhtasib, checked the apothecaries, and the surviving inspection manuals tell him how to detect a drug cut with something cheaper, how to test weights, and which substitutions count as fraud. Making up medicines had become a separate occupation from prescribing them, with its own literature, its own shops and its own ways of being caught out.

lights.t: Baghdad examined its physicians after one patient died
lights.s: The physician and historian Ibn abi Usaybi'a, writing in the thirteenth century, reports that in 931 a man in Baghdad died through a practitioner's mistake, and the caliph al-Muqtadir ordered that nobody practise medicine until examined. The task went to Sinan ibn Thabit, of a famous scholarly family, who tested the practitioners of the city and is said to have passed more than eight hundred and sixty. Those who failed were barred, with exemptions for physicians of established reputation. Sinan also arranged for doctors to visit prisons and sent staffed dispensaries out to the villages of the Iraqi countryside. The account is a later one and the round number should be read as a round number, but the principle in it is clear: a licence to practise, granted by examination.
lights.d: Baghdad · 931 CE, reported by Ibn abi Usaybi'a

lights.t: He walked from Malaga to Damascus collecting plants
lights.s: Ibn al-Baytar was born at Malaga near the end of the twelfth century, learned botany in Seville, then worked his way east through North Africa, Egypt, Syria and Anatolia, collecting and identifying plants and questioning the people who used them. He ended as chief herbalist to the ruler of Egypt and died in Damascus in 1248. His compendium of simple drugs lists roughly fourteen hundred substances, several hundred of them not described in Arabic before, arranged alphabetically, with earlier authorities named and his own findings marked as his own. Where he had checked a claim in the field and found it false, he said so. It stayed the fullest work of its kind in any language for centuries, and botanists were still mining it for identifications in the nineteenth.
lights.d: Ibn al-Baytar · Malaga to Damascus, died 1248

lights.t: What the surgeons used for pain is less than claimed
lights.s: It is often said that Muslim surgeons invented general anaesthesia. What the sources attest is narrower and worth knowing accurately. Opium, henbane, mandrake and related drugs were given to dull pain and make a patient drowsy, and recipes exist for a sponge soaked in a decoction, dried, then moistened and held under the nose. Recipes of that kind appear in Latin and in Arabic medical writing in overlapping centuries, and which way they travelled is not settled. There is no evidence of measured dosing, of controlled unconsciousness, or of anything a modern anaesthetist would recognise. The surgical texts assume a patient who feels the operation, work to keep it short, and describe assistants holding him still. General anaesthesia arrived in the 1840s with ether, and it was new then.
lights.d: Arabic and Latin surgery · 9th to 13th centuries

lights.t: An Iraqi oculist drew a cataract out through a needle
lights.s: Eye disease was the commonest serious illness across the region, and it produced a specialist, the kahhal, with a literature of his own. Hunayn ibn Ishaq's Ten Treatises on the Eye, from the ninth century, carries what are thought to be the earliest anatomical diagrams of the eye, though the surviving copies are later than the author. Around 1010 Ammar ibn Ali al-Mawsili described removing a soft cataract by suction through a hollow metal needle and named the patients he had done it on. Ali ibn Isa's notebook for oculists, from Baghdad, worked through more than a hundred conditions and was translated into Latin and used for centuries. Pushing the clouded lens aside with a needle was old, Indian and Greek before them. The refinement and the record keeping were theirs.
lights.d: Ammar al-Mawsili and Ali ibn Isa · c. 1000 CE

lights.t: The earliest named Muslim nurse worked in a tent
lights.s: Early biographical works, chiefly Ibn Sa'd's Tabaqat, name a woman of the Aslam tribe, Rufayda al-Aslamiyya, who cared for the wounded in a tent pitched near the Prophet's ﷺ mosque in Madinah, and report that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, wounded at the Battle of the Trench, was placed in her care so that he could be visited. Other women of Madinah are named in the same sources doing similar work. What those reports say is short. The fuller modern picture, of a training school with a syllabus and enrolled students, is a twentieth century elaboration and ought to be labelled as one. The attested part is enough on its own. In the 620s a woman ran a place for treating the injured at the centre of the town, and everybody knew her name.

lights.t: Umar turned an army around at the edge of a plague
lights.s: In 638 plague broke out at Amwas in Syria and killed on a scale the chroniclers count in the tens of thousands, among them the commander Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah. Umar ibn al-Khattab was travelling towards Syria and halted at Sargh on the border. He consulted those with him, and the argument put to him was that to go on was to walk into a plague. When he ordered the return, Abu Ubayda asked whether he was fleeing the decree of God, and Umar answered that he was fleeing from the decree of God to the decree of God. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf then reported the Prophet's ﷺ instruction not to enter a land where plague has broken out, and not to leave it if you are already there. The rule cuts both ways, and Muslim authorities cited it again in 2020.
lights.src: Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Tibb; Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Salam

lights.t: A Granadan doctor argued contagion from what he could see
lights.s: When the Black Death reached Granada in 1348, some scholars argued that a disease cannot pass from person to person, because that would put the cause somewhere other than in the hands of God. Lisan al-Din ibn al-Khatib, vizier and physician, wrote a short treatise in reply. He set out the evidence of the senses: that whoever nurses the sick catches it and whoever stays away does not, that it arrives in a port with a ship, that it runs through a household and through a quarter, that people cut off by desert or by sea escape it. He wrote that a proof drawn from transmitted authority has to be reconsidered when experience contradicts it. His colleague Ibn Khatima wrote a similar account at Almeria the following year. Ibn al-Khatib died in a prison cell in Fez in 1374, in a political quarrel.

lights.t: Three thousand books carry his name and he wrote few
lights.s: Jabir ibn Hayyan is said to have lived in Kufa in the eighth century and to have studied with Ja'far al-Sadiq. Some three thousand treatises circulated under his name. In 1942 the scholar Paul Kraus showed from internal evidence that they cannot be the work of one man of that period: they quote translations made later, and most of the corpus belongs to the late ninth and tenth centuries, the product of a school rather than a person. What the corpus contains is a landmark all the same. Substances are classified, apparatus is described, and procedures are set out in order, calcination, sublimation, crystallisation, distillation. One passage, in Holmyard's translation, says that whoever does not perform practical work and make experiments will never attain the least degree of mastery. The Latin books signed Geber are different works again, written in Europe.

lights.t: The still was Greek, the words for it are Arabic
lights.s: Distilling apparatus existed in Greco-Egyptian alchemy centuries before Islam, and one of its practitioners, Maria the Jewess, is credited with the water bath that a cook still calls a bain-marie. What happened in the Arabic laboratories was refinement and scale: better condensation, glass that would take the heat, and distillation run as an industry for rosewater, essential oils, naphtha and medicines. Al-Razi's book of secrets lists the equipment like a workshop inventory. The vocabulary crossed into Europe with the technique. Alembic is al-anbiq, itself from a Greek word. Alkali is al-qali, the ash of a saltwort plant. Elixir is al-iksir. Alcohol is al-kuhl, which meant the fine dark powder used on the eyes and came to mean the spirit of wine only later, in European usage.

lights.t: A philosopher wrote a hundred recipes for perfume
lights.s: Al-Kindi, the first of the major philosophers to write in Arabic, also wrote the Book of the Chemistry of Perfume and Distillations. It survives in a single manuscript in Istanbul and was edited and translated into German by Karl Garbers in 1948. It holds more than a hundred recipes and methods: aromatic waters and oils, the apparatus, the timings, and a section of substitutes, cheaper imitations of costly scents and medicines for people who could not pay for the real thing. He treated smell as a manufacturing problem with quantities in it. He did something similar in another work on compound drugs, trying to put numbers to how the strengths of the ingredients in a mixture add up, one of the first attempts to make pharmacy arithmetic rather than judgement.

lights.t: Frequency analysis came out of Arabic dictionary work
lights.s: Counting letters was a habit of Arabic linguistics before it was a weapon. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, who died around 786, built the first Arabic dictionary by working through the permutations of the roots, and is credited with a book on ciphers that has not survived. Scholars of the Qur'an counted words and letters as a matter of course. So when al-Kindi wrote his treatise on deciphering messages in the ninth century, he could assume readers who already thought of a language as a distribution: take a long ordinary text, count how often each letter occurs, count the symbols in the cipher, and match them in order. The tradition ran on for centuries through Ibn Adlan and Ibn al-Durayhim into the Ottoman chancery manuals. Al-Kindi's own treatise was thought lost until a copy turned up in an Istanbul archive in 1987.
lights.d: Al-Khalil to Ibn al-Durayhim · 8th to 14th c.

lights.t: Three brothers designed machines that regulated themselves
lights.s: Muhammad, Ahmad and al-Hasan, the sons of Musa ibn Shakir, were astronomers and patrons in ninth century Baghdad who paid translators out of their own pockets. Around 850 they produced the Book of Ingenious Devices, about a hundred machines. Most are vessels and fountains that do something unexpected, which makes them look like toys, and the surprise is nearly always a hidden control: a float that rises with the liquid and closes a valve, a siphon that empties a chamber at a set level, a lamp that trims its own wick and draws up its own oil. That is feedback, a machine holding a condition steady with no hand on it. They also describe a grab for lifting objects off a riverbed. Donald Hill translated the book into English in 1979.

lights.t: His famous crank turns up on a Roman relief
lights.s: Al-Jazari, chief engineer to the Artuqid court at Diyarbakir, finished his book of mechanical devices in 1206 with instructions detailed enough to build from, and wrote that he described nothing he had not made himself. Historians of technology long credited him with the earliest known crank and connecting rod, the linkage in his twin cylinder pump that turns rotation into a push and a pull. Then a carved relief from Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, studied and published in the 2000s, showed a water powered stone saw using the same linkage in the third century of the common era. The credit for the mechanism moves back. What does not move is the book: the earliest surviving set of engineering drawings that explains segmental gears, cams and valves well enough for somebody else to copy.

lights.t: A Persian water tunnel older than Islam spread west with it
lights.s: A qanat is a tunnel driven gently downhill from groundwater under a hillside out to the fields, so that water arrives by gravity and does not evaporate on the way. A line of vertical shafts marks its course across the desert, sunk to lift out the spoil and to let the diggers breathe. The technique is Iranian and pre-Islamic, at least two and a half thousand years old, and the one at Gonabad is still delivering water. Under Muslim rule it spread east and west and took local names: falaj in Oman, foggara in Algeria, khettara in Morocco, karez further east. Madrid drank from galleries of this kind into the nineteenth century. Around the year 1000 the mathematician al-Karaji wrote a book on finding hidden water and building these tunnels, with surveying instruments and rules for ventilation.
lights.d: Qanats · Iran and westward, from c. 500 BCE

lights.t: The water wheel came west and left its words behind
lights.s: Two machines raised water from Iran to Spain. The saqiya is a chain of pots turned by an ox through right angled gearing. The noria is a wheel with pots on its rim, driven by the current of the river itself and needing no animal at all. Seventeen of them still stand at Hama on the Orontes in Syria, the largest about twenty metres across, and they groan as they turn. They were not new in the Islamic period: a mosaic at Apamea, dated 469, already shows one. What the Muslim centuries added was their spread and the law of water shares that went with them, measured in time rather than volume. The words travelled too. Spanish noria is na'ura and acequia is al-saqiya, and irrigation ditches in New Mexico are still called acequias and still run by their own elected associations.

lights.t: The oldest windmills stood on a plain of constant wind
lights.s: In Sistan, on what is now the border of Iran and Afghanistan, a wind blows from the north for about a hundred and twenty days each summer, and the mills built there were made for it. They turn on a vertical shaft, sails set like doors inside a walled housing that funnels the wind onto one side of them, with the millstone below. Arabic geographers of the ninth and tenth centuries describe the windmills of the region as a known feature. Mills of the same design at Nashtifan in eastern Iran are still standing and were still grinding within living memory. European windmills, which appear in the records of the 1180s, turn on a horizontal shaft and are a different machine, so most historians treat them as a separate development rather than a borrowing.
lights.d: Sistan and Nashtifan · attested from the 9th c.

lights.t: The story of papermakers captured at Talas is probably legend
lights.s: Papermaking is Chinese. The usual account of how it reached the Muslim world says that Chinese papermakers taken prisoner at the battle of Talas in 751 taught the craft at Samarkand. That story is first told by al-Tha'alibi, writing nearly three hundred years afterwards, and historians of the subject now doubt it, because paper was already circulating in Central Asia before 751 and one group of captives is a thin explanation for an industry. The route and the consequence are not in doubt. Samarkand paper became famous, a mill was working in Baghdad by the 790s, and the craft moved on to Damascus, Cairo, Fez, then Xativa in Spain and Fabriano in Italy. Arabic papermakers worked from rags and linen rather than bark, and Europe received paper through their mills rather than from China directly.

lights.t: The flap on an old book cover is structural, not decoration
lights.s: The Islamic book got a binding of its own. Its boards are pasteboard, layers of waste paper pasted up rather than the wooden boards of the European codex, so the book is light. The sewing runs without cords across the spine, which leaves the back flat. The cover has a fifth part, a flap that comes off the back board, crosses the fore edge and tucks under the front, closing the book against dust and holding the text block square. Books were shelved flat, so titles were written on the fore edge rather than the spine. Decoration was stamped into damp leather with cut brass tools and, from the fifteenth century, tooled in gold. Historians of binding trace European gold tooling back to these workshops, reaching Italy by way of Venice and Naples.

lights.t: Muslin, damask and mohair are place names or Arabic words
lights.s: Textiles were the largest manufacturing industry of the medieval Muslim world, and the trade left its vocabulary in European languages. Muslin is named for Mosul and damask for Damascus. Mohair is mukhayyar, meaning choice or selected. Taffeta is the Persian taftah. Cotton is qutn, and sash is shash, a length of fine cloth wound as a turban. Some other favourites are guesswork: gauze from Gaza and satin from the Arabic name for the Chinese port of Quanzhou are marked uncertain in the dictionaries, and should be repeated with that attached. State workshops wove bands of inscription, tiraz, into robes, naming the ruler and the year, and a robe from the ruler's own wardrobe was a political act as much as a gift. The dyers left words as well. Crimson comes through Arabic qirmiz, the insect that gave the red.

lights.t: Damascus steel was made from Indian ingots and analysed in 2006
lights.s: The watered blades were forged at Damascus, Isfahan and elsewhere, but the steel itself arrived as cakes of crucible metal from southern India and Sri Lanka, the material English writers called wootz. The pattern in the finished blade comes from bands of carbide in the metal. The technique lapsed in the eighteenth century, and the best explanation offered is that a particular ore, carrying the trace elements that make those bands form, stopped coming through the trade. In 2006 a group at Dresden dissolved a fragment of a seventeenth century sabre in acid and reported carbon nanotubes and cementite nanowires in what was left, published in Nature. The finding is real; what it means is argued over, and nobody claims the smiths knew. They knew which ore, which heat, and how slowly to let it cool.
lights.d: Wootz steel · India to Damascus, analysed 2006

lights.t: He named a new science before writing the history
lights.s: The Muqaddimah is only the introduction to Ibn Khaldun's history, and it is the part still read. In it he announces a subject nobody had named, the science of human social organisation, and then sets about doing it. He argues that a state's revenue is largest when its rates of tax are low and shrinks as the rates rise, an observation Arthur Laffer credited to him when the same idea shaped American tax argument in the 1980s. He explains prices by supply and by the labour inside a good. He tests old chronicles against what an economy could actually feed and rejects their numbers as impossible. He also reasons from climate to character in ways no reader accepts now. The book was translated into French in the 1860s and into English by Franz Rosenthal in 1958.

lights.t: The first great travel book was written as penance
lights.s: Ibn Jubayr, a secretary in Granada, set out for Makkah in 1183 and came back two years later by way of Baghdad, Damascus, Acre and Sicily. He wrote it up day by day, and the result set the shape of the rihla, the travel book, for everybody after him, including Ibn Battuta, who copied passages from it without saying so. The story that he went in penance, having been made to drink wine by his governor, is told in the sources and may well be true. What makes the book unusual is that he wrote down things that did not suit him. Passing through Crusader ruled Palestine he found Muslim farmers under Frankish lords paying a fixed tax and otherwise left alone, said their condition looked better than that of their brothers under Muslim lords, and admitted that it troubled him.

lights.t: Ibn Battuta did not write the book that carries his name
lights.s: In 1355 at Fez, on the order of the sultan, Ibn Battuta dictated his travels to a young literary scholar, Ibn Juzayy, who wrote them up and said openly that he had polished the language. He also lifted long passages describing Damascus and Makkah straight out of Ibn Jubayr, writing a century and a half earlier, which was ordinary practice then and is disconcerting now. Nothing in Ibn Battuta's own hand survives, and he was recalling three decades of travel with few notes. Historians therefore argue about particular stretches: whether he really reached Bulghar on the Volga, how much of China he saw, how the Anatolian dates fit together. It remains the fullest description of the fourteenth century Muslim world anybody left, and it has to be read knowing how it was made.

lights.t: A Seville farmer wrote down what he had actually grown
lights.s: Ibn al-Awwam's Book of Agriculture, written near Seville in the later twelfth century, is the longest farming manual to survive from the medieval world. It covers roughly five hundred and eighty five plants and fifty fruit trees, with chapters on soils and how to judge them by hand and by taste, on manures, on grafting, on irrigation, on pests, on cattle and on bees. He names the authorities he is drawing on, among them Ibn Bassal, who had run the royal garden at Toledo and written from what he grew, and he marks his own trials separately: this I have tested. A Spanish translation appeared in Madrid in 1802 and a French one in the 1860s, and nineteenth century agronomists read them for practical advice rather than as history.

lights.t: Historians still argue whether there was a farming revolution
lights.s: In 1974 the economic historian Andrew Watson proposed that between the eighth and the tenth centuries a group of crops moved west across the Muslim world and changed how land was worked: sugar cane, cotton, rice, hard wheat, citrus, bananas, aubergines, spinach, watermelon, together with irrigation that allowed a summer crop where the fields had rested. He called it an agricultural revolution and the phrase stuck. Michael Decker and others have since argued from archaeology and from Roman farming manuals that several of those crops were already grown in the Roman east, so what happened was spread and intensification rather than novelty. The argument is not settled. Both sides agree the crops and the irrigation moved, that the Arabic farming manuals record real practice, and that much of it ended up in Spain and then in the Americas.

lights.t: The Qur'an was gathered into one book after a battle
lights.s: After the battle of Yamama in the year 12 of the Hijra, in which a large number of those who had memorised the Qur'an were killed, Umar ibn al-Khattab went to the caliph Abu Bakr and pressed him to have the text collected in one place. Abu Bakr sent for Zayd ibn Thabit, who had written down revelation for the Prophet ﷺ. Zayd's own account, preserved by al-Bukhari, says he found the task heavier than being asked to move a mountain, and that he gathered the Qur'an from palm stalks, thin white stones and the chests of men who had learned it. The sheets he produced stayed with Abu Bakr, then Umar, then Umar's daughter Hafsa.
lights.d: Zayd ibn Thabit · Madinah, c. 633 CE

lights.t: Uthman sent a master copy to each garrison city
lights.s: Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman came back from campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan alarmed at how differently the soldiers from Syria and Iraq were reciting. He went straight to the caliph Uthman and asked him to save the community before it split over its book the way earlier communities had split over theirs. Uthman borrowed the sheets held by Hafsa, had copies made by a small committee that again included Zayd ibn Thabit, and sent one to each of the main centres with a reciter to teach from it. Other manuscripts in circulation were withdrawn. Every printed Qur'an descends from that decision, taken by a man who had watched an army argue on the road home.
lights.d: Uthman ibn Affan · Madinah, c. 650 CE

lights.t: The book makes a claim about its own survival
lights.s: In Surah al-Hijr the Qur'an calls itself al-Dhikr, the Reminder, and says that it was sent down and that its keeping is undertaken by the One who sent it. The sentence is short and it is not a claim about paper. Muslims read it as covering the whole apparatus that grew around the text: children who learn it by heart before they can parse it, chains of teachers who will not certify a student until they have heard every letter, the standard copies, the counting of verses, the arguments over a single vowel that were written down rather than suppressed. The verse comes early, in a Makkan chapter, before any of that existed.

lights.t: Birmingham's two leaves belong to a book kept in Paris
lights.s: The two parchment leaves in Birmingham that were radiocarbon dated in 2015 to between 568 and 645 CE are not a stray find. Alba Fedeli identified them during doctoral work as having been bound by mistake into a different manuscript, and François Déroche of the Collège de France confirmed that they belong with sixteen leaves in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, catalogued as Arabe 328(c). One codex, eighteen surviving leaves, split between two European cities and reunited on paper rather than in a case. The Birmingham pages carry part of Surah al-Kahf, the closing verses of Surah Maryam, and the opening forty verses of Surah Ta-Ha.

lights.t: A wall in Sana'a gave up a paper hoard in 1972
lights.s: In 1972 workers repairing the roof of the Great Mosque of Sana'a in Yemen broke into the space between the ceiling and the roof and found it packed with old parchment and paper. The material was swept into sacks and left on a staircase. A conservation project funded by the German foreign ministry ran from 1980 to 1989, with the conservator Ursula Dreibholz sorting and flattening fragments, and it recovered tens of thousands of pieces from what had served as the mosque's store for worn out copies of scripture, which are set aside rather than destroyed. Among them are some of the earliest Qur'anic manuscripts known anywhere, kept safe by being walled up and forgotten.

lights.t: One Sana'a manuscript was written over an older text
lights.s: One of the Sana'a manuscripts is a palimpsest: the parchment was scraped clean and reused, and ultraviolet imaging brings back the erased lower layer. That lower text is Qur'anic, but it puts the chapters in a different order and differs from the standard text in wording at many points, mostly in ways that do not change the sense. Scholars read it as a companion's personal codex from before Uthman standardised copies, of the kind the early sources describe and name. What follows from that is argued over, from confirmation of the sources' own account to much wider claims. A leaf from the same manuscript was radiocarbon dated to between 578 and 669 CE with 95 per cent probability.

lights.t: A Tübingen fragment holds a quarter of the Qur'an
lights.s: The university library at Tübingen holds a Qur'anic manuscript catalogued as Ma VI 165, which reached Germany through the nineteenth century consul and collector Johann Gottfried Wetzstein. In 2014 the library published radiocarbon results for it: 649 to 675 CE with 95.4 per cent probability, which places the parchment within about forty years of the Prophet's death. The fragment is not a scrap. It runs continuously from Surah al-Isra to Surah Ya-Sin, roughly a quarter of the whole text, in an early script with sparse dotting. Radiocarbon dates the animal skin and not the ink, so it gives an earliest possible date rather than an exact one, and that caution belongs on every result of the kind.

lights.t: The Istanbul codex called Uthman's was written later
lights.s: Topkapi Palace in Istanbul holds a very large early Qur'an, missing only two pages of the entire text, which tradition names as one of the copies Uthman had made. The Turkish scholar Tayyar Altikulac produced a full facsimile and study of it, and later work has gone further. The vowel marking and the dotting it carries were developed after Uthman's lifetime, and the letter forms point to the eighth century rather than the seventh. Manuscripts in Istanbul, Cairo, Tashkent and Mashhad all carry the same attribution and none of them survives that test. They are genuinely early and genuinely important. What is disputed is the label, not the age.

lights.t: A Qur'an went from Samarkand to Russia and back
lights.s: The Samarkand codex, a large Kufic Qur'an long said to be Uthman's own copy, was kept at a shrine in Samarkand and was believed to have been brought there by Timur. After the Russian capture of Samarkand in 1868 a Russian general acquired it and sent it to the Imperial Library in Saint Petersburg. Following the revolution it was handed back to Muslims in Ufa, and after petitions from Turkestan it reached Tashkent in 1924, where about a third of it is kept at the Hast Imam library. Leaves from the same manuscript are now in New York, Toronto, Doha, Paris and Gotha. Radiocarbon and letter forms both place it well after Uthman's death.

lights.t: The Qur'an most people read was typeset over seventeen years
lights.s: In 1907 the Egyptian government set a committee of scholars from al-Azhar to work on a reliable printed Qur'an for state schools, where the copies in use were full of errors. The senior reciter Muhammad ibn Ali al-Husayni al-Haddad was among the leading figures. The edition appeared in July 1924 from the government press in Cairo. It follows the reading of Hafs from Asim, uses the Kufan way of dividing and numbering the verses, and fixes the pause marks and the spelling. It was not a new text. It was a decision about which inherited conventions to print, and almost every Qur'an published since, by Sunni and Shia publishers alike, follows it.

lights.t: The first printed Arabic Qur'an survives in a single copy
lights.s: Paganino and Alessandro Paganini printed an Arabic Qur'an in Venice between August 1537 and August 1538, the first anywhere produced with movable type. It was a commercial venture, apparently aimed at markets in the Ottoman lands, and it failed. The typesetting was full of errors, some of them mangling the Arabic beyond use, which made it worthless to any Muslim buyer. For centuries it was thought every copy had been destroyed, and a story circulated that the pope had ordered them burned. In 1987 the scholar Angela Nuovo found a surviving copy in the library of the Franciscan friars on the island of San Michele in Venice, where it had sat for four hundred years.

lights.t: A blind Andalusian put the seven readings into verse
lights.s: Qasim ibn Firruh al-Shatibi was born in Xativa in eastern al-Andalus in 538 of the Hijra, which is 1144 CE, and the biographers describe him as blind. He settled in Egypt and died there in 1194. His contribution was a poem, Hirz al-Amani, known to every student as the Shatibiyya, which takes the technical detail of the seven canonical readings and encodes it in over a thousand lines of rhymed verse, using letter symbols to stand for the readers so that the metre holds. Students still memorise it before they are permitted to teach the readings. A body of exact technical information was made portable by being turned into something a person can sing.

lights.t: The first words revealed sit at chapter ninety six
lights.s: The Qur'an is not arranged in the order it came down. Its 114 chapters run roughly from longest to shortest, with al-Baqarah at 286 verses near the front and the three verse al-Kawthar near the back. The passage identified as the first revelation, five verses opening with the command to read, sits at chapter 96, close to the end of the book. Some of the last material revealed is found in the middle. The effect is that a reader meets the material by theme rather than by date, and anyone who wants the historical sequence has to reconstruct it, which is what the science of the occasions of revelation was built to do.

lights.t: The Qur'an names one of its own chapters in passing
lights.s: In Surah al-Hijr, a Makkan chapter, the Prophet ﷺ is told that he has been given seven of the oft repeated, and the great Qur'an. Commentators from the earliest period read the seven as the seven verses of al-Fatiha, the short opening chapter recited in every unit of every prayer. The phrase gives that chapter one of its many names, al-Sab al-Mathani. It is also called Umm al-Kitab, the mother of the book, and al-Shifa, the cure. Anyone praying the five obligatory prayers recites it seventeen times a day. It is spoken from the reader upward, praise and then request, which is unusual in a book that mostly speaks downward.

lights.t: The longest verse in the Qur'an is about debt
lights.s: Verse 282 of Surah al-Baqarah is the longest single verse in the Qur'an, longer than most of the short chapters. Its subject is not prayer or paradise. It is a commercial instruction: when you contract a debt for a fixed term, write it down, let a scribe write it justly, let the one who owes dictate, bring witnesses, and do not think it beneath you to write it down whether the sum is small or large. The verse anticipates objections, allows for a debtor who cannot dictate, and permits a pledge instead of a written record when travelling. The most space given to any one subject in a single verse goes to keeping an accurate record of what one person owes another.

lights.t: Different cities counted the verses differently
lights.s: Printed Qur'ans following the Cairo edition give 6,236 verses. Other totals circulate, and they come from old regional traditions of verse division associated with Kufa, Basra, Madinah, Makkah and Damascus, which differ from one another by a few dozen. The difference is never about the words. It is about where one verse stops and the next begins: whether a phrase closes one verse or opens the next, and whether the opening formula counts as a verse of the chapter. Reciters were trained in one system and transmitted it. Anyone comparing two translations that give different numbers for the same sentence is looking at the tail of an argument between early schools of recitation.

lights.t: Some chapters are built as a ring around a centre
lights.s: Hamiduddin Farahi, an Indian scholar who died in 1930, argued that each chapter of the Qur'an has a single organising theme and a deliberate shape, and his student Amin Ahsan Islahi worked the idea through the whole book in an Urdu commentary. Later scholars, among them Michel Cuypers on Surah al-Ma'ida and Raymond Farrin on al-Baqarah, have described the pattern as ring composition: sections mirror each other outward from a middle, so that the first answers the last and the pivot sits at the centre. The approach is one reading among several and is contested. What it does is treat the jumps between subjects as a shape to be found rather than a defect to be explained.

lights.t: Most chapter names come from one word, not the theme
lights.s: Surah al-Baqarah is called the Cow after an episode of seven verses in a chapter of 286, in which Musa tells his people to sacrifice a cow and they ask a series of questions to avoid doing it. Surah al-Nahl is the Bee, from two verses about where the bee is taught to build. Surah al-Naml is the Ant, from a single ant who warns her colony to get out of Sulayman's way. Surah al-Ankabut is the Spider, from one image of a fragile house. The names work like handles. They pick a word that appears nowhere nearby, so anyone can find the chapter. They are not summaries, and reading them as summaries misleads.
lights.d: Chapter names taken from a rare word

lights.t: Only one woman is named in the Qur'an
lights.s: Chapter 19 is called Maryam, and Mary is the only woman in the Qur'an referred to by her own name. Every other woman appears by relation: the wife of Imran, the wife of Fir'awn, the queen who came to Sulayman, the mothers and daughters and wives of prophets. Maryam is named directly, and the chapter carrying her name opens with the birth of Yahya and then gives her the longest continuous account of any woman in the book, including her withdrawal to a distant place, the palm tree, and her return to her people carrying the child. She is also the one person told she has been chosen above the women of the worlds.

lights.t: One Qur'an in Ibn al-Bawwab's hand survives, in Dublin
lights.s: Ibn al-Bawwab worked in Baghdad around the year 1000 and took the proportional system of Ibn Muqla and made it supple. Contemporaries said he was a doorkeeper's son who learned to decorate rooms, then to write, and that he could match another calligrapher's hand well enough to replace a missing volume without anyone noticing. Of everything he wrote, one complete Qur'an survives carrying his name, copied in Baghdad in the year 391 of the Hijra, which is 1000 to 1001 CE. It is the earliest surviving Qur'an in naskh, the cursive book hand that took over from angular Kufic for scripture. It has been in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin since the collector acquired it.

lights.t: Umar tried to stop a man reciting and was corrected
lights.s: Umar ibn al-Khattab heard Hisham ibn Hakim reciting Surah al-Furqan in a way he had not been taught. He waited for the prayer to finish, took him by the cloak and marched him to the Prophet ﷺ. Both men recited. Both were told they were right. The Prophet ﷺ then said the Qur'an was sent down in seven ahruf and they should recite whichever was easier. What an harf is has been argued for twelve centuries: dialects, wordings, a category of permitted variation, something else again. Al-Suyuti collected dozens of opinions on it. The report stands in the strongest collections, and its plain effect was to license difference in a community newly unified around a book.

lights.t: A Baghdad scholar chose seven readings out of many
lights.s: Around the year 930 in Baghdad, Ibn Mujahid wrote Kitab al-Sab'a, the Book of the Seven, in which he selected seven reciters whose readings he judged both soundly transmitted and widely followed, and set out their differences systematically. He took three from Kufa and one each from Makkah, Madinah, Basra and Damascus, so the geography of the early community was represented. His seven were not the only readings in use and he never claimed they were. The number stuck anyway, partly because it echoed the report about seven ahruf, and later scholars had to keep explaining that the two sevens are not the same thing. Ibn Mujahid died in 936.

lights.t: The Qur'an in Morocco is recited differently from Egypt
lights.s: Each canonical reading is transmitted through named students, usually two of them, so ten readings arrive as twenty transmissions. The one most of the world reads is Hafs from Asim, both men of Kufa, which the Cairo edition of 1924 printed and which spread with it. In Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania and much of West Africa the reading is Warsh from Nafi of Madinah, and a printed Warsh Qur'an looks noticeably different on the page, with different vowel signs and spellings. Parts of Libya read Qalun from the same Nafi. Sudan and the Horn read al-Duri from Abu Amr. The same text, in more than one transmitted form, on shelves a few hours' flight apart.

lights.t: One man's book settled the readings at ten
lights.s: Ibn al-Jazari, born in Damascus in 1350 and dead in Shiraz in 1429, spent his life on the readings of the Qur'an. He argued that three further readings met the same standards as Ibn Mujahid's seven, and his book al-Nashr fi'l-Qira'at al-Ashr fixed the number at ten, where it has stayed. He set out three tests a reading must pass: it must fit the consonantal skeleton of the Uthmanic copies, it must be defensible in Arabic, and its chain of transmission must be sound. He also compiled Ghayat al-Nihaya, a biographical dictionary of thousands of reciters listed generation by generation, so that the chains could be checked rather than asserted.

lights.t: The command to recite slowly created a whole discipline
lights.s: In an early Makkan chapter addressed to the Prophet ﷺ standing at night, the instruction is to recite the Qur'an in tartil, measured and unhurried. Tajwid, the science that grew from that word, comes from a root meaning to make something well. It is not about having a fine voice. It is a precise phonetic system: which letters are held and for how many counts, where the nasal sound called ghunna is sustained, which consonants merge into the next, which are hidden, which are formed at the back of the tongue against the soft palate. It is taught by ear and corrected by ear, and it has held the pronunciation of a seventh century text steady across languages that contain none of those sounds.

lights.t: Arabic sounds were mapped by where they are made
lights.s: Reciters learn the makharij, the exact points in the mouth and throat where each Arabic consonant is formed, and the sifat, the qualities each sound carries: whether it is voiced, whether air escapes around it, whether the tongue rises behind it. A student is asked to hold a letter and told which surface to touch. The system was worked out by early grammarians and reciters together, and it is the same analysis that let al-Khalil ibn Ahmad order the first Arabic dictionary by the throat rather than the alphabet. Scholars have counted the points differently, and the count used in teaching recitation is seventeen.

lights.t: The small letters above the line tell you where to stop
lights.s: Open a printed Qur'an and small letters float above the text: a mim, a jim, a lam with an alif, a cluster of three dots that appears twice. They are not part of the revealed text. They are pause marks, worked out so that a reciter taking a breath at the end of a phrase does not break the sense, and the system in widest use is credited to Muhammad ibn Tayfur al-Sajawandi, who died in the twelfth century. There is a compulsory stop, a permitted stop, a place where stopping is forbidden, and a pair where you may stop at one but not at both. A reader who ignores them can turn a clause into a sentence that says something else.

lights.t: A reciter's licence lists every teacher back to the source
lights.s: To be certified in recitation a student sits with a teacher and recites the entire Qur'an aloud, letter by letter, and is corrected. At the end the teacher issues an ijaza, a licence, which names the student, names the teacher, then names the teacher's teacher, and continues back through the generations to the Prophet ﷺ. The document is a list of people. Nothing in it rests on a manuscript. The same instrument is used in hadith, and it is why Muslim scholarship produced such large biographical dictionaries: if a chain is a claim, every name in it has to be a person whose dates, teachers and reliability can be checked by somebody else.

lights.t: Printed Qur'ans keep a spelling a thousand years old
lights.s: The consonantal skeleton of the Uthmanic copies is preserved on purpose, even where it no longer matches how Arabic is written. The word salah carries a waw where modern spelling uses an alif. Some words carry a letter nobody pronounces, others drop one that is pronounced. Copyists were instructed not to modernise, and printed editions follow the same rule, adding vowel signs and dots on top of an unchanged skeleton rather than tidying it up. The result is that a page printed in Cairo last year and a seventh century parchment agree letter for letter in their consonants, which is what makes comparing them possible at all.

lights.t: Arabic got its dots and vowels after the Qur'an
lights.s: The earliest Qur'anic manuscripts have almost no dots and no vowel marks. Arabic script distinguishes several consonants only by dots above or below an identical shape, and the short vowels are not written at all, so an unpointed text is a memory aid for somebody who already knows it. The sources credit Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, who died around 688, with introducing coloured dots for the vowels, and reciters working under the governor al-Hajjaj with systematising the consonant dots. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad later replaced the vowel dots with the small shapes still used. Who did what is reported differently in different sources. The order is not in doubt: recitation first, notation built to serve it.

lights.t: He measured letters in dots and lost his writing hand
lights.s: Ibn Muqla was born in Baghdad around 885 and served three times as vizier to the Abbasid caliphs. He is credited with putting Arabic calligraphy on a geometric footing: the rhombic dot made by pressing the reed pen once becomes the unit of measure, the alif is a set number of dots tall, and a circle whose diameter is that alif governs the proportions of every other letter. Scripts written this way were called al-khatt al-mansub, the proportioned hand. Politics ended badly for him. He was imprisoned, his right hand was cut off, his tongue was cut out afterwards, and he died in prison in July 940. His system was still being taught five hundred years later.
lights.d: Ibn Muqla · Baghdad, c. 885 to 940 CE

lights.t: He cut the pen at an angle and changed the letters
lights.s: Yaqut al-Musta'simi was taken as a boy, probably from Amasya in Anatolia, and became secretary to al-Musta'sim, the last Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. When the Mongols took the city in 1258 he is said to have sheltered in a minaret and gone on practising. His technical contribution was small and consequential: he trimmed the nib of the reed pen to an oblique angle instead of a straight one, which varies the thickness of every stroke as the hand turns and gives the letters their tapering weight. He reworked the six standard scripts on that basis, and for two centuries afterwards calligraphers identified themselves by which of his students they descended from.

lights.t: An Ottoman calligrapher copied forty seven Qur'ans
lights.s: Shaykh Hamdullah was born in Amasya in 1436 and knew the future sultan Bayezid II when they were both young men there. When Bayezid took the throne he brought him to Istanbul. In 1485 the sultan set a group of Yaqut al-Musta'simi's writings in front of him and asked for something better. Hamdullah went away, worked, and came back with a reformed naskh that became the Ottoman standard and stayed so into the twentieth century. He is said to have copied forty seven complete Qur'ans. An Ottoman saying held that the Qur'an was revealed in the Hijaz, recited in Egypt and written in Istanbul, and it was Hamdullah's line of students that earned the third clause.

lights.t: Ramadan was when the text was checked against its source
lights.s: Ibn Abbas said the Prophet ﷺ was the most generous of people, and most generous of all in Ramadan, when Jibril used to meet him every night of the month and go through the Qur'an with him. The report sits at the very front of Sahih al-Bukhari, as the sixth hadith in the collection. It is the origin of the tarawih habit of reciting a portion each night until the whole book is finished, and of the practice called mudarasa, in which two people take turns reciting to one another and correcting. The annual review is why Ramadan is a month of recitation and not only a month of hunger.
lights.d: Ibn Abbas, on the Prophet ﷺ in Ramadan

lights.t: One sentence about memory is repeated four times over
lights.s: Surah al-Qamar, the fifty fourth chapter, tells four stories of communities that rejected the messengers sent to them: the people of Nuh, of Hud, of Salih, and of Lut. After each one the same sentence lands. We have made the Qur'an easy to remember, so is there any who will take heed. Four times, unaltered, at verses 17, 22, 32 and 40. The refrain works structurally, closing each panel, and it makes a claim that can be tested. Children who speak no Arabic memorise the entire book, and the number of living people who have done so runs into the millions. Very few texts of that length are carried whole in ordinary memory.

lights.t: The measure given was learning it and passing it on
lights.s: Uthman ibn Affan reported the Prophet ﷺ saying that the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. The sentence is short and its shape is the point: not the one who learns it, and not the one who teaches it, but the one who does both. It became the charter for an institution found in every Muslim town, the kuttab or maktab where children learn to recite before they learn to read. Teachers in that system are often unpaid or barely paid, and the chain of transmission runs through them. A body of knowledge that could have stayed with specialists was made everybody's business by a sentence with two verbs in it.

lights.t: The opening formula appears exactly 114 times
lights.s: Every chapter of the Qur'an opens with the basmala, in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, except chapter 9, Surah al-Tawba, which begins without it. So the formula heads 113 chapters. It occurs once more inside the text, in Surah al-Naml, where the queen of Saba reads out the letter that has reached her and quotes its opening: it is from Sulayman, and it is in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. That brings the total in the book to 114, the number of chapters. The one occurrence that is not a heading is a quotation from a letter between two heads of state.

lights.t: Twenty nine chapters open with letters nobody can explain
lights.s: Alif Lam Mim. Ha Mim. Kaf Ha Ya Ayn Sad. Nun. Twenty nine chapters of the Qur'an begin with strings of disconnected Arabic letters, recited by name rather than sounded as a word. Fourteen of the twenty eight letters are used, in fourteen different combinations, and Alif Lam Mim and Ha Mim each appear six times. The classical commentators offer many readings: names of God, abbreviations, a challenge pointing out that the book is built from the same letters its opponents use, a signal that recitation is beginning. A great many early scholars declined to explain them and said their meaning rests with God. It is the one part of the text that has never been decoded.
lights.src: Commentators differ widely over the disconnected letters, and many of the earliest authorities declined to interpret them at all.

lights.t: He was asked which verse was greatest and answered at once
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b which verse of the book of Allah was the greatest. Ubayy answered with the verse of the Throne, verse 255 of Surah al-Baqarah. The Prophet ﷺ struck him on the chest and told him that knowledge should be pleasant for him. The verse itself is one sentence made of negations: no god but Him, no drowsiness takes Him and no sleep, no intercession without His permission, nothing of His knowledge grasped except as He wills, no fatigue in holding the heavens and the earth. It sits in the middle of the longest chapter, surrounded by rules about debt, warfare, marriage and charity.

lights.t: The verse after the Throne verse forbids compelling belief
lights.s: Verse 255 of Surah al-Baqarah is the fullest description of God in the Qur'an. Verse 256, immediately after it, opens with the words there is no compulsion in religion, and continues that right guidance has become clear from error. The placement has been noticed by commentators since the earliest period. The largest possible statement of divine power is followed at once by a limit on what human beings may do to each other about belief. The classical discussion of what the verse forbids and whom it addresses is long, and it works from a reported occasion of revelation involving families in Madinah whose sons had been brought up in another faith.

lights.t: A verse about nearness sits inside the rules on fasting
lights.s: Surah al-Baqarah gives the law of Ramadan in a short run of verses: who must fast, who is excused, what to do when ill or travelling, when the fast begins and when it ends. In the middle of that legal passage, at verse 186, the register changes completely. When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me. There is no intermediary in the sentence and no instruction to go through anyone, and unlike most answers in the Qur'an it does not begin with the command to say. It is set between rules about food and rules about the first light.

lights.t: The verse of light sits between rules about privacy
lights.s: Surah al-Nur is a legal chapter. It sets penalties, deals with a false accusation made against Aisha, tells believers to lower their gaze, and instructs people not to enter houses without asking permission and giving greeting. At verse 35, in the middle of all that, comes the passage that gives this site its name. Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is a niche in which there is a lamp, the lamp in glass, the glass like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree neither of the east nor of the west. The image is an ordinary household object, seen at night.

lights.t: Seven oaths in a row open one short chapter
lights.s: Surah al-Shams begins with the longest run of oaths in the Qur'an. By the sun and its morning brightness, by the moon when it follows it, by the day when it displays it, by the night when it covers it, by the sky and what built it, by the earth and what spread it, by the soul and what proportioned it. Seven verses, seven oaths, moving from the largest visible object down to the interior of one person, and the last of them puts the human soul in the same series as the sun. Only then does the thing sworn to arrive: he has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it.

lights.t: One of the earliest chapters swears by the pen
lights.s: Surah al-Qalam opens with a single letter, Nun, and then an oath: by the pen and what they inscribe. Many early authorities place it among the very first chapters revealed, close behind the five opening verses of Surah al-Alaq, which themselves end with the statement that God taught by the pen. Makkah at that time was a trading town with limited literacy and no scholarly tradition of its own. The oath is sworn on an instrument and on the act of using it, in a chapter that goes on to defend the Prophet ﷺ against the charge of madness. What grew from those verses included paper mills, libraries and a copying trade.

lights.t: A three verse chapter swears by time itself
lights.s: Surah al-Asr has three verses. It swears by al-asr, which carries the age, or time, or the late part of the afternoon, and then states that mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do right and counsel one another to truth and counsel one another to patience. That is the entire chapter. A remark attributed to al-Shafi'i and quoted by Ibn Kathir in his commentary says that if people weighed only this chapter it would be enough for them. Companions are reported to have recited it to each other on parting. The exception clause is the shortest complete account of what the Qur'an asks: belief, action, truth between people, endurance.

lights.t: The word for a verse is the word for a sign
lights.s: An ayah is a verse of the Qur'an. It is also the word the Qur'an uses for a sign in the world: the alternation of night and day, ships running on the sea, rain that revives dead ground, sleep, lightning, and the diversity of your languages and your colours. One noun covers a sentence in a book and a fact about the world, which puts them in the same category. A person reading is looking at ayat. A person looking at the sky is also looking at ayat. It is a choice of vocabulary that makes the natural world part of the same exercise as the text, and both of them things to be read rather than only used.
lights.d: Ayah, a verse and a sign

lights.t: Mercy and the womb come from the same three letters
lights.s: The root r h m gives rahma, mercy, and rahim, the womb. It gives al-Rahman and al-Rahim, the two names of God that open every chapter of the Qur'an, and it gives the ordinary Arabic word for kinship, since relatives are the people connected through a womb. The Prophet ﷺ reported God saying that He is al-Rahman, that He created the rahim and derived its name from His own name, and that whoever keeps it joined He will keep joined, and whoever cuts it off He will cut off. The formula recited before every reading of the Qur'an rests on the same three letters as the organ that carried the reader.
lights.d: Root r h m, mercy and the womb

lights.t: Patience in Arabic is a word about restraint
lights.s: Sabr is usually translated as patience, which suggests sitting still and letting time pass. The root s b r means to bind, to hold something in place, to keep it from going where it wants to go. The same root names a bitter plant and supplies the verb for holding a person to a commitment. So sabr sits closer to self restraint under pressure than to endurance: keeping the tongue off complaint, the body at its task, the hand from retaliation. The Qur'an says the patient will be given their reward without reckoning. The word describes somebody doing something difficult, not somebody waiting for it to be over.
lights.d: Root s b r, to bind and restrain

lights.t: God consciousness is built on a word meaning to shield
lights.s: Taqwa is usually rendered piety or fear of God. Its root is w q y, to guard, to shield, to put something between yourself and harm. A wiqaya is a protective covering, and the same root gives modern Arabic its term for preventive medicine. Read that way taqwa is not a feeling but a practice of keeping a barrier between yourself and what damages you. The Qur'an makes the image explicit twice. In the middle of the rules for pilgrimage it tells travellers to take provision, and says the best provision is taqwa. In a passage about clothing it calls taqwa a garment, and the best of garments. A shield, a supply and something you wear.
lights.d: Root w q y, to guard and to shield

lights.t: The Qur'an's name for itself is a word about memory
lights.s: The root dh k r means both to remember and to mention, and Arabic does not separate the two: bringing a thing to mind and saying it aloud are one act. Dhikr therefore covers remembrance and recitation at once. The Qur'an uses the word as one of its own names, calling itself al-Dhikr, the Reminder. It also uses it for the practice: remember Me and I will remember you, and the statement that in the remembrance of God hearts find rest. What grew out of that root includes litanies counted on the fingers, phrases repeated after prayer, and the habit of saying a short formula aloud before eating, travelling or sleeping.
lights.d: Root dh k r, to remember and to mention

lights.t: Faith and safety are the same word in Arabic
lights.s: The root a m n gives iman, faith, and amn, safety. It gives amana, a trust placed in somebody's keeping, and amin, trustworthy, which was what the Makkans called the Prophet ﷺ before he had recited a single verse to them. It gives the word said at the end of al-Fatiha. A mu'min, a believer, is at root somebody who has been made safe and who makes others safe. The Qur'an sets the pair side by side in the short chapter about Quraysh, thanking God for feeding them against hunger and making them safe from fear. Belief and security are not two subjects in this language. They share a skeleton.
lights.d: Root a m n, faith and safety

lights.t: The word for prayer also means blessing the Prophet
lights.s: Salah is the ritual prayer performed five times a day. The same word from the same root is what God and the angels are said to do for the Prophet ﷺ, and what believers are told to do when they say the formula asking for peace upon him. The lexicographers connect the root with supplication and with turning towards. The Qur'an gives the purpose of the prayer in three words in Surah Ta-Ha: establish the prayer for My remembrance. Not for reward, not for protection, not for good order. The verse makes the standing and bowing and prostrating an instrument of memory, which puts salah and dhikr into one sentence.

lights.t: The word for alms means growth, not deduction
lights.s: Zakat is the obligatory portion of accumulated wealth handed over each year. The root z k w means to grow and to increase, and also to be pure, and the noun is used of a plant that thrives. Arabic takes purity and increase from the same three letters because a thing cleaned of what spoils it grows better. So the term for taking a fortieth out of your savings is a word about the pile getting larger. The Qur'an uses the same verb of the self in the chapter of the sun: he has succeeded who causes it to grow, and he has failed who buries it. One verb covers a bank balance and a person.
lights.d: Root z k w, growth and purity

lights.t: Islam and peace and the greeting share three letters
lights.s: The root s l m carries wholeness, soundness, being intact. From it come salam, peace, and the greeting exchanged between Muslims; salim, sound and unbroken, as in the sound heart that the Qur'an says is the only thing worth arriving with; istislam, surrender; and islam itself, which is the act of handing something over whole. Al-Salam is one of the names of God listed at the end of Surah al-Hashr. A Muslim is one who gives himself over, and the word for what he gives and the word for the state he is meant to reach are built from one skeleton. The greeting is the religion's own name, conjugated.
lights.d: Root s l m, wholeness and peace

lights.t: The Qur'an uses the word for disbeliever to mean farmer
lights.s: The root k f r means to cover and to conceal. A kafir in ordinary Arabic is somebody who covers a thing over, and the Qur'an uses exactly that sense in Surah al-Hadid, comparing the life of this world to rain whose resulting growth pleases al-kuffar, meaning the farmers, the men who cover seed with soil. The same root gives kaffara, an expiation, which covers a fault. Applied to belief the word describes covering over something known rather than failing to know it, which is why the classical discussions of kufr turn on knowledge and rejection rather than on ignorance. Old Arabic poetry calls the night kafir because it covers what lies under it.
lights.d: Root k f r, to cover over

lights.t: Gratitude shares a root with a beast that thrives on little
lights.s: The lexicons record an old use of the root sh k r: a she camel called shakur is one that yields plenty of milk on scant fodder, and an animal described with the same word visibly puts on condition from a small ration. The image behind shukr, gratitude, is therefore a return larger than what was given. It is not acknowledgement, it is output. The Qur'an keeps the accounting sense in Surah Ibrahim: if you are grateful I will certainly increase you. Ingratitude in Arabic is kufr, from covering, so the opposite of gratitude in this language is not indifference but concealment of what was received.
lights.d: Root sh k r, a return larger than the gift

lights.t: Trust in God uses a word from commercial law
lights.s: Tawakkul is usually translated as reliance on God. The root w k l is the ordinary vocabulary of agency. A wakil is the agent you appoint to act on your behalf, and in Arabic today a wakil is a lawyer or a proxy or a company representative, while a tawkil is a power of attorney. Tawakkul is appointing God as your agent in a matter, which assumes there is a matter and that you have done your part of the paperwork. The Qur'an puts it after an instruction to act: once you have decided, rely on God. And elsewhere, whoever relies on God, He is enough for him.
lights.d: Root w k l, to appoint an agent

lights.t: Excellence was defined as working as if you were watched
lights.s: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about islam, then about iman, then about ihsan. The answer to the third was that you worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you. The questioner was Jibril, and the report is the standard summary of the religion in three levels: practice, belief, and the quality of both. Ihsan comes from the root h s n, which covers what is good and what is well made in one word. Arabic offers no convenient way to say that a thing is morally right but badly done.

lights.t: Manners and literature are the same word in Arabic
lights.s: Adab today means good manners, courtesy, knowing how to behave. It also means literature. A professor of Arabic adab teaches poetry and prose, and a faculty of adab is a faculty of arts. The lexicographers connect the root with ma'duba, a banquet to which people are invited, so that adab began as the conduct proper to somebody invited to a table and widened into the whole body of things a cultivated person should know. Medieval books of adab teach both at once: how to sit, what to quote, how to open a letter, when to stay quiet. The manners and the reading were never filed as separate subjects.
lights.d: Root a d b, banquet, manners, letters

lights.t: One name of God means keeping your temper
lights.s: Hilm is the quality of somebody who has the power to react and does not: deliberate, slow to anger, not easily provoked. Pre Islamic Arabs prized it as the opposite of jahl, which is usually translated as ignorance but in that setting means hot headedness, the readiness to be roused. Al-Halim is one of the names of God in the Qur'an, and it is repeatedly paired with al-Ghani, the one free of need. The pairing has a logic to it. Somebody who needs nothing from you has no reason to be provoked by you. The verse that pairs them is about not following a gift with a reminder of the favour.

lights.t: Provision in Arabic is a portion allotted, not earned
lights.s: Rizq means provision: food, income, whatever sustains a life. The root r z q carries the sense of a share handed out, and classical usage applies it to the daily ration issued to a soldier. It is not a word about earning. The Qur'an says there is no creature moving on the earth whose provision is not upon God, and it places rizq in the sky alongside what has been promised. What follows in practice is a division of labour that runs through Muslim ethics: the effort belongs to the person, the outcome does not. Somebody who works and does not receive has not failed at rizq, because rizq was never the thing he was doing.
lights.d: Root r z q, an allotted share

lights.t: Blessing comes from the word for a camel kneeling down
lights.s: Barakah is usually translated as blessing, and it means something more specific: a good that settles, stays, and goes on producing beyond what its size accounts for. The root b r k gives baraka, the verb used when a camel folds its legs and lowers itself to the ground to remain there, and birka, a pool, water that has stopped moving and stayed. Both images are about something coming to rest rather than passing through. The Qur'an uses the noun for what would have been opened on a town from the sky and the earth had its people believed and been mindful. Barakah is the difference between an amount and what it does.
lights.d: Root b r k, to kneel and to settle

lights.t: The word for human nature also means breaking a fast
lights.s: The root f t r means to split open, to cleave. From it comes fatir, the originator, used as a name of God and as the title of chapter 35, the one who splits creation into being out of nothing. From it also comes iftar, the breaking of the fast at sunset, which splits the day's abstention in two. And from it comes fitrah, the original pattern on which people were made, named in Surah al-Rum: the fitrah of God, upon which He originated mankind, with no altering of the creation of God. The same three letters carry the first act of creation and the meal a fasting person eats at dusk.
lights.d: Root f t r, to split open

lights.t: The Qur'an names three states of the self
lights.s: Nafs is the self, the soul, the person. The root n f s is the root of breath: nafas is a breath, tanaffasa is to breathe, and Surah al-Takwir swears by the morning when it breathes. The same root gives nafis, precious, and munafasa, competition, the state of two people breathing hard for the same thing. The Qur'an describes the nafs in three conditions, which the later tradition read as stages: the one that commands to evil, in the story of Yusuf; the one that reproaches itself, at the opening of Surah al-Qiyamah; and the one at rest, addressed in Surah al-Fajr and told to return to its Lord.
lights.d: Root n f s, breath and self

lights.t: The Arabic word for heart means the thing that turns
lights.s: Qalb comes from the root q l b, to turn something over, to invert it. The same root gives inqilab, which in modern Arabic is a coup, and taqallub, fluctuation. The organ is named in Arabic for instability rather than for steadiness, which is the reverse of what the English word heart suggests. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have prayed often with the words: O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion. Asked why he needed to say it, he answered that hearts are between two of the fingers of the Merciful, turned as He wills. The supplication is built on the same root as the noun.
lights.d: Root q l b, to turn over

lights.t: Spirit, wind and relief are one word family in Arabic
lights.s: The root r w h gives ruh, spirit; rih, wind; rawh, relief or mercy; rayhan, a fragrant herb; istiraha, rest; and rawah, the going home in the evening. Everything in the family involves air moving or a pressure lifting. When the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the ruh, the answer given in Surah al-Isra is short and closes the subject: the ruh is of the affair of my Lord, and you have been given only a little knowledge. Yaqub, waiting for news of Yusuf, tells his sons not to despair of the rawh of God, using the same root, so that relief and breath and spirit arrive in one word.
lights.d: Root r w h, breath, wind, relief

lights.t: Arabic dictionaries file every word under a three letter root
lights.s: Ibn Manzur, an Egyptian judge who died around 1311, spent much of his life compiling Lisan al-Arab, which fills twenty volumes in modern printings. It is not alphabetical in the way an English dictionary is. Words are filed under their root, usually three consonants, so that everything grown from k t b sits in one place: kataba, he wrote; kitab, a book; katib, a writer; maktab, a desk or an office; maktaba, a library; kitaba, the act of writing. Looking a word up means first stripping it back to its skeleton, which is a small act of analysis. The reader who finds the word also finds its relatives, and the relatives usually explain it.

lights.t: Arabic builds tools by pouring a root into a mould
lights.s: Arabic takes a root of three consonants and pours it into fixed patterns, and the pattern carries as much meaning as the root. The pattern mif'al makes an instrument: from f t h, to open, comes miftah, a key; from w z n, to weigh, mizan, a scale; from n sh r, to saw, minshar, a saw. The pattern maf'al makes a place: from k t b comes maktab, an office; from s j d, to prostrate, comes masjid, the place of prostration, which English took in as mosque. A speaker who meets an unfamiliar word can often work out both halves of it, the family and the function, before reaching for a dictionary.

lights.t: One missing letter changes the King into the Owner
lights.s: In the fourth verse of al-Fatiha, recited in every prayer, the word describing God in relation to the day of judgement is read two ways. Hafs from Asim, the reading in most printed copies, has maliki with a long first vowel, meaning owner or master. Nafi of Madinah and Ibn Kathir of Makkah read it short, meaning king. Both are canonically transmitted, both were recited from the beginning, and the difference is a single alif that the earliest manuscripts did not write in either case. A king rules what is not his. An owner possesses it. The verse is recited both ways every day by hundreds of millions of people.
lights.src: The canonical readings differ: Hafs from Asim reads maliki with the alif, Nafi and Ibn Kathir read maliki without it.

lights.t: The word for a Qur'an copy also gives journalist
lights.s: Muslims distinguish the Qur'an, which is the recitation, from the mushaf, which is the physical book on the shelf. The word comes from the root s h f, which gives sahifa, a sheet or a page, and suhuf, the pages that the Qur'an says were given to Ibrahim and Musa. The same root gives modern Arabic sahafa, journalism, and sahafi, a journalist, somebody whose work is pages. Early reports say the companions weighed several words for the bound volume before settling on mushaf.
