The distinction still does work: a mushaf can wear out and be buried or replaced, and none of that touches the Qur'an, which is what is recited.
lights.d: Root s h f, sheet, codex, press

lights.t: The toothbrush of the sunnah is a frayed twig
lights.s: The siwak is a short stick cut from the arak tree, chewed at one end until the fibres open into bristles. The Prophet ﷺ used it on waking, before prayer, and when he came home. He said that if it would not have been hard on his community, he would have ordered them to use it before every prayer, which is five times a day. The instruction concerns the mouth, not the soul, and he gave it the weight of a near obligation. Dental researchers have since studied arak fibres for their natural fluoride, silica and antibacterial compounds, and the World Health Organization has recognised the chewing stick as an effective tool for oral hygiene. It is one of the few seventh century objects still sold in markets for exactly its original use.

lights.t: A boy's hand wandering across a dish got three instructions
lights.s: Umar ibn Abi Salamah was a child in the household, the son of Umm Salamah from her first marriage. He remembered eating beside the Prophet ﷺ and letting his hand roam over the whole platter. The correction he received was three clauses long: say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you. He kept those rules for the rest of his life and taught them as he had received them. Nothing about the words is grand. They are what an adult says to a child at a shared dish, which is why they survived. The boy grew up, people asked him how the Prophet ﷺ ate, and he told them about his own hand being sent back to its own side of the plate.
lights.d: Umar ibn Abi Salamah, as a boy · Madinah

lights.t: He drank in three breaths and said it was better
lights.s: Anas ibn Malik, who served in the household for ten years, said the Prophet ﷺ took the cup from his mouth three times while drinking rather than swallowing it down in one draught, and that he found it more thirst quenching and easier on the stomach. He also told people not to breathe into the vessel itself. The habit can be tested at any kitchen tap. Water taken in three separate breaths sits differently from water gulped, and anyone who has drunk too fast on a hot day knows the difference. It is a small piece of table manners with a physical reason attached, reported by a servant who watched it happen at close range for a decade, and it costs nothing to keep.

lights.t: He never once spoke against a plate of food
lights.s: Abu Hurayra said the Prophet ﷺ never found fault with food. If he wanted it he ate it, and if he did not want it he left it. Not one complaint about the cooking, the quantity or the temperature is recorded from him in a lifetime of eating what other people set in front of him, often in poor households that had stretched to feed a guest. The rule has an obvious target: the person who did the cooking. Whole cuisines have been built on seasoning at the table with criticism. His practice removed it entirely and left the diner two options, both of them silent.

lights.t: He mended his own sandal and helped in the house
lights.s: Aisha was asked what the Prophet ﷺ did at home. Her answer was that he was in the service of his family, and when the call to prayer came he went out to it. In other reports preserved from her he is described mending his sandal, patching his own garment and milking the sheep, doing in his house what any of you does in his. These accounts are given no chapter of their own in the law books because they establish nothing legal. They survive because someone asked a plain question about a private man and got a plain answer, and because the answer surprised people who expected a head of state to be waited on.
lights.d: Aisha, asked about him at home · Madinah

lights.t: Greet the ones you know and the ones you do not
lights.s: A man asked the Prophet ﷺ which part of Islam was best. The answer named two things: that you feed people, and that you give the greeting of peace to those you know and those you do not know. The second half is the harder one. Greeting an acquaintance is ordinary courtesy. Greeting a stranger is the deliberate removal of the line between the two. In a tribal society, whom you greeted announced whom you counted as yours, and the instruction erases that calculation. It is repeated in the reports as a habit he kept himself, on roads, in markets, and walking past groups of children. It is also the cheapest of all recommended acts, costing one word.
lights.d: Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As · Madinah

lights.t: He greeted children first and kept doing it
lights.s: Anas ibn Malik used to pass groups of boys and give them the greeting of peace, and he told people he did it because the Prophet ﷺ used to do it. That is the whole report. An adult of standing initiating the greeting to children ran against the convention, which sends the greeting upward from the lesser to the greater. He reversed the direction. Elsewhere he is described stopping for children in the street, carrying them, joking with a small boy about a pet bird that had died, and cutting his own prayer short because he heard an infant crying at the back of the mosque. The pattern is consistent enough that his companions treated greeting children as a practice to copy rather than a personal quirk.

lights.t: The lowest branch of faith is clearing the road
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ described faith as having some seventy branches, the highest being the declaration that there is no god but Allah and the lowest being the removal of something harmful from the road. Modesty, he added, is one of the branches. Putting road maintenance on the same list as the creed is a decision about where religion is supposed to operate. In another report a man walking past a thorny branch in the path pulled it aside so that it would not injure anyone, and was forgiven for it. Neither act is witnessed, ceremonial or expensive. Both involve a person alone with a piece of rubbish, making a decision about strangers he will never meet.
lights.src: Bukhari 9; the man and the branch, Muslim 1914

lights.t: A smile counts as charity in the ledger
lights.s: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari came from a poor tribe and had almost nothing to give away. He was told by the Prophet ﷺ that smiling in the face of his brother was an act of charity, and that he should not think little of any good deed, even meeting another person with a cheerful face. The point was practical rather than sentimental. Abu Dharr worried openly that the rich were buying rewards he could not afford. The answer changed the currency. What is asked for is attention rather than money, and the poorest man in the mosque had as much of that as anyone else in it.

lights.t: Five things one Muslim owes another, and one is a visit
lights.s: Asked what a Muslim owes a Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ listed five duties: return the greeting, visit him when he is ill, follow his funeral, accept his invitation, and answer him when he sneezes. They are small, public, and impossible to perform at a distance. Illness is the one that costs time. Later scholars gathered the etiquette of the visit from the reports around it: keep it short, sit near him, do not tire him, pray for him. In a system that could have asked for donations, what was asked for was presence, which is the thing a sick person actually lacks.

lights.t: Sleep was treated as a departure with instructions
lights.s: Al-Bara ibn Azib was taught a sequence for going to bed: perform the washing you would perform for prayer, lie down on your right side, then say a short prayer that ends by placing yourself in the care of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ told him that if he died that night he would die in a natural state of belief, and to make those words the last thing he said. The framing is exact. Sleep is treated as a small death, which is also how the Qur'an speaks of it. Nothing in the sequence requires equipment or company. It can be done in a tent, a barracks or a hospital ward, and it puts the last conscious sentence of the day under the sleeper's own control.

lights.t: He cupped his hands, recited three suras, and wiped
lights.s: Aisha described what he did every night before sleeping. He brought his palms together, blew into them, recited the last three chapters of the Qur'an, Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas, then wiped his hands over as much of his body as he could reach, beginning with his head and face, and repeated the whole thing three times. During his final illness, when he could not do it himself, she recited and used his own hands to wipe him, because it was his hands that carried the blessing rather than hers. The practice takes under a minute. It is one of the few of his private habits recorded with enough physical detail that a reader fourteen centuries later can copy the movement exactly.

lights.t: The last third of the night is when the door opens
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ said that each night, when the last third of it remains, our Lord descends to the nearest heaven and says: who is calling on Me, that I may answer him, who is asking of Me, that I may give him, who is seeking My forgiveness, that I may forgive him. Muslim scholars have argued for centuries about how the descent is to be understood, and have generally refused either to explain it away or to describe it physically. What is not disputed is the timetable. The report puts the best hour of the whole day at the point when nobody is watching, no congregation has gathered, and the only witness to a person getting up is the person himself.
lights.d: Abu Hurayra · the last third of the night

lights.t: The deeds He loves most are the small repeated ones
lights.s: Aisha reported that the acts most beloved to Allah are those done consistently, even if they are few, and that the practice of the Prophet ﷺ was steady rather than dramatic. When he took on a devotion he kept it. The household reports show the same shape: a fixed number of units of prayer at night, a fixed set of words in the morning, a fast on the same two days most weeks. It is a standard that penalises the intense week followed by nothing, and rewards the two minutes a day that survive a bad month. Anyone who has abandoned an ambitious plan by the second week can recognise the diagnosis behind the instruction.

lights.t: A man urinated in the mosque and was left alone
lights.s: A bedouin walked into the mosque at Madinah and began to urinate in it. The companions shouted and moved to stop him. The Prophet ﷺ told them to leave the man alone and let him finish, then to pour a bucket of water over the spot. Afterwards he called him over and explained, without raising his voice, that mosques are not for this but for prayer and the remembrance of Allah. Two things were being weighed against each other: the floor, and the man. Interrupting him mid stream would have spread the mess and humiliated a stranger who did not know where he was standing. The floor was easy to fix. It was the correction that had to be done well.
lights.d: Anas ibn Malik · the mosque at Madinah

lights.t: A man asked for advice and got two words, repeated
lights.s: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him for advice. He said: do not become angry. The man asked again and got the same answer. He asked several times, and each time the reply was the same two words. The report is short and the repetition is the content. Given one instruction to carry away for life, the man was handed neither a doctrine nor a devotion but a temper. Elsewhere the Prophet ﷺ defined strength in the same terms: the strong man is not the one who throws people in wrestling, but the one who controls himself when he is angry. That is an unusual definition in a warrior society, and it is stated as a correction to what everybody there assumed.
lights.src: Bukhari 6116; the definition of strength, Bukhari 6114

lights.t: A woman was punished over a cat she shut in
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ told his companions about a woman who was punished on account of a cat. She confined it and did not feed it, and did not let it go so that it could eat the small creatures of the earth. He was not describing an obscure legal case. He was telling people who kept animals in a hard climate that a locked door and an empty bowl are a moral act. The same collections record the opposite case, of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and the general principle he stated: in every living creature there is a reward for the one who helps it.

lights.t: A man climbed into a well for a thirsty dog
lights.s: A man walking on a very hot day found a well, went down into it, drank, and came up to find a dog panting and eating the wet earth from thirst. He judged that the dog was as thirsty as he had been. He went down again, filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth to climb out, and gave the dog a drink. He was forgiven for it. The companions asked whether they were rewarded for animals as well, and were told that in every living creature there is a reward. The report is precise about the mechanics: the sock, the climb, the teeth. The mercy in it is not a feeling. It is a man doing a hard physical task twice for an animal that could not thank him.
lights.d: Abu Hurayra · reported in two collections

lights.t: The longest verse in the Qur'an is a loan agreement
lights.s: Verse 282 of Surah Al-Baqarah is the longest single verse in the Qur'an, and its subject is debt. It instructs believers who take on a loan for a fixed term to write it down, to have a scribe record it justly, to have the borrower dictate rather than the lender, to bring witnesses, and not to consider it beneath them to set the sum down whether it is small or large. It ends by allowing a pledged security when no scribe is available. A book that spends far fewer words on many devotional matters gives its longest passage to contract law, because unwritten debt between neighbours has destroyed more households than most disasters.

lights.t: He died with his armour pledged to a Jewish neighbour
lights.s: Aisha reported that when the Prophet ﷺ died, his shield was still held as security by a Jewish man of Madinah against a debt of barley taken for his family. The report is in the sound collections and was preserved partly as a legal precedent for pledging property, and partly for what it says about the last weeks of a man who by then headed a state. He owed money for food. He had borrowed from a neighbour of another religion in an ordinary transaction with an ordinary security, and he died before it was settled. In the law that grew from his teaching, debts owed to human beings are not cancelled by death.

lights.t: A stranger entering could not tell which man he was
lights.s: The reports about how the Prophet ﷺ sat are unusually consistent. He sat wherever there was room in the gathering rather than at its head, so that visitors arriving and asking for him had to be told which of the men he was. He disliked people standing up when he came in, and told them not to do what the foreign courts did for their rulers. When a man stood trembling in front of him he said, be at ease, I am the son of a woman who ate dried meat. These accounts come through several chains in the collections of Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, and they lie behind the discomfort many Muslims still feel about a reserved chair at the front of a room.

lights.t: He never saw me without smiling at me
lights.s: Jarir ibn Abdullah al-Bajali was a tall man of the tribe of Bajila who came to Islam late, in the ninth year after the migration. His summary of his time with the Prophet ﷺ was two facts. He was never once refused anything he asked for, and he was never seen by him without being smiled at. Abdullah ibn al-Harith, another companion, said he had never met anyone who smiled more. What comes out of these small statements is not a solemn man. Several reports describe him laughing until his back teeth showed, though nobody describes him laughing loudly, and none of his recorded jokes are at anybody's expense.

lights.t: The meal before dawn was made a practice on purpose
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ told his companions to eat before dawn, because in that meal there is blessing. He also kept the gap between the end of it and the call to prayer short. Zayd ibn Thabit said they ate with him and then stood for prayer, and when Anas asked how long the interval had been, Zayd measured it as the time it takes to recite about fifty verses. A fast kept without the pre dawn meal is still valid. It is the practice, not the fast, that the instruction protects, and the reason given is not medical but a blessing placed in the act of getting up in the dark to eat with your household.
lights.d: Anas and Zayd ibn Thabit · Ramadan

lights.t: Break the fast early and the community stays well
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ said that people will remain in a good state as long as they hasten to break the fast, meaning that they eat the moment the sun has set rather than waiting to be extra certain. He broke his own fast before praying the sunset prayer, with fresh dates if he had them, dried dates if not, and otherwise a few mouthfuls of water. The rule cuts against a religious instinct that more is always better. An extra ten minutes of hunger looks like extra devotion and is treated here as a fault, because the fast has a fixed end, and a person who invents a stricter one is not being more obedient.

lights.t: Leaving food is not wanted if false speech stays
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does not give up false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of his leaving his food and drink. The sentence is blunt about what the fast is for. Going without water in a hot country is hard enough to feel like an achievement in itself, and the report refuses to accept it as one. In another narration he told a fasting person who is insulted or dragged into an argument to say, twice, that he is fasting, and to leave it there. The same reports describe Ramadan as a month of restraint in speech and temper, with the hunger as its most visible and least important part.

lights.t: He was most generous in Ramadan, like a loosed wind
lights.s: Ibn Abbas said the Prophet ﷺ was the most generous of people, and that he was at his most generous in Ramadan, when the angel Jibril met him every night of the month to go through the Qur'an with him, and that in those nights he was more generous with good than a wind sent forth. The image is weather rather than accounting. The report also records something else in the same breath: an annual review of the text with the one who had brought it, night after night, for a whole month. The connection between the two halves is not explained. Generosity and the revision of the revelation are simply placed in one sentence about the same weeks of the year.

lights.t: He spent the last ten nights of Ramadan in the mosque
lights.s: Aisha reported that the Prophet ﷺ kept i'tikaf, seclusion in the mosque, during the last ten days of Ramadan every year until the end of his life. She also said that when those ten nights came he would tighten his waist wrapper, stay awake at night, and wake his family. I'tikaf is a physical withdrawal. A man with a household, a mosque and a state took ten days a year and did not leave the building. The schools differ on the minimum period, some holding it to be a single night and others a day. What the reports agree on is that he did not treat the last third of the month like the first two.
lights.d: Aisha · the last ten nights of Ramadan

lights.t: Aisha asked what to say if she found the night
lights.s: Aisha asked the Prophet ﷺ what she should say if she knew which night was Laylat al-Qadr. She was not told to ask for anything material. The words he gave her ask for pardon: O Allah, You are the one who pardons and You love to pardon, so pardon me. The Arabic verb is afw, which carries the sense of erasing a thing rather than overlooking it while still remembering it. On the night the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months, the request recommended to her was that a record be wiped. The report is in the collections of Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, and Tirmidhi himself graded it hasan sahih.
lights.d: Aisha · the last ten nights of Ramadan

lights.t: No days are better for good work than these ten
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ said there are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these ten, meaning the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah. The companions asked whether not even struggle in the path of Allah matched them. He said not even that, except for a man who goes out with his life and his wealth and comes back with none of it. The days belong to everyone, not only to the pilgrims. Somebody in a flat in Manchester and somebody standing on the plain of Arafah are inside the same ten days, and the report places ordinary acts done at home above what was normally treated as the highest deed available.
lights.d: Ibn Abbas · the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah

lights.t: Hajj done cleanly returns a person to day one
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever performs the pilgrimage and does not speak or act obscenely, and does not commit wickedness, returns as he was on the day his mother bore him. The two named faults are worth noticing. Neither is a ritual error. They are coarseness and losing your temper with the people around you, which is the likeliest thing to happen to anyone who has spent five days in a crowd of millions in great heat, sleeping on the ground and queueing for water. The hardest part of the pilgrimage is not the walking, and the condition attached to the reward is conduct rather than technique.

lights.t: Neither the meat nor the blood reaches Him
lights.s: The animals sacrificed at the end of the pilgrimage, and by families across the world on the same days, are the subject of one line in Surah Al-Hajj: it is not their meat nor their blood that reaches Allah, but the God consciousness from you that reaches Him. The verse closes off the older reading of sacrifice as feeding a deity. What is left is a distribution of food. The practice attached to it divides the meat into shares, one for the household, one for relatives and neighbours, one for the poor, which means that the rite ends with several kilograms of protein arriving at doors that do not usually receive any.

lights.t: Umar was told which verse deserved a festival
lights.s: A Jewish man said to Umar ibn al-Khattab that there is a verse in your book which, had it come down to us, we would have taken that day as a festival. Umar asked which verse. He recited the words: this day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you. Umar answered that he knew both the day and the place it came down. The Prophet ﷺ was standing at Arafah, and it was a Friday. The exchange is preserved near the beginning of Bukhari's collection, and it fixes one of the most quoted lines in the Qur'an to an afternoon on a hill outside Makkah in the year 632.

lights.t: He found a fast in Madinah and joined it
lights.s: Ibn Abbas reported that when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah he found the Jewish community fasting on the day of Ashura. He asked what the day was. They told him it was the day Allah saved Moses and his people from Pharaoh, so Moses fasted it. He said that the Muslims had a closer claim to Moses, and he fasted the day and told them to fast it. Quraysh had also marked the tenth of Muharram before Islam. What is being described is not the invention of a fast but the adoption of one, with an explanation of why an older prophet's rescue belongs to a newer community as well.

lights.t: The best fast after Ramadan is in the month of Allah
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ was asked which fast is best after Ramadan and said: the month of Allah which you call Muharram. In the same report he said the best prayer after the obligatory ones is the prayer at night. Muharram is one of the four months the Qur'an calls sacred, in which fighting was forbidden long before Islam and remained forbidden after it. The recommendation is voluntary and the month is not a second Ramadan. What it does is place a marked stretch of fasting at the start of the year rather than the middle, an arrangement recognisable to anyone who has watched resolutions collapse in January.
lights.d: Abu Hurayra · the month of Muharram

lights.t: Four months of the twelve were declared off limits for war
lights.s: The Qur'an states that the number of months with Allah is twelve, fixed on the day He created the heavens and the earth, and that four of them are sacred. The four are Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab, three consecutive and one standing alone. The truce they carried was older than Islam and was kept by tribes who agreed on very little else. Caravans moved, pilgrims travelled, and blood feuds paused for a quarter of every year. The verse confirms the arrangement rather than creating it. It is an early example of a calendar doing the work of a peace treaty, in a place where no authority was strong enough to enforce one.

lights.t: One prayer on him returns as ten
lights.s: The Qur'an instructs believers to send prayers and peace upon the Prophet ﷺ, and he told them what happens when they do: whoever sends one prayer upon me, Allah sends ten upon him. That is the reason for the small formula written after his name throughout Muslim literature, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, and represented in modern typesetting by a single character. Scribes have added it by hand in the margins of manuscripts for more than a thousand years. It is one of the few devotional acts with no fixed time, place, direction, state of purity or number attached to it, which is why it turns up in the middle of ordinary sentences.

lights.t: Asked about fasting Mondays he named the day he was born
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ was asked about fasting on Mondays. He answered that it is the day he was born and the day he was sent, or the day revelation came down upon him. He fasted Mondays and Thursdays as a habit, and another report explains those two days as the days on which deeds are presented. The reference to his birth is the only place in the sound collections where he marks it, and what he does with it is fast. Rabi al-Awwal, the month he was born in, is also the month he died in and the month he reached Madinah, which is why the same weeks in the calendar carry three different memories.
lights.d: Abu Qatada al-Ansari · Monday and Thursday

lights.t: The first Muslim was a businesswoman of forty
lights.s: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid ran a caravan trade in Makkah and hired Muhammad ﷺ to take her goods to Syria before she proposed marriage to him. When he came back from the cave of Hira shaking and asked to be covered, she did not ask him for evidence. She wrapped him, listened, and told him that Allah would never disgrace him, because he kept ties of kinship, carried the weak, gave to the poor, honoured the guest and helped people through hardship. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqah, a Christian scholar, for a second opinion. That order of operations, comfort first and verification afterwards, is preserved in the opening pages of Bukhari's collection.
lights.d: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid · Makkah, c. 610 CE

lights.t: Senior companions came to her with their hardest questions
lights.s: Aisha bint Abi Bakr was widowed in her early twenties and lived nearly fifty years more in Madinah, in a house attached to the mosque. Abu Musa al-Ashari said that whenever the companions found a report difficult they asked Aisha, and found knowledge with her. Her nephew Urwa ibn al-Zubayr said he had never seen anyone more learned in law, in medicine or in poetry. She corrected other narrators, including senior ones, when she judged that they had misremembered a ruling, and later scholars gathered those corrections into books of their own. Over two thousand reports are transmitted from her, which places her among the largest single sources for the practice of the Prophet ﷺ.
lights.d: Aisha bint Abi Bakr · died 58 AH, 678 CE

lights.t: Her advice saved the treaty at Hudaybiyyah
lights.s: In 628 at Hudaybiyyah the Prophet ﷺ accepted terms his companions found humiliating: no pilgrimage that year, a ten year truce, and a clause returning defectors to Quraysh. He told the men to slaughter their animals and shave their heads, which would end the state of pilgrimage. Nobody moved. He went into his tent and Umm Salamah, who was travelling with him, advised him to say nothing further to them, to go out, slaughter his own camel and call his barber. He did. When they saw it they got up and did the same, some of them shaving one another. The episode is preserved in Bukhari's account of the treaty, with her advice named as the thing that broke the deadlock.
lights.d: Umm Salamah bint Abi Umayyah · Hudaybiyyah, 628

lights.t: She went to Uhud with a waterskin and ended up fighting
lights.s: Nusaybah bint Ka'b of the Banu Najjar, known as Umm Ammarah, went out to Uhud in 625 to carry water and tend the wounded. When the Muslim lines broke and the Prophet ﷺ was exposed, she took up a sword and a bow and stood among the small group that held their ground, taking a deep wound to the shoulder that took a year to heal. Her husband and her sons were beside her. Eight years later, at Yamama in 633, she fought again in her sixties and lost a hand. The early biographers Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Hisham name her and record him saying that wherever he turned at Uhud, right or left, he saw her defending him.
lights.d: Nusaybah bint Ka'b, Umm Ammarah · Uhud, 625

lights.t: She tore her belt in two and gained a name
lights.s: When the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr in 622, Abu Bakr's daughter Asma carried food out to them. She had nothing to tie the bundle with, so she cut her waist belt in two and used one half for the food and the other for the waterskin. From that she was called Dhat al-Nitaqayn, the woman of the two belts. She was pregnant during the migration and gave birth at Quba on arrival. Seventy years later, blind and about a hundred years old, she is reported to have told her son Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, besieged in Makkah and asking whether to surrender, that a sheep does not suffer from being skinned once it has been slaughtered.
lights.d: Asma bint Abi Bakr · died 73 AH, 692 CE

lights.t: Her dowry was that he become Muslim
lights.s: Umm Sulaym bint Milhan of Madinah was widowed with a small son, Anas, whom she sent to serve the Prophet ﷺ. When Abu Talha, then still a pagan, proposed to her, she told him she would not refuse a man like him, but that she could not marry an unbeliever, and that if he accepted Islam that would be her dowry and she would ask for nothing else. He did, and the marriage went ahead. The report is preserved by an-Nasa'i and others, and early scholars cite it in the chapters on what may count as a valid dower. She went out at Hunayn while pregnant, carrying a dagger, and told him she was keeping it for anyone who came near her.

lights.t: A tent in the mosque was the first field hospital
lights.s: Rufaida bint Sa'd al-Aslamia, of the tribe of Aslam in Madinah, had learned medicine from her father and set up a tent inside the Prophet's ﷺ mosque to treat the wounded. When Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was struck in the arm by an arrow at the battle of the Trench in 627, the Prophet ﷺ ordered that he be carried to her tent so that he could visit him easily. The early biographers record that she trained other women and was given a share of the spoils for her service. Nursing histories now cite her as the earliest named Muslim nurse. The detail worth keeping is the location. The wounded were treated inside the mosque, not away from it.

lights.t: She asked for a servant and was taught a formula
lights.s: Fatimah bint Muhammad came to her father with hands blistered from working a hand mill, to ask for a servant from among the captives who had arrived. He did not give her one. He told her instead to say, when she went to bed, subhanallah thirty three times, alhamdulillah thirty three times and allahu akbar thirty four times, and said that it would be better for her than a servant. Ali, her husband, reported that he never left it off after hearing it. The household in question was the Prophet's ﷺ own daughter and his cousin. Whatever the decision meant for the wider question of servants, it meant that the exemption did not start at home.

lights.t: The first person killed for this religion was a slave woman
lights.s: Sumayyah bint Khayyat was an enslaved woman in Makkah, married to Yasir and the mother of Ammar. The family were among the earliest converts and had no clan able to protect them, which is why they were tortured in the open while men of the great families were not. The biographers record that Abu Jahl killed her with a spear. She was elderly. Muslim tradition counts her as the first person to be killed for the faith, before any battle and before the migration. The same reports preserve the Prophet ﷺ passing the family under torture and telling them to be patient, that their appointed place was Paradise. He could not stop it. He had no clan strong enough either.
lights.d: Sumayyah bint Khayyat · Makkah, c. 615 CE

lights.t: He appointed a caller to prayer for her household
lights.s: Umm Waraqah bint Abdullah of the Ansar had collected the Qur'an, and the Prophet ﷺ used to visit her at her house and called her the martyr. The report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says that he appointed a mu'adhdhin for her and instructed her to lead the people of her household in prayer. Scholars have argued over it for centuries, both about the chain and about whether her household included men, and the schools reach different conclusions on women leading prayer as a result. She was killed at home by two of her servants during the caliphate of Umar, which is why the title he had given her was remembered.
lights.src: Abu Dawud 592; the chain turns on al-Walid ibn Abdullah ibn Jumay, graded acceptable by some and weak by others

lights.t: He heard Bilal's footsteps ahead of him in Paradise
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ asked Bilal ibn Rabah to name the deed he most hoped for, because he had heard the sound of his sandals in front of him in Paradise. Bilal said he had done nothing he counted on more than this: that he never performed the ritual washing at any hour of the night or the day without praying with that washing whatever had been written for him to pray. It is not an impressive answer. No fasting record, no battle, no charity. An Abyssinian former slave who had been dragged over hot stones in Makkah for refusing to recant named a small private habit kept at odd hours, and that is the deed the report preserves.
lights.d: Abu Hurayra, of Bilal ibn Rabah · Madinah

lights.t: He crossed three countries looking for one man
lights.s: Salman al-Farisi was born near Isfahan, the son of a Zoroastrian landowner who locked him in the house to stop him leaving. He left anyway, followed a Christian monk to Syria, and served a succession of teachers, the last of whom told him a prophet was about to appear in a land of date palms between two fields of black rock. On the way he was betrayed and sold as a slave, and ended up in Madinah, where he recognised the description of the place before he met the man. His freedom was bought under a contract requiring three hundred date palms and a weight of gold, and the Prophet ﷺ planted the palms with him. He later proposed digging the trench that saved the city.

lights.t: He handed over everything he owned to be allowed to leave
lights.s: Suhayb ibn Sinan was an Arab boy captured by Byzantine raiders and raised in their territory, which is why Makkah called him ar-Rumi, the Roman. He was freed, became a merchant and grew wealthy. When he tried to migrate to Madinah, Quraysh stopped him and told him he had arrived among them with nothing and would not leave with a fortune. He asked whether they would let him go if he gave them all of it. They agreed, and he told them where the money was buried and rode out with nothing. Early commentators connect his case to the verse about the man who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, and the reports say the Prophet ﷺ told him twice that the sale had been profitable.
lights.d: Suhayb ibn Sinan ar-Rumi · Makkah to Madinah, 622

lights.t: He carried two bricks while everyone else carried one
lights.s: When the mosque at Madinah was being built, Ammar ibn Yasir carried two mud bricks at a time while the others carried one. The Prophet ﷺ brushed the dust off him and said that the transgressing party would be the ones to kill him. Ammar had watched both his parents die under torture in Makkah. He lived to be over ninety and was killed at Siffin in 657, fighting on Ali's side against the army of Muawiya, and the statement about his death was quoted by both camps immediately afterwards, because whichever side had killed him stood named in it. It is one of the few prophetic sayings that became a live political argument within a single generation.
lights.d: Ammar ibn Yasir · Madinah, then Siffin 657

lights.t: The only companion named in the Qur'an was a freed slave
lights.s: Zayd ibn Haritha was taken as a boy in a raid and sold in Makkah, where he ended up in the household of the Prophet ﷺ. When his father and uncle found him and came with a ransom, he was given the choice and chose to stay. He was freed, and for a time was called Zayd ibn Muhammad, until the Qur'an ended the practice of giving adopted sons the name of the adopter and told believers to call them by their own fathers. He is the only one of the companions mentioned by name in the Qur'an, in Surah Al-Ahzab. He commanded the army at Mu'ta in 629 and was killed there.
lights.d: Zayd ibn Haritha · died at Mu'ta, 629 CE

lights.t: He asked after one man and found him among the dead
lights.s: Julaybib was a poor man of unknown lineage in Madinah, short and thought unattractive, with no family to speak for him. The Prophet ﷺ arranged his marriage himself, going to a man of the Ansar to ask for his daughter and receiving a refusal until the girl herself agreed to it. After a battle he asked the companions whether they had lost anyone. They named their dead. He said that he had lost Julaybib, and went looking until he found him lying beside seven men he had killed before they killed him. He carried the body himself and said: he is of me and I am of him. Nobody else had counted him.
lights.d: Abu Barza al-Aslami, of Julaybib · Madinah

lights.t: He insulted a man's mother and had to be corrected
lights.s: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari abused a servant by referring to his mother's colour. When the Prophet ﷺ heard of it he said that Abu Dharr was a man in whom something of the age before Islam still remained, and told him: they are your brothers, Allah has placed them under your hand, so feed them from what you eat, clothe them from what you wear, and do not burden them with more than they can bear, and if you do, then help them. The correction was kept because of what came next. Al-Ma'rur ibn Suwayd met Abu Dharr years later, found him and his servant wearing the same cloth, and asked why. That is how the report reached us.
lights.d: Al-Ma'rur ibn Suwayd, of Abu Dharr · Rabadha

lights.t: A blacksmith asked when the help was coming
lights.s: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt made swords in Makkah and was among the first to accept Islam. He was enslaved, and his owner is reported to have pressed him down onto heated stones. He came to the Prophet ﷺ, who was resting in the shade of the Ka'ba with his cloak folded under his head, and asked him to seek help for them and to pray for them. The answer was not comfort. He described believers before them combed with iron combs and sawn in half who did not leave their religion, then said that Allah would complete this matter until a rider could travel from Sana to Hadramawt fearing nobody but Allah, but that you are being hasty.

lights.t: A blind man interrupted and the Qur'an took his side
lights.s: Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum was blind and poor. He came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was occupied with the leading men of Quraysh, hoping they might accept Islam, and interrupted with a question of his own. He was frowned at and turned away from. The opening of Surah Abasa records the incident: he frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. That passage stands in the Qur'an that Muslims recite in prayer. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have greeted him by asking whether he needed anything, and he twice left him in charge of Madinah while he was away from the city.

lights.t: Offered half of another man's wealth, he asked for the market
lights.s: When the migrants reached Madinah with nothing, the Prophet ﷺ paired each of them with a man of the city. Sa'd ibn al-Rabi offered Abdurrahman ibn Awf half of his property. Abdurrahman answered: may Allah bless you in your family and your wealth, show me the market. He went to it, traded in dried yoghurt and butter, and before long came to the Prophet ﷺ with the yellow trace of perfume on him and said that he had married. He was told to hold a wedding meal even if only with one sheep. He died among the wealthiest men in Madinah, and the whole of it began with a refusal of charity.

lights.t: Ten years of service and not one rebuke
lights.s: Anas ibn Malik was about ten when his mother brought him to the Prophet ﷺ to serve him, and he stayed for ten years. His summary: he never said uff to me, and never asked why I had done a thing or why I had not done it. Another report from him adds that when he was sent on an errand and went off instead to play with boys in the street, the Prophet ﷺ came up behind him, took hold of the back of his neck, and asked with a smile whether he had gone where he was told. Anas lived into his nineties at Basra and is the source of well over a thousand reports about how the household actually ran.
lights.d: Anas ibn Malik · Madinah, ten years

lights.t: He told the truth about staying behind and lost fifty days
lights.s: Ka'b ibn Malik had no excuse for missing the expedition to Tabuk in 630. He had meant to go, put it off, and stayed. More than eighty other men came back with excuses and were accepted. He told the truth and was told to wait. For fifty nights he and two others were cut off. Nobody in Madinah spoke to them, their wives were sent away from them, and Ka'b described the earth becoming strange to him. Then the Qur'an announced their forgiveness in the verse about the three who were left behind until the earth, vast as it is, closed in upon them. He said afterwards that he never told a lie again, and his own account of it runs for pages in Bukhari.
lights.d: Ka'b ibn Malik · Tabuk and Madinah, 630 CE

lights.t: He wrote to the enemy and Badr saved him
lights.s: In 630, while the march on Makkah was being prepared in secret, Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a sent a letter warning Quraysh. It was intercepted by riders sent after the woman carrying it. Asked why he had done it, Hatib said he had no doubt about the religion, but that he had no clan in Makkah to protect his family and had wanted a favour owed to him there. Umar asked permission to strike his neck. The Prophet ﷺ refused, saying that Hatib had been at Badr, and that Allah had looked upon the people of Badr and forgiven them. He was not executed, and the report is preserved with his excuse intact, including the part where he admits the letter was his.
lights.d: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a · Madinah, 630 CE

lights.t: They cursed a man for drinking and were told to stop
lights.s: A man in Madinah was brought in repeatedly for drinking and lashed for it. On one occasion someone in the crowd said, may Allah curse him, how often he is brought here. The Prophet ﷺ said: do not curse him, for by Allah, I know that he loves Allah and His Messenger. The punishment was carried out and the contempt was refused. Two separate things are being held apart: what a community does about an offence, and what it is entitled to conclude about the person committing it. Umar transmitted the report, and Bukhari placed it in the chapters on legal punishments, which is where the collector thought a prohibition on cursing belonged.

lights.t: The first mosque was built by hand at Quba
lights.s: When the Prophet ﷺ reached the outskirts of Yathrib in 622, he stopped for several days at Quba, a settlement of palm groves south of the town, and a mosque was built there before he went on. It was a simple enclosure of palm trunks and mud brick, and the reports describe him carrying stones for it himself. The commentators generally identify it with the mosque the Qur'an calls founded on God consciousness from the first day. He kept visiting it after moving into the town, and the practice of going out to Quba on a Saturday is recorded from him. The building on the site now is modern. The foundation date is not.
lights.d: Quba, outside Yathrib · Rabi al-Awwal, 622 CE

lights.t: The Qur'an recorded the defeat at Uhud in detail
lights.s: At Uhud in 625, a year after the victory at Badr, the Muslims were beaten. Archers left the hill they had been told to hold, the line was turned, some seventy men were killed including the Prophet's ﷺ uncle Hamza, and he himself was wounded in the face. What is unusual is what happened to the account. Surah Al Imran goes through the day at length and assigns the cause: they had disputed and disobeyed after being shown what they wanted. The community's own scripture preserves its worst military day, with the reasons named. Very few religious traditions keep a defeat in the canon and refuse to explain it as anyone else's fault.
lights.d: Mount Uhud, north of Madinah · 625 CE

lights.t: A Persian idea kept ten thousand men out of Madinah
lights.s: In 627 a coalition of Makkan and allied tribes, put by the sources at around ten thousand men, marched on Madinah. Salman al-Farisi, who had grown up in Persia, proposed digging a trench across the open northern approach, the only side not protected by lava fields and palm groves. It was not an Arab tactic and the cavalry had no answer to it. The Muslims dug for weeks in cold weather and hunger, the Prophet ﷺ working in the line with them. The siege broke up after about a month without a general battle, and a storm scattered the camp. The idea came from a former slave who had been born a Zoroastrian near Isfahan.

lights.t: A treaty that looked like defeat was called a victory
lights.s: In 628 the Prophet ﷺ set out for Makkah to perform the lesser pilgrimage and was stopped at Hudaybiyyah. The terms he accepted looked bad to his companions: turn back this year, a ten year truce, and any Makkan who defected to him must be returned while any of his who went the other way need not be. Umar objected openly. Even the wording was conceded, with the document dropping the titles Quraysh refused. Surah Al-Fath, revealed on the way back, calls it a clear victory. Within two years the truce had let people move and talk freely, conversions rose sharply, and Makkah was taken with almost no fighting.

lights.t: The city that expelled him was told to go home
lights.s: In Ramadan of the eighth year after the migration, 630 CE, the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah with a large force and the city fell with very little fighting. He had been driven out of it eight years earlier and members of his family had been killed by people now standing in front of him. According to the accounts he asked what they expected, was told they expected good from a generous brother, and said: go, you are free. A general amnesty followed, with a short list of exceptions, most of whom were also pardoned. Bilal, who had been tortured in that city as a slave, climbed onto the roof of the Ka'ba and called the prayer.

lights.t: The farewell sermon was delivered from the back of a camel
lights.s: In Dhul Hijjah of the year 632, on the plain of Arafah, the Prophet ﷺ addressed the largest gathering he ever spoke to, from the back of his camel, with a man repeating his words to the crowd behind. Jabir ibn Abdullah, then a young man, gave a long account of the whole pilgrimage that runs to several pages in Muslim's collection. The sermon cancelled outstanding blood feuds, starting with a claim owed to his own family, cancelled the interest owed to his own uncle first of all, told the men that their wives have rights over them, and in the version preserved in other collections stated that no Arab has any superiority over a non Arab except in God consciousness. He died within three months.
lights.d: Plain of Arafah · Dhul Hijjah, 10 AH, 632 CE

lights.t: Abu Bakr answered the crisis of his death with a verse
lights.s: The Prophet ﷺ died in Madinah in the month of Rabi al-Awwal in the eleventh year after the migration, which is 632 CE, in Aisha's room, and was buried where he died. The exact day is given as the twelfth by most of the sources, though some give the first or the second, and the conversions disagree. Umar refused at first to accept that he was dead. Abu Bakr came in, uncovered his face, then went out and recited the verse in Surah Al Imran which says that Muhammad is only a messenger, that messengers have passed away before him, and asks whether they would turn back if he died. Umar said his legs would not carry him.

lights.t: The year he lost his wife and his uncle
lights.s: Around 619 CE, in the space of a few months, the Prophet ﷺ lost Khadijah, who had been his wife for some twenty five years and his first believer, and Abu Talib, the uncle whose clan protection had kept him alive in Makkah. The sources call it the Year of Sorrow. The exact year is usually given as 619 and sometimes as 620. With the protection gone he went to Ta'if to look for support and was driven out by a crowd that stoned him until his sandals filled with blood, and he returned to a city where he could now be attacked openly. The migration to Madinah followed about three years later.

lights.t: Seventy reciters died and the Qur'an was gathered
lights.s: At Yamama in 633, in the fighting against Musaylima, a large number of the men who had memorised the Qur'an were killed. The figure usually given is about seventy. Umar went to the caliph Abu Bakr and argued that if this kept happening, parts of the text would be lost with the men who carried them, and that it should be written into one collection. Abu Bakr hesitated, on the ground that the Prophet ﷺ had not done it. Then he agreed, and gave the work to Zayd ibn Thabit, who said that moving a mountain would have been lighter. He gathered it from written pieces and from the memories of the men who had it, and the sheets stayed with Abu Bakr, then Umar, then Umar's daughter Hafsa.

lights.t: The Haram at Makkah began as an open space between houses
lights.s: In the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ the Kaaba stood in a small courtyard with private houses pressed around it and no enclosing wall. Around 638 the caliph Umar bought the nearest houses, had them pulled down and put a low wall around the cleared ground. Uthman widened it again. The Abbasid caliph al-Mahdi spent heavily between 777 and 781 to enlarge the courtyard and bring the Kaaba nearer its centre. The arcades most photographed in old prints were Ottoman work of the 1570s. Saudi expansions since 1955 have taken the enclosure past 350,000 square metres, and each stage removed older fabric, including most of those Ottoman arcades, which historians of architecture objected to at the time.
lights.d: Masjid al-Haram, Makkah · 638 CE to the present

lights.t: Zamzam is a shallow well in a dry valley floor
lights.s: The well of Zamzam sits about twenty metres east of the Kaaba, in the bed of the Wadi Ibrahim. It is roughly thirty metres deep. The upper part passes through the loose sand and gravel that the valley floor is made of, and the lower part is cut into fractured rock, which is where most of the water enters. Pilgrims once drew it by bucket, then by hand pump. Today the well head is sealed below the circumambulation floor, the water is pumped, treated with ultraviolet light and piped to taps and to a bottling plant at Kudai. The Saudi Geological Survey monitors the water level continuously, because heavy pumping during Hajj draws it down and it recovers afterwards.

lights.t: Two hills of a woman's search now stand inside a mosque
lights.s: Safa and Marwa are two rock outcrops a little under four hundred metres apart. Muslims walk between them seven times during Hajj and Umrah, a distance of roughly three kilometres, in memory of Hagar going back and forth looking for water for her son Ismail. The Qur'an names both hills and calls them among the symbols of God. For most of history the walk was along an open street with shops on it. The Saudi expansions enclosed the whole route inside the mosque, air conditioned it and later stacked it on several levels to move larger crowds. The bare rock of Safa is still exposed at one end, fenced behind glass, so that what people are walking between can still be seen.

lights.t: A pilgrim who misses this afternoon has missed the Hajj
lights.s: Arafat is a flat, stony plain about twenty kilometres southeast of Makkah, with a granite hill at its edge that people call Jabal al-Rahmah. Pilgrims stand there from midday until sunset on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah, and that standing is the one rite the Hajj cannot be completed without. The Prophet ﷺ delivered the sermon of his farewell pilgrimage there in 632. A hadith reports him saying that Hajj is Arafat. The plain is empty and closed for most of the year. For a few hours it holds more than two million people, all standing outdoors in the same place at the same time, doing nothing except asking.
lights.src: Sunan al-Tirmidhi and Sunan Abi Dawud, Books of Hajj

lights.t: Mina is a city of tents empty fifty weeks a year
lights.s: Mina is a narrow valley five kilometres east of Makkah where pilgrims sleep for three or four nights of the Hajj and throw pebbles at three stone markers. After a fire in 1997 killed hundreds of people, the canvas was replaced with fibreglass coated tents on fixed steel frames, about a hundred thousand of them, laid out in numbered streets with their own hospitals and fire mains. The Jamarat itself has been rebuilt twice. The current structure, finished between 2006 and 2009, is a multi level bridge with separate ramps for each direction, designed for a flow measured in hundreds of thousands per hour. It was built because crowds crushed on the old bridge, most severely in 1990 and again in 2015.

lights.t: The Prophet's mosque began with palm trunks and a gravel floor
lights.s: When the Prophet ﷺ reached Yathrib in 622 he bought a plot used for drying dates and built on it: mud brick walls, columns of palm trunks, a roof of palm fronds that leaked, a floor of earth and gravel. A shaded bench along one wall, the Suffa, housed companions who had nowhere else. Umar and Uthman enlarged it. The Umayyad governor rebuilt it between 707 and 709, adding the concave prayer niche and minarets and taking in the room where the Prophet ﷺ was buried. A dome was raised over that room in 1279 and painted green in 1837. The building now holds more than a million people, around a plot bought for drying dates.

lights.t: He walked out to Quba every Saturday to pray two units
lights.s: Quba was a settlement on the southern edge of Yathrib. The Prophet ﷺ stopped there for several days before entering the town in 622 and had a mosque built, the first built after the migration. Bukhari and Muslim both record that afterwards he went out to Quba every Saturday, sometimes riding and sometimes walking, and prayed two units there. Many commentators identify Quba with the Qur'anic phrase about a mosque founded on God consciousness from the first day, though others read that verse as referring to his own mosque in the town. The present building on the site is modern, rebuilt in the 1980s, and stands about three kilometres from the Prophet's mosque.
lights.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Books of Prayer

lights.t: The cave of the first revelation is smaller than most rooms
lights.s: Hira is a cleft near the top of Jabal al-Nour, a steep hill about four kilometres northeast of the Kaaba. The climb takes most people over an hour. The cave itself is small, roughly the length of a man lying down and about a metre and a half wide, with an opening that faces toward the Kaaba. The Prophet ﷺ used to withdraw there for nights at a time before revelation began, and the first verses came to him in that space during Ramadan. Thousands of pilgrims climb it each season. Visiting it is not part of Umrah or Hajj and carries no rite, which scholars in Makkah repeat every year.

lights.t: The cave in the Qur'an held two men for three nights
lights.s: Jabal Thawr rises south of Makkah, higher and harder to climb than Jabal al-Nour. In 622 the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid in a cave near its summit for three nights while search parties from Quraysh combed the roads north, and only then set out for Yathrib by a coastal route. The Qur'an refers to the episode directly, describing the second of two when they were in the cave and one said to his companion not to grieve. The familiar detail of a spider's web and nesting doves across the entrance comes from later biographical literature, not from the Qur'an, and hadith scholars have long noted that its chains are weak.

lights.t: A mountain the Prophet said loves us and we love it
lights.s: Uhud is a red granite ridge a few kilometres north of the Prophet's mosque, running for several kilometres and standing apart from the ranges around it, which is where its name, meaning single or alone, is usually traced. The battle fought at its foot in 625 cost the Muslims about seventy dead, among them the Prophet's uncle Hamza, after archers left the small hill they had been told to hold. That hill, Jabal al-Rumat, is still there, a rise of a few metres beside the cemetery of the fallen. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet ﷺ saying of it that this is a mountain that loves us and we love it.
lights.d: Jabal Uhud, Madinah · battle 3 AH, 625 CE

lights.t: Badr was a watering stop on the road to Syria
lights.s: Badr lies about 130 kilometres southwest of Madinah, near the coastal route that Makkan caravans took to Syria. It mattered because it had wells. Whoever held them controlled where an army could stand and where it could not, and on 17 Ramadan in year 2 of the Hijra the smaller Muslim force reached them first and filled in the rest. The place is an ordinary town today, with a mosque, a museum and a walled graveyard holding the fourteen Muslims who died in the battle. Historians still argue about exactly which depressions in the ground were the wells. What is not in doubt is that the whole engagement turned on water in a dry valley.

lights.t: Al-Aqsa is the whole enclosure, not only the silver dome
lights.s: In Muslim usage al-Masjid al-Aqsa names the entire walled enclosure in Jerusalem, about fourteen and a half hectares, which includes the Dome of the Rock, the silver domed congregational hall at the southern end, courtyards, fountains, cisterns and colonnades. The Qur'an calls it the farthest mosque in the verse about the Prophet ﷺ being taken by night. The congregational hall has been destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly, mainly by earthquakes: the shocks of 748 and 1033 each brought much of it down, and its present columns and arcades are largely eleventh century work with Fatimid, Crusader, Ayyubid and modern repairs on top. The wooden pulpit installed by Salah ad-Din's order was burned in an arson attack in 1969 and replaced in 2007.

lights.t: Four religions built on the same rectangle in Damascus
lights.s: The Great Mosque of Damascus stands inside a walled rectangle that began as an Aramean temple precinct to the storm god Hadad, was rebuilt as a Roman temple of Jupiter, and by the fourth century held a Christian basilica dedicated to John the Baptist. After the Muslim conquest of 635 the two communities used parts of the site alongside each other for about seventy years. In 705 the caliph al-Walid took over the church and built the mosque that stands now, finished around 715. Sources differ on the terms, some reporting compensation and other churches given in exchange, others plain seizure. A shrine inside is said to hold the head of John the Baptist, and Christian as well as Muslim visitors still stop at it.

lights.t: Cordoba's double arches made short columns carry a high roof
lights.s: Abd al-Rahman I began the mosque of Cordoba in 785 on the site of a church, which the sources say was first shared and then bought. His builders had a supply of Roman and Visigothic columns that were too short for the height they wanted, so they stacked two tiers of arches on each column, a lower horseshoe and an upper semicircle, banded in red brick and pale stone. It worked, and it was extended three times, ending with around 850 columns. Cordoba fell to Castile in 1236 and the building became a cathedral. In 1523 a Renaissance nave was cut into the middle of the hall. Mass is said there daily, and Muslim prayer in the building is not permitted.

lights.t: One sentence is carved thousands of times across the Alhambra
lights.s: The Alhambra was built on a ridge above Granada by the Nasrid sultans, mostly between 1238 and 1391. Its walls are not carved stone but moulded plaster, cut and painted while damp, which is why so much detail was possible and why so much of it has had to be repaired. Running through that decoration, in cursive and in angular script, in courtyards and over doorways, is the Nasrid motto: there is no victor but God. Scholars who have counted the inscriptions put its repetitions in the thousands. It was the family slogan of a dynasty that survived by paying tribute to Castile, and they wrote it on every wall of the palace they lost in 1492.

lights.t: The oldest standing minaret is a square tower in Tunisia
lights.s: Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan in 670 as a garrison in the Tunisian steppe. Its great mosque was rebuilt several times, most substantially by the Aghlabid ruler Ziyadat Allah I around 836, and that is essentially the building that stands. Its massive three tiered square tower is generally taken to be the oldest minaret still standing anywhere, with a lower section that may be older still. The prayer hall rests on roughly four hundred columns carried in from Roman and Byzantine ruins across the region, no two bays quite alike. Around the prayer niche are lustre tiles brought from Iraq in the ninth century. The city became the centre where Maliki law was written down, in Sahnun's Mudawwana.

lights.t: The world's oldest working library reopened in 2016
lights.s: The library attached to the Qarawiyyin in Fez holds about four thousand manuscripts, among them a ninth century copy of Malik's Muwatta written on parchment and a fourteenth century copy of Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah. It has been in use since the medieval period, which makes it one of the oldest libraries anywhere still doing the job it was built for. By 2012 it had broken gutters, damp in the walls and a collection at risk. The restoration was led by Aziza Chaouni, a Canadian trained engineer and architect from Fez, who put in a new drainage system, solar panels and climate control for the manuscript room, and kept the old door of the manuscript room with its four locks, whose keys are held by four different people. It opened to readers again in 2016.

lights.t: She spent an inheritance on a mosque that became a university
lights.s: Fatima al-Fihri came from a family that migrated from Kairouan to Fez in the early ninth century. When her father died she used her share of his estate to build a mosque in 859 in the quarter where the migrants had settled, and tradition holds that she fasted while the work went on. That mosque, al-Qarawiyyin, acquired teaching circles, then a library, then salaried professors and issued certificates, and it has never closed. UNESCO and Guinness both list it as the oldest existing degree granting institution. Almost everything told about Fatima herself comes from Ibn Abi Zar's chronicle written some five centuries later, and historians say plainly that earlier evidence for her life is thin.

lights.t: A whole town replasters its mosque in a single morning
lights.s: The Great Mosque of Djenne in Mali is the largest mud brick building in the world. Its walls are made of sun dried bricks and coated in banco, a mud and rice husk plaster that the rainy season washes away every year. So each spring the town replasters it. Masons of the local guild direct the work, young men carry the mud, women bring water, and the bundles of palm wood that stick out of the walls, the toron, are the permanent scaffolding they climb. It is done in one day. The present building dates from 1906 and 1907, raised on the footprint of a much older mosque, and how closely it follows the earlier one is still debated by historians of the region.

lights.t: A dated inscription of 1107 sits in a Zanzibar village mosque
lights.s: In the fishing village of Kizimkazi at the southern tip of Zanzibar there is a small mosque whose prayer niche carries a foundation inscription in floriated Kufic script. It gives a date corresponding to 1107, which makes it the oldest dated Islamic inscription known in East Africa. The letters are cut into coral stone, the local building material along the whole coast, quarried soft from the reef and hardening in the air. Excavations further north at Shanga on the Kenyan coast have found the postholes of a timber mosque dating from around the eighth century, rebuilt in stone later. Islam arrived on this coast by sea and by trade, and it left dated stone behind it.
lights.d: Kizimkazi, Zanzibar · inscription dated 500 AH, 1107 CE

lights.t: The minaret in Xi'an is a wooden pagoda in a garden
lights.s: The Great Mosque of Xi'an sits in the old Muslim quarter of the city, at the eastern end of what was the Silk Road. Tradition dates a mosque here to 742, and the buildings standing now are mostly Ming work from 1384 onward with later repairs. It looks nothing like a mosque in Cairo or Istanbul. It is a Chinese temple compound: four walled courtyards on a long axis, timber halls with upturned tiled roofs, memorial arches, stone tablets, a garden. The minaret is a three storey octagonal wooden pavilion. There is no dome. The axis runs east to west rather than north to south, because the prayer hall at the far end has to face Makkah.

lights.t: A 1531 endowment in Sarajevo still pays for its own library
lights.s: In 1531 Gazi Husrev-beg, the Ottoman governor of Bosnia, endowed a mosque in Sarajevo and, in the same deed, a madrasa, a library, a public bath, a soup kitchen and a covered market whose rents were to pay for the rest. The endowment survived empires and still funds the library, which now holds more than ten thousand manuscripts in Arabic, Turkish, Persian and Bosnian. During the siege of Sarajevo between 1992 and 1995 the collection was moved by hand between hiding places, box by box, and came through intact. The city's National and University Library was less fortunate: it was shelled and burned in August 1992, and something like a million and a half books and periodicals were lost.

lights.t: The green dome over Rumi covers a museum, not a lodge
lights.s: Rumi died in Konya in December 1273 and was buried beside his father. A tomb was raised over him with Seljuk patronage, crowned by a fluted cone of turquoise glazed tiles that the city has been repairing ever since. Around it grew the mother lodge of the Mevlevi order, with cells, a kitchen where novices were trained for a thousand and one days, and a hall for the turning ceremony. In 1925 the Turkish Republic closed all dervish lodges. The building reopened in 1926 as a museum and remains one, receiving well over a million visitors a year, more than any other museum in the country in some years. The ceremony is now performed as a cultural programme, most fully in the week of his death.

lights.t: A brick tower in Bukhara has stood since 1127
lights.s: The Kalyan minaret in Bukhara was finished in 1127 for the Karakhanid ruler Arslan Khan. It is baked brick, about forty six metres high, tapering, set on a deep foundation packed with reeds, and its whole surface is worked into fourteen bands, each with a different geometric pattern laid up in the brickwork itself rather than applied to it. The city was destroyed by the Mongols in 1220 and the minaret was left standing. A well known story says Genghis Khan ordered it spared after his hat fell off as he looked up, which is a good story with no early source behind it. The mosque beside it was rebuilt in the sixteenth century. The tower is the older thing on the square by four hundred years.

lights.t: Tigers and a human faced sun sit above a college door
lights.s: The Registan in Samarkand is a public square hemmed in on three sides by colleges. Ulugh Beg built the first in 1420 and taught astronomy in it. Facing it, the Sher-Dor madrasa was finished in 1636, and its portal carries two great cats stalking deer, each with a rising sun on its back, and each sun has a human face. Figural images on a madrasa front were unusual, and the tiling has survived to be argued about. The third side, Tilya-Kori, was finished around 1660 and its prayer hall is gilded. In 1932 a leaning minaret at the Ulugh Beg madrasa was pulled back upright with cables and jacks rather than dismantled, an operation engineers still write about.

lights.t: Isfahan's great mosque sits at an angle to its square
lights.s: Shah Abbas began laying out the Naqsh-e Jahan square in Isfahan in 1598. It measures roughly 160 by 510 metres, and the stone goalposts of the polo ground are still standing at either end. Three buildings and a bazaar gate open onto it. The problem the architects had was that the square is aligned to the city and the qibla is not. Their answer is visible from the air: the portal of the Shah Mosque sits square with the plaza, and behind it the entire building swings about forty five degrees to face Makkah, the turn taken up inside a short vestibule. The smaller Sheikh Lotfollah mosque, built for the court, does the same trick and has neither minaret nor courtyard.

lights.t: Delhi's first mosque was built from demolished temples and says so
lights.s: The Quwwat al-Islam mosque in Delhi was begun in 1192 by Qutb al-Din Aibak, and its courtyard is ringed with carved columns taken from Hindu and Jain temples that his forces pulled down. An inscription over the eastern gate states this outright, giving the number of temples as twenty seven. Some of the figures on the columns were defaced, others were left. Beside the mosque rises the Qutb Minar, begun in 1199 and finished under Iltutmish, seventy two and a half metres of fluted red sandstone and marble, the tallest brick minaret in the world. In the courtyard stands an iron pillar cast around the fourth century, centuries before the mosque, still almost free of rust because of the phosphorus in its metal.

lights.t: Akbar built a sandstone capital and left it fourteen years later
lights.s: Akbar began Fatehpur Sikri in 1571 near the hermitage of the Sufi Salim Chishti, whose white marble tomb sits in the courtyard of the mosque there. The city is built almost entirely of the local red sandstone, cut like carpentry, with brackets and screens copied from Gujarati and Rajput work. In its hall of worship Akbar had Muslim scholars debate Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests, sometimes into the night. The gateway he added after his Gujarat campaign carries an inscription attributing to Jesus the words that the world is a bridge, and that one should pass over it and build no house upon it. By about 1585 the court had moved on. Historians usually cite water supply and northwestern campaigns.

lights.t: The Blue Mosque was criticised because its patron had won nothing
lights.s: Sultan Ahmed I began his mosque in Istanbul in 1609, on the site of the old Byzantine palace and directly facing Hagia Sophia. The architect was Sedefkar Mehmed Agha, trained in Sinan's office. Inside are more than twenty thousand tiles from the kilns at Iznik, and the order was so large that the workshops raised their prices and the sultan capped them. Six minarets went up, matching the number then at Makkah, which caused comment at the time. The sharper criticism was financial. A sultan's mosque was expected to be paid for from the spoils of a victory, and Ahmed had no victory, so the money came from the treasury, and jurists said so.

lights.t: Hagia Sophia has been four things in fifteen hundred years
lights.s: Justinian's church was finished in 537, designed by two men trained in geometry rather than building, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. Its first dome fell in 558 and was rebuilt steeper. It was the cathedral of Constantinople for nine hundred years, and it was looted in 1204 by a Christian army of the Fourth Crusade. After the Ottoman conquest of 1453 Mehmed II converted it into a mosque, and it served as one for nearly five centuries, with Sinan adding buttresses that are part of why it is still standing. In 1934 the Turkish government made it a museum, and the covered mosaics were uncovered. In 2020 it became a mosque again, with the mosaics curtained during prayer.

lights.t: He became chief architect at fifty and worked fifty more years
lights.s: Sinan was born around 1490 to a Christian family in Anatolia, taken into Ottoman service through the levy of boys, and spent his early career as a military engineer building bridges on campaign. He was made chief court architect in 1538, at about fifty. The registers of his office credit him with roughly three hundred buildings, many of them the work of assistants under his name. He called the Selimiye in Edirne, finished in 1575, his masterwork, and set out to make its dome match the span of Hagia Sophia, which by careful measurement it very nearly does. He also rebuilt the water supply of Istanbul. He is buried in a small stone tomb he built himself, beside one of his own water channels.

lights.t: A waqf takes property permanently out of the market
lights.s: A waqf is founded by a deed that freezes a piece of property forever. Once the deed is registered the thing cannot be sold, given away or inherited, and only its income may be spent, on whatever the founder wrote down: a mosque, a school, a hospital, a fountain, blankets for the poor in winter, feed for stray cats. The founder names the trustee and the rules, and courts enforce them centuries later. The legal starting point is a report in Bukhari and Muslim in which Umar acquires land at Khaybar and is told by the Prophet ﷺ to hold the property itself and give away its produce. By the nineteenth century a large share of the cultivated land in some Ottoman provinces was held this way.
lights.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Books of Conditions

lights.t: A soup kitchen endowed in 1552 is still serving in Jerusalem
lights.s: Hurrem Sultan, wife of Suleiman and known in Europe as Roxelana, endowed a complex in Jerusalem in 1552: a mosque, a hostel for travellers and a public kitchen. The deed she registered assigned the revenue of named villages and shops to pay for it and specified what was to be cooked, how much bread each person got, and who was to be served first. The kitchen fed several hundred people a day in the sixteenth century. It has run, with interruptions and much reduced, ever since, and meals are still handed out from the Haseki Sultan foundation in the Old City. The endowment outlived the empire that produced it because the deed made the property unsellable.

lights.t: A Damascus hospital of 1154 charged nobody and taught medicine
lights.s: Nur al-Din Zangi founded the bimaristan that carries his name in Damascus in 1154. Like the other great hospitals it was paid for out of waqf, the rents of shops, bathhouses and farmland assigned to it in perpetuity, which meant its budget did not depend on a ruler staying alive or generous. Treatment was free. The rules of these institutions record admission without regard to religion, origin or means, separate wards by illness including wards for patients with mental disorders, and a resident staff of physicians, oculists, surgeons and pharmacists. Students walked the wards with their teachers and were examined before they could practise. The building still stands in the old city of Damascus and now houses a museum of medicine.

lights.t: Baghdad's 1233 college taught four schools of law at once
lights.s: The Mustansiriya was opened in Baghdad in 1233 by the caliph al-Mustansir, on the east bank of the Tigris. Its innovation was to house all four Sunni schools of law in one building, each with its own professor, its own students and its own corner of the courtyard, rather than one school per college as had been usual. It also had teaching in Qur'an, hadith, medicine and mathematics, a hospital, a kitchen that fed the students, a bath, stipends, and a large library. Over the entrance was a water clock that marked the hours for the whole quarter. The building survived the sack of 1258 and is still standing on the riverbank in Baghdad.

lights.t: The certificate was written on your copy of the book
lights.s: In the Muslim scholarly tradition the qualification belonged to a person, not to a building. A teacher who was satisfied that a student had read a book with him, correctly and in full, wrote an ijaza on the student's copy: a licence to transmit that text, naming the teacher's own teachers back to the author. Some ijazas run for pages and list a chain of thirty names across seven centuries. There was a separate licence to teach law and issue legal opinions, which is the nearest thing to a professional qualification. The historian George Makdisi argued that this practice shaped the European licence to teach; other historians think the resemblance is not close enough to prove a debt.

lights.t: An observatory in Iran hired astronomers from as far as China
lights.s: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi persuaded the Mongol ruler Hulagu to fund an observatory at Maragha in northwest Iran, begun in 1259. It was not one instrument but an institution: a staff drawn from Damascus, Mosul, Tus and Andalusia, a Chinese astronomer among them, a library, a workshop for making instruments, and thirty years of funding. The star tables produced there, the Zij-i Ilkhani, were finished in 1272 and used for centuries. The astronomers of Maragha also built new geometric models to fix the parts of Ptolemy they thought incoherent, and the same devices turn up later in Copernicus. How they reached him is still argued, and no document of the transmission has been found.

lights.t: Istanbul's observatory was built in 1577 and demolished in 1580
lights.s: Taqi al-Din, an astronomer from Damascus who had become chief astronomer to the Ottoman court, was given money by Sultan Murad III to build an observatory in Galata. It was finished in 1577, with a staff of about fifteen and instruments comparable to those Tycho Brahe was using in Denmark in the same years. Taqi al-Din observed the great comet of that autumn and read it as favourable. What followed was plague and a costly war. In January 1580 the observatory was demolished by order, after the chief mufti gave an opinion against it.
