Historians who have worked on the episode read the destruction as a court quarrel as much as a religious one, but the instruments went all the same.

lights.t: The postmaster's real job was reporting on the governor
lights.s: The barid was the state post, a chain of relay stations along the main roads with fresh mounts waiting at each. It carried official mail, not private letters. Its second function was intelligence: the postmaster in each province reported directly to the caliph on prices, harvests, unrest and the conduct of the governor he lived beside. One such official, Ibn Khurradadhbih, used the road registers to write the earliest surviving Arabic geography of routes, listing stages and distances across the empire. The Mamluks rebuilt the system under Baybars in the thirteenth century, moving despatches from Cairo to Damascus in about four days, with a parallel pigeon service and towers built to receive the birds.

lights.t: Manuals told inspectors exactly how bakers water the dough
lights.s: The muhtasib was the official who walked the markets. His brief covered weights and scales, adulterated bread, milk and saffron, blocked streets, unsafe buildings, the cleanliness of butchers and the honesty of money changers. Manuals were written to train him. Al-Shayzari's twelfth century handbook and Ibn al-Ukhuwwa's fourteenth century one from Egypt go trade by trade, explaining how each is cheated: how a baker adds water to increase weight, how a miller mixes in cheap grain, how a cloth seller stretches a bolt. They also cover schoolteachers, and instruct the inspector to test physicians against the questions in Hunayn ibn Ishaq's textbook before letting them practise.

lights.t: Frontier forts on the Tunisian coast doubled as retreat houses
lights.s: A ribat was a fortified post on a threatened frontier, most often a coast. The ones at Monastir, founded in 796, and Sousse, built in 821, still stand in Tunisia: square blocks of stone with a courtyard, cells on two storeys, a prayer hall and a watchtower. They were held by volunteers who came for a term of service rather than by a standing garrison, and the same men spent their nights in prayer and Qur'an study, so the buildings functioned as barracks and retreat houses at once. The towers were close enough to pass a signal fire along the coast within a night. In later centuries the word ribat shifted meaning and came to name a Sufi lodge with no walls to defend.

lights.t: Anatolian road inns were spaced one day's walk apart
lights.s: The Seljuks of Anatolia built stone inns along their trade roads at intervals of about thirty kilometres, a day with loaded animals. The largest, the Sultan Han near Aksaray, was built in 1229 for Kayqubad I and covers some four and a half thousand square metres: an open courtyard with arcades and stables, a vaulted hall for winter, and a small mosque raised on four piers in the middle of the yard so that the animals could be led underneath it. The endowment deeds that paid for these buildings provide for lodging without charge for a set period, commonly three days, with food, fodder, a bath, medicine for the sick and shoeing for horses.

lights.t: Cairo put a school for children above the drinking fountain
lights.s: Ottoman Cairo built hundreds of small corner buildings of a single type: a sabil below and a kuttab above. The sabil was a public cistern with bronze grilles onto the street, where anyone could take a cup of cold water for nothing. Above it, open to the air, sat a room where children learned to read the Qur'an. The cistern underneath held the year's supply, filled at the Nile flood and carried in by water sellers. The best known, built by Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda in 1744, still stands where the main street of the old city forks. A report in the Sunan collections has the Prophet ﷺ answer that the best charity is water, and founders of fountains have quoted it for centuries.
lights.src: Sunan Abi Dawud and Sunan Ibn Majah

lights.t: A sultan wrote the advertisement for his own fountain
lights.s: In front of the outer gate of Topkapi Palace stands a square marble pavilion built in 1728 for Sultan Ahmed III. Each of its four faces has a tap and a basin, and each corner has a grilled window where an attendant handed cups of water to passers by without charge. The whole surface is carved with tulips, cypresses and inscriptions, and the closing couplet is attributed to the sultan himself: open the tap with the name of God, drink the water, and pray for Khan Ahmed. The city had hundreds of such endowed fountains, fed by aqueducts and cisterns that Sinan and others had rebuilt, and the men who staffed them, the sebilci, were paid from the same endowments.

lights.t: The House of Wisdom was probably a library, not an academy
lights.s: Baghdad's Bayt al-Hikma is often described as a great research academy where Greek learning was translated by teams of salaried scholars. The evidence is thinner than that picture. Early sources mention it mainly as a palace library, in existence under Harun al-Rashid and expanded under al-Ma'mun, associated above all with translation from Persian and with astronomical work. Dimitri Gutas and others have shown that most Greek to Arabic translation was commissioned privately, by wealthy families such as the Banu Musa, who reportedly paid Hunayn ibn Ishaq in gold matching the weight of the books he produced. The translation movement was real, expensive and enormous. It simply was not run out of one building with a famous name.

lights.t: A Damascus library's own catalogue survives with 2,000 titles
lights.s: Attached to a mausoleum in thirteenth century Damascus was a modest library called the Ashrafiya. Its catalogue survived, bound into a manuscript now in Istanbul, and it is the most detailed library catalogue to come down to us from the medieval Muslim world. It lists roughly two thousand titles by about twelve hundred authors, ordered by the size of the volume and then alphabetically by the first letter of the title, with notes on condition and on multiple copies. The shelves held law and hadith as expected, and also poetry, cookery, chess, veterinary medicine, popular epics and Christian texts. Konrad Hirschler edited it in 2016, which means we can now read what an ordinary reader in Damascus could borrow.

lights.t: A Qur'an written in gold on indigo dyed parchment
lights.s: The Blue Qur'an is a manuscript whose parchment leaves were dyed a deep indigo blue and then written on in gold Kufic script, with silver rosettes marking the verses that have since tarnished to grey. It was made in the ninth or tenth century and was recorded in the library of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, where an inventory of 1294 describes a Qur'an in blue and gold. Where it was actually produced is still disputed between North Africa, Iraq and Muslim Spain. The volume has been broken up. Its leaves are now scattered across museums in Tunisia, Europe and the United States, and single pages appear at auction, which is why no one can say how long the complete book once was.

lights.t: Arabic was block printed centuries before Gutenberg, on amulets
lights.s: About sixty printed Arabic texts survive from medieval Egypt and Syria, most of them dug up at Fustat, the old settlement under Cairo. They are narrow strips of paper carrying Qur'anic verses, the names of God and prayers for protection, printed from carved blocks between roughly the tenth and fourteenth centuries and rolled into metal amulet cases. So the technology of printing on paper existed and was practised in Arabic before it existed in Europe. It stayed confined to amulets sold by street sellers, a trade of low standing, and never moved to books. Historians give various reasons, from the prestige of the copyist's hand to the economics of a strong manuscript trade, and none of them is settled.

lights.t: A room in Topkapi has had a reciter since 1517
lights.s: The Chamber of the Sacred Trusts in Topkapi Palace holds objects venerated as relics: a mantle and a staff attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, hairs of his beard, swords attributed to his companions, the keys and gilded fittings of the Kaaba door, and letters said to be his to foreign rulers. Most arrived after 1517, when Selim I took Cairo and the sharif of Makkah sent the keys of the sanctuary. Historians cannot establish the provenance of most of the objects by ordinary evidence, and museum labels are careful about this. What is documented is the practice around them: Qur'an has been recited in that room continuously, in shifts, since the trusts arrived, and reciters are still appointed to do it.

lights.t: Damascus steel was made from Indian ingots and then lost
lights.s: The blades called Damascus steel carry a watered pattern of light and dark bands in the metal itself. They were forged from wootz, a crucible steel made in South India and Sri Lanka and traded west as small cakes of metal, so the city gave the blades a name rather than a birthplace. Production faded in the eighteenth century and the method was lost. In the 1990s John Verhoeven and Alfred Pendray reproduced the pattern and showed it depends on trace elements, vanadium among them, present in particular ores, which explains why the craft died when a supply changed. A 2006 paper reported carbon nanotubes in one sabre sample. That finding is still discussed, and it does not mean the smiths knew what they had.
lights.d: Wootz steel · South Asia and Syria

lights.t: A carpet signed by its maker holds 26 million knots
lights.s: Two carpets were woven for the shrine of Shaykh Safi al-Din at Ardabil in northwest Iran and finished in 1539 or 1540. Both carry a date and an inscription naming the work of the servant of the threshold, Maqsud of Kashan, with a couplet of Hafiz above it, which is rare because carpets are usually anonymous. The larger, now in London, is about ten and a half metres long and contains something near twenty six million knots, roughly three hundred and fifty in every square inch, each one tied by hand around two warp threads. Persian workshops used an asymmetric knot looped around one warp, Turkish workshops a symmetric knot around two, and the difference can still be read off the back of any old rug.

lights.t: Honeycomb vaults were drawn as flat plans before they were built
lights.s: Muqarnas is the tiered cluster of small niches that fills the corner where a square room becomes a round dome. It looks improvised and is not. A scroll now in Topkapi, made in Iran or Central Asia around the fifteenth or sixteenth century, contains sheet after sheet of geometric drawings including muqarnas designs set out as flat plans, the view from directly below, which a mason could scale up and build from. In the same period the mathematician al-Kashi in Samarkand devoted a section of his arithmetic textbook to muqarnas, classifying the types and giving a method for measuring their surfaces so that a builder could estimate materials. The ornament was a calculation before it was a ceiling.

lights.t: A 1453 Isfahan shrine carries a pattern that never repeats
lights.s: In 2007 Peter Lu and Paul Steinhardt published a paper in Science on the tilework of the Darb-i Imam shrine in Isfahan, finished in 1453. They showed that its patterns can be generated from a set of five decorated tiles, and that the result is close to a quasiperiodic tiling, a pattern with fivefold symmetry that never exactly repeats, of the kind Roger Penrose described in the 1970s and physicists later found in real crystals. What the paper did not claim is that the craftsmen had the modern concept. Emil Makovicky had described related patterns in a Maragha tomb in 1992, and other geometers disputed how much of the tiling is quasiperiodic. What is certain is that the geometry is on the wall.

lights.t: One sentence in one book is all we know of her
lights.s: An astrolabe is the sky rendered in brass. Turn its rotating grid against an engraved plate for your latitude and it will give you the time from the height of the sun, the hour of sunrise, the direction to look for a star, and the hours for prayer. More than a thousand survive from the Muslim world, and the oldest dated ones are from the tenth century. In his catalogue of books written around 987, Ibn al-Nadim lists instrument makers and names among them Mariam, daughter of al-Ijli the astrolabist, who worked at the court of Sayf al-Dawla in Aleppo. That is the whole record. No instrument of hers is known. An asteroid discovered in 1990 was later named for her.

lights.t: A Damascus timekeeper computed the qibla for every latitude
lights.s: Finding the direction of Makkah from anywhere else is a problem in spherical trigonometry, and Muslim astronomers knew it. In the fourteenth century Shams al-Din al-Khalili, the timekeeper at the Umayyad mosque in Damascus, computed a table of about 2,880 entries giving the qibla for every degree of latitude and every degree of longitude difference from Makkah. When David King checked the values against exact modern computation, almost all were correct to within a minute or two of arc. Ordinary travellers used simpler things: brass compass boxes made in Istanbul and Isfahan, with a needle, a list of cities and the angle to set for each. Early mosque qiblas vary, and surveyors are still measuring them.

lights.t: Fez has a water clock nobody has managed to restart
lights.s: On a street in Fez, opposite the Bou Inania madrasa, is a wall with thirteen carved cedar beams jutting out of it and twelve brass bowls set below them. It is the front of a water clock built in 1357 for the Marinid sultan Abu Inan, and the building behind it is still called Dar al-Magana, the house of the clock. On the hour a weight is thought to have released a ball onto a bowl, so the hours were counted by sound. The mechanism inside is gone. Several restorations have cleaned and stabilised the facade, and the working of it remains a matter of competing reconstructions, none of them proved. Elsewhere al-Jazari's manual preserves the drawings that Fez lacks.

lights.t: Made from water every living thing
lights.s: Surah al-Anbiya says that We made from water every living thing. What biology observes is that water is the medium the whole business runs in. A human body is around sixty percent water by mass, a jellyfish closer to ninety five, and every chemical reaction inside a cell happens in solution. When astronomers search other worlds for life, the first thing they look for is liquid water, because nobody has a working model for life without a solvent that behaves as water does. None of this needs the verse to have anticipated it. A community living in a dry valley knew perfectly well that water and life go together. The verse asks them to notice that ordinary fact and say who arranged it.

lights.t: Clouds joined, then heaped, then hail out of mountains
lights.s: A verse in Surah al-Nur describes God driving clouds, then joining them together, then piling them into a heap, with rain coming out from the middle of it, and hail sent down from mountains in the sky. Meteorologists describe a thunderstorm in a similar order. Small cumulus cells merge, the merged cell grows vertically into a tower that can reach twelve kilometres, and hailstones form inside that tower, carried up and down through freezing layers until they are heavy enough to fall. The word in the verse for the heaped cloud, rukam, is an ordinary word for a pile. Anyone standing in Arabia in a summer storm could watch this happen. The verse is pointing at what is already visible.

lights.t: Your languages and your colours are listed among the signs
lights.s: Surah al-Rum puts the making of the heavens and the earth in one clause and the differences of human languages and colours in the next, and calls both of them signs. There are roughly seven thousand languages spoken now, and about forty percent of them have fewer than a thousand speakers left. On colour, geneticists find that human variation is continuous rather than banded, that most of the variation in our species is found within any one population rather than between populations, and that skin tone is governed by a small number of genes tracking ultraviolet exposure across latitudes. The verse ranks nothing. It lists difference as evidence, in the same breath as the sky.

lights.t: Two seas meet and a barrier lies between them
lights.s: Surah al-Rahman says He released the two seas, meeting, and between them a barrier they do not overrun. Where a river runs into the sea, oceanographers do find a boundary: fresh water is lighter and rides over a wedge of salt water, and the two keep separate identities for a distance, sometimes with a visible line on the surface where sediment collects. Similar density fronts exist between water masses in the open ocean. What should not be said is that the verse predicted this. These boundaries are not walls, they mix steadily by turbulence and diffusion, and the classical commentators, long before any of it was measured, read the passage as saying that sweet water and salt each keep their character.

lights.t: A drink of varying colours in which there is healing
lights.s: Surah al-Nahl describes the bee taking from every fruit, and a drink of varying colours coming out of it, in which there is healing for people. Honey does vary in colour, from near white to almost black, according to the flowers worked. It is also genuinely hostile to bacteria: it is supersaturated with sugar so it pulls water out of cells, it is acidic, and bee enzymes make small amounts of hydrogen peroxide in it. Sterilised medical grade honey is licensed as a wound dressing and used in hospitals, with the best evidence in partial thickness burns. It is not a cure for everything, and it should never be given to a baby under one year, because of the risk of infant botulism.

lights.t: By the stars they are guided
lights.s: Surah al-Nahl mentions landmarks, and adds that by the stars they are guided. This was a working technology, not a figure of speech. The altitude of the pole star above the horizon equals your latitude, so a sailor who can measure that angle knows how far north he is. Indian Ocean pilots did it with the kamal, a small wooden plate on a knotted string held at arm's length, one knot per port. Ahmad ibn Majid, a pilot from Julfar who wrote navigation manuals in the fifteenth century, set out star bearings and courses in verse so that crews could memorise them. The sextant refined the same measurement, and warships still teach it in case the satellites go dark.

lights.t: One word in Surah al-Dhariyat is often pushed too far
lights.s: The verse says the heaven We built with power, and that We are musi'un. The word comes from a root meaning breadth or capacity, and the classical commentators, al-Tabari among them, read it as We are able, or possessed of vastness. After Hubble published his measurements in 1929, translators began rendering it as We are expanding it, and it is now quoted as though the Qur'an announced cosmic expansion. The observation itself is solid: distant galaxies recede, and the further away they are the faster, which is what an expanding space looks like from inside. But hanging that on one contested word makes the credibility of scripture depend on the next revision of cosmology, which is a poor trade.

lights.t: Mountains are called pegs, and a peg is a tent peg
lights.s: Surah al-Naba pairs the earth as a resting place with the mountains as awtad, pegs. The image is a tent peg, an object every listener owned and hammered into the ground each evening. It is often claimed that this predicts isostasy, the fact that a mountain range floats on a deep root of lighter crust, which under the Himalaya reaches more than seventy kilometres down. The geology is real, and it was worked out from survey measurements in India in the 1850s. The verse is not doing geology. Mountains do not stop continents moving, and peg imagery for hills is common in older Arabic poetry. Read as it stands, the verse is about a world made steady enough to live on.

lights.t: The frailest of houses is the house of the spider
lights.s: Surah al-Ankabut compares taking protectors other than God to a spider taking a house, and says the frailest of houses is the spider's house. Spider silk is not frail. Weight for weight, dragline silk has a tensile strength in the range of steel, and it absorbs far more energy before breaking, which is why materials scientists have spent decades trying to make it in factories. The verse does not say the thread is weak. It says the house is, and it is: an orb web keeps out no rain, no wind and no cold, is torn by a passing bird, and is usually eaten and rebuilt by its owner within a day. The comparison is about shelter, not tensile strength.

lights.t: We sent down iron, and what that verb does elsewhere
lights.s: Surah al-Hadid says that We sent down iron, in it great strength and benefits for people. The same verb, anzala, is used in the Qur'an for cattle and for clothing, and classical commentators read it in the sense of bestowal from above rather than as a statement about where the metal came from physically. Astrophysics does say that all the iron in the earth was forged inside stars and scattered by their deaths, long before the planet gathered. Iron also arrived more directly on occasion: the dagger buried with Tutankhamun was analysed in 2016 and its nickel content shows the blade was made from a meteorite, worked centuries before anyone in Egypt could smelt iron ore.

lights.t: They ask about the crescents and the answer is about time
lights.s: When people asked the Prophet ﷺ about the phases of the moon, Surah al-Baqarah gave an answer about function rather than astronomy: they are timings for people, and for the Hajj. The moon returns to the same phase every 29.53 days on average, which is why Islamic months run to 29 or 30 days and never to a fixed number. Whether the new crescent can actually be seen on a given evening depends on how far the moon has moved from the sun, how high it sits when the sky darkens, and how clear the air is, and astronomers have published visibility criteria for exactly this. Communities still divide over whether to sight it or to calculate it, and the calculation is not in dispute.

lights.t: A companion tested the verse with two threads under his pillow
lights.s: Surah al-Baqarah tells those fasting to eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread of dawn. Bukhari and Muslim report that Adi ibn Hatim took this literally, put a white string and a black string under his pillow and looked at them in the dark until he could tell them apart, and that the Prophet ﷺ told him it meant the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day. What he was being pointed at is astronomical twilight: the first horizontal band of light on the horizon before sunrise. Modern timetables fix it by how far the sun is below the horizon, commonly eighteen degrees, and because that figure is argued, printed times for the same city can differ by twenty minutes.

lights.t: The sun is called a radiance and the moon a light
lights.s: Surah Yunus says He made the sun a radiance, diya, and the moon a light, nur, and measured out phases for it so that people could count years and reckon time. Arabic uses two different words there, and commentators noticed and discussed the difference long ago. It is sometimes offered as proof that the Qur'an knew the moon shines by reflection before science did. That is not fair to the astronomers. Greek writers had already explained lunar phases by reflected sunlight, and al-Biruni set the geometry out with diagrams in the eleventh century, as did Ibn al-Haytham in a treatise on moonlight. The knowledge was in the world and was hard won. The verse asks that the counting of months be noticed as a gift.

lights.t: Night is wound over day with the verb for a turban
lights.s: Surah al-Zumar says He winds the night over the day and winds the day over the night. The verb, yukawwir, comes from a root used for coiling a rope and for winding a turban round a head, and exegetes writing centuries before telescopes discussed what that shape implies. It is worth being careful about what follows. Muslim astronomers did not need the verse to tell them the earth is a ball. Al-Biruni measured its radius from a mountain in what is now Pakistan and got a figure close to the modern one, and no serious astronomer of the period held any other view. The verse gives an image of one thing wrapped over another, and the geographers went out and measured the thing.
